# PageV1P46
anchors:
- Root: م-س-ح (m-s-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To wipe, pass the hand over a surface; to erase or remove by wiping.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In devotional acts, masḥ denotes a physical gesture of blessing (barakah) seeking contact with the divine through the body.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in the sense of physical wiping; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to the face as a means of transmitting the barakah of dhikr or duʿā.
- Root: ر-ق-ي (r-q-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To ascend, to recite a charm or incantation (ruqyah) for healing or protection.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ruqyah is a licit spiritual remedy, distinct from sorcery, performed through Quranic recitation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for climbing; metaphorical for the spiritual elevation of the one who recites and the one upon whom it is recited.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional clause (sharṭ) with fā’ al-jazā’ — the apodosis following the condition is introduced by fa-, indicating a consequent action, as in «فإذا فرغتم فامسحوا» (when you finish, then wipe).
translation:
I say — may Allah guide us and you — this is the sixth station: if one cannot attain the most excellent deed, then at least let him not fall short of a deed that is praiseworthy and striving (nāḍil). For Allah — exalted is He — has said: {«فإذا فرغتم فامسحوا بها وجوهكم»} (And when you have finished, wipe your faces with it) [Quran 5:6].

The Gnostic of Allah, Shams al-Dīn al-Balā’ī — may Allah have mercy on him — said: One wipes his face with both palms, due to what Abū Dāwūd, al-Bazzār, Ibn Ḥibbān, Ibn Mājah, and al-Ḥākim in al-Mustadrak narrated with very good chains of transmission (asānīd jayyidah jiddan) with this exact wording. Likewise, the Sayyid Muftī of Tunis, al-Burzulī, said: The ḥadīth of al-Tirmidhī supports wiping the face after supplication. And likewise, my master al-Qāsim al-ʿUqbānī transmitted the preference (tarjīḥ) of Ibn Rushd for wiping the face after supplication, based on the one who performed ruqyah with the Opening of the Book (Fātiḥah al-Kitāb) and wiped, and based on the one who wiped with his palms over as much of his body as he could after reciting over them, and based on the ḥadīth of ʿUthmān ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ. But he did not attribute this transmission to Ibn Rushd; rather, he attributed it to some of the shaykhs. Then he said: This shaykh had no need for this kind of derivation (takhrij), because we have already established that wiping the face is part of the wiping in ruqyah, so that no derivation is needed. Then he said: And we say: And among the etiquettes of supplication are such-and-such...

[Footnote references to the narrators and their biographical details are omitted here, as they pertain to the scholarly apparatus of the original text.]

# PageV1P47
anchors:
- Root: م-س-ح (m-s-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pass the hand over something; wiping, stroking, or touching with the palm.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ritual wiping (masḥ) as a physical act of seeking blessing (tabarruk) through contact with the sacred.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) physical wiping; here used literally, not metaphorically.
- Root: ق-ل-د (q-l-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To adorn with a necklace; to imitate blindly, to follow without evidence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Taqlīd — acceptance of another's opinion without proof; contrasted with following evidence (ittibāʿ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of placing a collar; metaphorical sense of blind adherence.
- Root: د-ع-و (d-ʿ-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To call, invoke, supplicate; the act of raising hands in prayer.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Duʿāʾ — the servant's humble petition to Allah, a station of worship.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal calling; metaphorically, the heart's turning to Allah.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ) — "If not... then at least..." (إن لم يكن... فلا أقل من...) establishes a graded obligation, parsed as a conditional with an implied apodosis.
translation:
I say — and this is the sixth station of the conduct of religiosity: If one cannot attain the most excellent act, then at the very least let him not fall short of performing an act that has been established [by the Sunnah].

It has come in this regard — also in the authentic report (al-khabar al-ṣaḥīḥ) — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when he raised his hands in supplication, would not lower them until he had wiped his face with them. He said: So you see in the authentic report how the wiping (al-masḥ) is affirmed. And with the affirmation of the report, it is not permissible for us to oppose it — especially since the Imām has already stated what I have mentioned.

And this [opposition] is to be understood as [arising from] the fact that the report had not reached him. For whenever a trustworthy [report] is found, it becomes obligatory to defer to it — just as al-Shāfiʿī said: "When a ḥadīth is authentic, then strike my opinion against the wall." Then he said: And the majority have adopted the wiping of the face with the hands immediately following supplication.

We have thus concluded on the matter of wiping after supplication that it is a point of divergence, and that the preponderant view (al-rājiḥ) is that which conforms to the authentic report — namely, its practice. It cannot be objected: "This applies only to the mujtahid; as for the muqallid, no." For we deny taqlīd in this particular matter, because the reality of taqlīd is the acceptance of another's statement without proof. As for what you have heard directly from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that is not taqlīd — for it is itself a proof (ḥujjah). And he mentioned that taqlīd pertains only to legal rulings (al-aḥkām); matters of etiquette (ādāb) are not of that category — extending to a lengthy discussion that he (may Allah have mercy on him) recorded.

I had intended to transmit the words of Ibn al-ʿArabī in "al-Sirāj"; then it occurred to me [otherwise]; so look at it at his statement — "a fallacy" — in the fifty-fourth name of "al-Sirāj." And there will come to me, in speaking of this station in the section on spiritual ascent (al-taraqqī), something similar from Ibn ʿArafah, al-Burzulī, the Shaykh of Shaykhs Ibn Labb, my master Ibn Sirāj, my master al-Muntūrī, and their shaykhs — my master al-Qayjāṭī and my master al-Ḥaffār — who deem light what al-Shāṭibī deemed heavy, and deem heavy what al-Shāṭibī deemed light.

And look also at what has been continuously practiced: the supplication following the obligatory prayers (adbār al-ṣalawāt) and the visitation of the grave of the deceased on the morning of the seventh day after burial. The Shaykh of Shaykhs Ibn Labb said: "Supplication after the obligatory prayers has never ceased to be practiced in all — or most — of the regions of the earth, without any disapproval — except that in times past, a man came to Granada, named so-and-so, who vehemently denounced this practice, among those who used to read upon him. And when he finished his session of speech before the prayer, they would rush out in crowds, fleeing from praying behind the imāms who supplicate after the prayers. And if one of them prayed behind them, he would rise immediately upon the imām's salutation — hurried and terrified, like one fearing that the supplication might touch him with hardship or punishment, or seize him by claw or fang. And that man also denounced other things that the people of this Andalusian region had long practiced — such as the morning visitation of the grave for seven days after burial." And his followers were even more severe in their denunciation than he was — until one of them said to me: "I was returning from the morning visitation of a grave, and at that time [he asked]: 'Do you do this? And is it unbelief (kufr)?'" — end of the text of the Shaykh of Shaykhs Ibn Labb. So observe the foolishness of these others.

Then he said after that: Thus it is completed.

والطلاق» فيما قصارى أمره أنه مباح مع مأخذ مقلده؛ القائل في الحلال والحرام أنه
إذا جرى عمل بقول مرجوح في النظر أنه لا يعرض للناس في ذلك.

وانظر أيضًا مما جرى به عمل ورشحه الفضلاء دون من شذ من جماعتهم:
تلفين الميت عند دفنه؛ قال القاضي أبو بكر بن العربي: هو فعل أهل المدينة

# PageV1P48
anchors:
- Root: ن-ض-ل (naḍala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To excel, surpass, or be superior in merit; a "nāḍil" is one who strives beyond the obligatory.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Denotes voluntary supererogatory acts (nawāfil) that elevate the believer's rank, distinct from obligatory duties (farāʾiḍ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "surpassing" in excellence; metaphorically used for any act of devotion exceeding the minimum requirement.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Responsive Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — "If not... then at least..." (fa-in lam... fa-lā aqall) establishes a graded hierarchy of obligation, with the apodosis implying a necessary minimum.
translation:
I say: The sixth station concerns the methodology of "lowering oneself" (al-tadallī) — that if one cannot perform an act of superior merit, then at the very least one should not fall short of performing an act of striving excellence (nāḍil). This is my refutation of the Grand Shaykh of Shaykhs, Ibn Lubb — upon whose fatwas we rely in matters of creed, lawful and unlawful, and upon whose school we depend regarding binding oaths and other rulings concerning blood, marriages, and divorce — for his position, at its utmost, is merely that such acts are permissible (mubāḥ), following the stance of his own legal authority (muqallid), who opined in matters of lawful and unlawful that if a practice has been acted upon according to a view deemed weaker (marjūḥ) in legal reasoning, then one should not reproach the people for it.

Consider also, from what has been established by practice and endorsed by the virtuous scholars — excluding those who deviated from their consensus — the following: the instruction (talqīn) of the deceased at his burial. Qāḍī Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī said: "This is the practice of the people of Medina and the righteous among the elite." Likewise, the recitation of {«Yā Sīn»} — transmitted by Abū Dāwūd and others — which the imams endorsed, interpreting away what was reported from Imam Mālik (concerning its prohibition).

I was once asked about a certain jurist of the desert who scrupled against reciting over graves. Then his situation deteriorated to the point that when a reciter stood to recite at a grave, he rebuked him violently and struck him with his hand. Before that, I had already responded that this is not his station, and that he must be disciplined — because he has treated all the imams who interpreted the reported wording from Imam Mālik as fools, and has cast among the people turmoil in their religion, distress in their souls, and ill suspicion toward their muftis. Not one of those imams deviated; none of them displayed such anger, nor claimed such a "reckoning" (ḥisbah). But for every falling thing there is one who picks it up — this man was prompted to claim his own ḥisbah, and so he increased in declaring things innovations (tabdīʿ), attacking hadith, and rejecting — until he wrote to the imam of the village of Darkal, mentioning his zeal on his behalf and what he felt within himself of defamation against me. He requested from me — as if asking whether I had any proof — and that was a slip (zallah) on my part. So I wrote to him a letter saying: Let him not feel in himself any objection against me, for my creed regarding my opponents is that I add nothing to them beyond "Peace" — except peace — in compliance with the command of God. Then I say: "Praise be to God, praise be to God," following the example of the best of creation — may God have mercy on him (i.e., al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī).

And among the meaning of what I informed him of, from my scholarly source, was that I said to him: "Beware, O my friend in God — then beware — lest any doubt creep into you or any suspicion occur to you that the deceased, when placed in his grave and his companions turn away from him, indeed hears the sound of their sandals (khaft nawālihim). Then two angels come to him and question him." And likewise the other authentic report — also from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, who said: "When you bury me, stand around my grave for the time it takes to slaughter a camel and distribute its meat, so that I may find comfort in your presence, and I may see with what I shall answer the messengers of my Lord."

# PageV1P49
anchors:
- Root: ل-ق-ن (la-qāfa-nūn)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To teach, to prompt, to instill a word or phrase into someone’s mind; specifically, the act of dictating the testimony of faith to a dying person or to the deceased at the grave.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the theological context, talqīn is a means of spiritual reinforcement for the deceased during the trial of the grave (fitnat al-qabr), aligning the soul’s final utterance with divine truth.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — verbal instruction; metaphorical (majāz) — the soul’s receptivity to divine mercy through the living’s intercession.
- Root: س-ك-ن (sīn-kāf-nūn)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Tranquility, stillness, calmness; the descent of divine peace (sakīnah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A special divine presence that accompanies the recitation of the Qur’an, as in the hadith cited.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical stillness; metaphorical — spiritual serenity and angelic presence.
- Sībawayh Rule: The conditional clause with «إذا» (idhā) in the hadith «ما اجتمع قوم...» — the protasis (condition) and apodosis (result) are both in the past tense, indicating a habitual or universal truth, not a single event.
translation:
I say — and success is from God alone:

Know, O my beloved in God, that the deceased in his grave is like a drowning man, awaiting the mercy of God or a supplication (duʿā’) from the living; if it reaches him, it is more beloved to him than the world and all that it contains. So beware, O my beloved in God — then beware — lest doubt overtake you or suspicion seize you that the Book of God is the most trustworthy intercessor and the most sufficient of aids, freely given and bountiful. And no rain of divine mercy is ever sought by any means more hopeful than it; and when mercy descends, it encompasses and includes all.

My shaykh al-Muntūrī narrated to me, saying: Shaykh al-Shuyūkh Ibn Lubb said: A good thought occurred to me — and even the sinner may have a good thought — so I desired to impose upon myself a regular devotion (wird) of remembrance (dhikr) or recitation (tilāwah), and I hesitated over which act of virtue was superior. Then I was inspired in a dream:

“When the appointed times have passed, the meeting is cut off — so what remains is only the benefit of the Book.”

When I awoke, I knew that the recitation of the Qur’an was the most virtuous.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs — al-Bukhārī and Muslim — and in al-Tirmidhī: While a man was reciting Sūrat al-Kahf, he saw his beast of burden galloping; he looked, and behold, there was something like a cloud or a mist. He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and mentioned that to him, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him: “That was the sakīnah (divine tranquility) descending with the Qur’an, or descending upon the Qur’an.”

And in another authentic hadith, the Messenger of God ﷺ said: “No people gather together reciting the Book of God and studying it among themselves, but that the sakīnah descends upon them, mercy envelops them, the angels surround them, and God mentions them to those with Him.” {«وَمَا اجْتَمَعَ قَوْمٌ فِي بَيْتٍ مِنْ بُيُوتِ اللَّهِ يَتْلُونَ كِتَابَ اللَّهِ وَيَتَدَارَسُونَهُ بَيْنَهُمْ إِلَّا نَزَلَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ السَّكِينَةُ وَغَشِيَتْهُمُ الرَّحْمَةُ وَحَفَّتْهُمُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ وَذَكَرَهُمُ اللَّهُ فِيمَنْ عِنْدَهُ»}

As for the text of Ibn al-ʿArabī: It is recommended (mustaḥabb) at that time, when the deceased is placed in his grave, to instruct him (yulaqqan). Ibn al-ʿArabī said: This talqīn is recommended. He said: It is the practice of the people of Madīnah and the righteous among the good. He said: Because it corresponds to the saying of God the Exalted: {«وَذَكِّرْ فَإِنَّ الذِّكْرَى تَنفَعُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ»} [al-Dhāriyāt: 55]. He said: And the servant is most in need of reminding at the time of the questioning by the angel. End of the text of “al-Masālik.”

And know, O my beloved in God, that the deceased in his grave is like a drowning man, awaiting the mercy of God or a supplication (duʿā’) from the living; if it reaches him, it is more beloved to him than the world and all that it contains. So beware, O my beloved in God — then beware — lest doubt overtake you or suspicion seize you that the Book of God is the most trustworthy intercessor and the most sufficient of aids, freely given and bountiful. And no rain of divine mercy is ever sought by any means more hopeful than it; and when mercy descends, it encompasses and includes all.

My shaykh al-Muntūrī narrated to me, saying: Shaykh al-Shuyūkh Ibn Lubb said: A good thought occurred to me — and even the sinner may have a good thought — so I desired to impose upon myself a regular devotion (wird) of remembrance (dhikr) or recitation (tilāwah), and I hesitated over which act of virtue was superior. Then I was inspired in a dream:

“When the appointed times have passed, the meeting is cut off — so what remains is only the benefit of the Book.”

When I awoke, I knew that the recitation of the Qur’an was the most virtuous.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs — al-Bukhārī and Muslim — and in al-Tirmidhī: While a man was reciting Sūrat al-Kahf, he saw his beast of burden galloping; he looked, and behold, there was something like a cloud or a mist. He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and mentioned that to him, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him: “That was the sakīnah (divine tranquility) descending with the Qur’an, or descending upon the Qur’an.”

And in another authentic hadith, the Messenger of God ﷺ said: “No people gather together reciting the Book of God and studying it among themselves, but that the sakīnah descends upon them, mercy envelops them, the angels surround them, and God mentions them to those with Him.” {«وَمَا اجْتَمَعَ قَوْمٌ فِي بَيْتٍ مِنْ بُيُوتِ اللَّهِ يَتْلُونَ كِتَابَ اللَّهِ وَيَتَدَارَسُونَهُ بَيْنَهُمْ إِلَّا نَزَلَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ السَّكِينَةُ وَغَشِيَتْهُمُ الرَّحْمَةُ وَحَفَّتْهُمُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ وَذَكَرَهُمُ اللَّهُ فِيمَنْ عِنْدَهُ»}

Ibn al-Kharrāṭ: ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd al-Azdī al-Asadī, known as Ibn al-Kharrāṭ al-Ishbīlī al-Mālikī. Born in the year 510 AH and died in 582 AH. Among his works: al-Aḥkām al-Ṣughrā fī al-Ḥadīth, al-Aḥkām al-Kubrā, Ibn al-Mubtadiʿ, Tahdhīb al-Maṭālib, al-Jamʿ bayn al-Ṣaḥīḥayn (al-Bukhārī and Muslim), al-Jamʿ bayn al-Kutub al-Sittah, Kitāb al-Tahajjud, Kitāb al-Raqāʾiq, Kitāb al-ʿĀqibah fī Dhikr al-Mawt, al-Mukhtaṣar fī al-Ḥadīth, al-Wāʿī fī Ḥadīth ʿAlī (may God honor his face).

# PageV1P50
anchors:
- Root: ن-ز-ل (n-z-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Descent from a height; the settling of something upon a place or people.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological context, the "descent" of divine mercy (sakīnah) as a tangible spiritual reality upon a gathering.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal descent (ḥaqīqah) for physical objects; metaphorical (majāz) for divine attributes—here, the "sending down" of tranquility as an act of divine favor.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ) — The construction "إن لم يكن... فلا" (If it is not... then there is no) establishes a logical entailment, with the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) omitted for rhetorical emphasis.
translation:
I say — and with Allah is success:

The Sixth Station: If there is no excellence in a deed, then there is no harm in it being a deed of perfection. Among them (the people of remembrance), when they gather, tranquility descends upon them, mercy envelops them, and Allah mentions them to those who are with Him. Ibn Ḥabīb added: "And the angels shade them with their wings and seek forgiveness for them." Then, O my beloved in Allah, the tranquility when it descends, and the angels when they shade and seek forgiveness, and the mercy when it envelops — all of this encompasses and is comprehensive.

This authentic ḥadīth is corroborated by another authentic ḥadīth: "Among them is a servant who has erred; he merely passes by and sits with them. Then the Majestic Lord, glorified be His majesty, says: 'I have forgiven him; they are a people whose companion is never wretched.'"

So, by a greater priority, O my beloved in Allah, if Allah wills, this applies to one for whose sake the gathering is held and for whom the recitation is made for Allah. It is established in the authentic collection, on the authority of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he said: "No Muslim dies, and forty men stand over his funeral prayer, not associating anything with Allah, except that their intercession is accepted for him."

My teacher al-Muntūrī narrated to me, from the professor Ibn ʿAmrah, from the professor Abū al-Ḥasan al-Qurṭubī, from the narrator Abū ʿUmar ibn Ḥawṭ Allah, from the judge Abū al-Khaṭṭāb, from Abū al-Qāsim ibn Bashkuwāl — [with a chain of transmission] — that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever recites the Quran and acts upon it, his parents will be clothed on the Day of Judgment with a light whose brilliance is better than the light of the sun in the dwellings of this world, if they were in them. So what do you think of the one who acts upon this?"

title_en: Section 39 — The Sixth Station: If One Cannot Perform the Best Deed, Then at Least a Virtuous Deed
arabic_text:
### | الصفحة 50

4 منهج التدلي/ المقام السادس: إن لم يكن في عمل أفضل فلا أقل من أنيكون في عمل فاضل
عن أي محمد بن بربوع”'!؛ عن أبي محمد بن خزرج”. عن أبي محمد الخزرجي'” قال:
أخبرني أبو عبد اله القروي في المسجد الجامع بقرطبة: قال: كنت بمصر؛ فأناني نعي أ

فوجدت عليه وجنا شديناء فبلغ ذلك الشيخ أا الطيب بن غلبون المقرئ””؛ فوجه بي؛ فاه
فجعل يصبرنيه ويذكرني ثواب الصبر على المصبية والرزية: ثم قال لي: ازجع إلى ماهو
أعود عليك وعلى الميت من أفعال الب والخير مثل الصدقة وما شاكلها؛ وأمرني أن أقرأ عنه

(قل هو الله أحد) عشر مرات في كل ليلة؛ ثم قال لي: أحدثك في ذلك بحديث» قال: كان
رجل معروف بالخير والقضل؛ فرأى في منامه كأنه في مقبرة مصرء وكأن الئاس قد نشروا من
مقابرهم؛ كأنه مشى خلفهم ليسألهم عن الشيء الذي أوجب نهوضهم إلى الجهة التي
.توجهوا إليها. فوجد رجلا على حفرته قد تخلف عن جماعتهم فسأله عن القوم إلى أين

لين وهبء أخيار إسماعيل القاضي؛ أخيار الأعمش» أخبار قضاة قرطبة: أخبار المحاسني»
تاريخ الأندلس مختصر» حديث من كذب على بطرقه؛ الحكايات المستغرية» ذكر من رو
الموطأ عن مالك؛ طرق حديث المغفر ثلاثة أجزاء غتبة الأسماء امبهمة الواقعة في متون
الأحاديث المستدة الغوامض والمبهمات فيما جاء ذكره في الحديث؛ كتاب الصلة في فيل
تاريخ علماء الأندلس لأبي الوليد الفرضي مطبوع.

(1) هو أبو محمد عبد لله بن أحمد بن يربوع الشتتريني ثم الاشبيلي؛ نزيل قرطبة المشوفى
اسنة 2ك

(2) هو عبد الله بن إسماعيل بن محمد بن خنزرج اللخمي؛ الإشيلي (أبو محمد) محدث؛ حافظ
مؤرخ؛ فقيه. توفي بإشبيلية في شوال.
مسن آثاره؛ شرحان على المدونة في فروع القفه المالكي؛ ومختصر رسالة ابن أبي زييد
القبرواني.

(3) هو قاسم بسن إبراهيم بن قاسم بن يزيسد بن يوسف الانصاري؛ الخزرجسي؛ ويعرف

لله

(4) هو عبد المنعم بن عبيد لله بن غلبون بن المبارك الحلبي؛ الشافعي (أبو الطيب) مقرئ. ولد

# PageV1P51
anchors:
- Root: ع-م-ل (ʿamal)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Exertion of effort in a task; any act, whether physical or spiritual, that produces a result.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ʿamal denotes the outward manifestation of faith (īmān) and obedience (ṭāʿah), as opposed to mere intention (niyyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical action; metaphorical (majāz) — the spiritual efficacy of deeds, such as charity (ṣadaqah) benefiting the deceased.
- Root: ف-ض-ل (faḍl)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Superiority, excellence, surplus; that which exceeds the obligatory minimum.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, faḍl denotes voluntary supererogatory acts (nawāfil) that elevate the believer's rank, as opposed to farḍ (obligatory).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — abundance; metaphorical — moral excellence and divine grace.
- Root: ص-ب-ر (ṣabr)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Restraint, endurance, withholding the soul from complaint and panic.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The virtue of steadfastness in tribulation (muṣībah), a prerequisite for true submission (islām) to divine decree.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical forbearance; metaphorical — spiritual patience in accepting qadar.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional sentence (sharṭ) with "in lam" — The protasis (condition) and apodosis (result) are linked by the particle "fa" in the response, indicating a logical consequence: if the higher station is unattainable, the lower one becomes obligatory.
translation:
I say — may Allah grant us success — this is the sixth station: If one cannot perform the best deed, then let him not fall short of performing a virtuous deed.

Narrated to us Abū Muḥammad ibn Barbūʿ — from Abū Muḥammad ibn Khazraj — from Abū Muḥammad al-Khazrajī, who said: Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Qarawī informed me in the Great Mosque of Cordoba, saying: I was in Egypt when news of a death reached me. I grieved intensely over it. This reached the Shaykh Abū al-Ṭayyib ibn Ghalbūn al-Muqriʾ, so he sent for me. He began to console me and remind me of the reward of patience (ṣabr) upon calamity and affliction. Then he said to me: "Return to that which is more beneficial for you and for the deceased — namely, acts of righteousness and goodness, such as charity (ṣadaqah) and the like." He commanded me to recite on his behalf {«Qul huwa Allāhu aḥad»} ten times every night. Then he said to me: "I shall relate to you a ḥadīth concerning this." He said: There was a man known for goodness and virtue. He saw in a dream as if he were in a cemetery of Egypt, and as if the people had been raised from their graves. He walked behind them to ask them about the matter that had compelled them to rise and proceed toward their destination. He found a man at his grave who had lagged behind the group, so he asked him: "Where are these people going?" [The man replied...]

[The remainder of the text is cut off in the manuscript, followed by a list of the author's other works and biographical notes on the narrators.]

BIOGRAPHICAL NOTES (from the manuscript's marginalia):
(1) He is Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd Allāh ibn Aḥmad ibn Barbūʿ al-Shantarīnī, then al-Ishbīlī, resident of Cordoba, died in the year 2[?] (AH).
(2) He is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Muḥammad ibn Khazraj al-Lakhmī, al-Ishbīlī (Abū Muḥammad) — muḥaddith, ḥāfiẓ, historian, jurist. Died in Seville in Shawwāl. Among his works: two commentaries on al-Mudawwanah in Mālikī jurisprudence, and an abridgment of the Risālah of Ibn Abī Zayd al-Qayrawānī.
(3) He is Qāsim ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Qāsim ibn Yazīd ibn Yūsuf al-Anṣārī, al-Khazrajī, known as Ibn al-Ṣābūnī. A scholar of the Qurʾān and ḥadīth, from Cordoba. Born in Ramaḍān, died in the city of [—]. Among his works: an abridgment of al-Jalīs wa al-Ṣāḥib, Faḍl al-ʿIlm, Faḍl al-Adhān, and Faḍāʾil ʿĀshūrāʾ.
(4) He is ʿAbd al-Munʿim ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ghalbūn ibn al-Mubārak al-Ḥalabī, al-Shāfiʿī (Abū al-Ṭayyib), a Qurʾānic reader (muqriʾ). Born in Aleppo twelve nights before the end of Rajab, moved to Egypt and settled there, died there in Jumādā al-Ūlā. Among his works: al-Miʿdāl, Irshād al-Mubtadī wa Tadhkirat al-Muntahī — both on qirāʾāt — and Ḥadīqat al-Balāghah wa Dawḥat al-Barāʿah.

title_en: Section 40 — On the Virtue of Reciting Qur'an for the Deceased and the Permissibility of Gifting Its Reward
arabic_text:
### | الصفحة 51

منهج التدلي/ المقام السادس: إن لم يكن في عمل أفضل نلا أقل من أن يكون في عمل فاشل ___95
يريدوث؟ فقال: رحمة جاءتهم يقتسمونهاء قال: فهلا مضيت معهم؟ فقال: إني قد فنعت بما
يأنيني من ولد عن أن أفاسمهم فيما أيهم من المسلمين» تقلت له: وما الذي يأنيك من
ولدك؟ فقال: يقرأ كل يوم (قل هو الله أحد) عشر مرات؛ ويهدي إلى ثوابها. فذكر الشيخ
ابن غلبون لي أنه منذ سمع هذه الحكاية كان يقرأ عن والدبه قل هو الله أحد) كل يوم عشر
مرات عن كل منهماء ولم يزل بهذه الحالة إلى أن مات أبو العباس الخباط: فجعل يقرأ كل
ليلة(قلل هو الله أحد) عشر مرات ويهدي إليه ثلبهاء قال الشيخ لبن غلبون: فمكثت على هذا
ثم عرض لي فتور قطعني عن َلك فرأيت أب اعباس في النوم. فقال لي: يا با الطيب»
الم قطعت عنا ذلك السكر الخالص الذي كنت توجه به إلينا؟فاتبهت من منامي» وقلت:
السكر الخالص كلام الله عز وجل؛ وإنما كنت أوجه إليه ثواب قل هو الله أحد» فجعلت
أقرأها عنه رحمه الله

وقال ابن رشد في " انصه إذا قرأ الرجل ووهب ثواب
جاز ذلك؛ وحصل للميث أجره؛ وحصل له نفعه. اه نصه.

.وانظر إذا كانت القراءة عند القبرء فقد تقدم أن سيب نزول الرحمة هي أرجى
اللنفع» ولوجه آخر قاله العلماء من ديوان ابن يونس ما نصه: أرواح المؤمنين خاصة

.وانظر تخصيص هذه الزيارة صبيحة سبعة أيام بعد دفن الميت في "شرح

رضي الله عنهم.

وقال به ابن بطال والقايسي” وأئمة تحقق صدقهم؛ وظتنا في مأخذهم أحسن

إا) هو أبو محمد عبد اله بن طاوس بن كيسان اليماني. الامام المحيّث القة. سمع من أيه

(2) ابن القابسي؛ أبو الحسن (324 - 403ه - 936- 1012م). أبو الحسن علي بن محمد بن

# PageV1P52
anchors:
- Root: ه-د-ي (h-d-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To guide, direct, or send toward; also a gift (hadiyyah) — the act of directing something toward another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, the "gifting" (ihdā') of reward (thawāb) — a transfer of spiritual benefit from one person to another by divine permission.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — sending a physical gift; metaphorical (majāz) — directing the reward of an act of worship to another's account.
- Root: ث-و-ب (th-w-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Return, recompense, reward — the return for an action, whether good or evil.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The eschatological reward (thawāb) granted by Allah for acts of obedience — a divine recompense that can be redirected by the performer.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the return of something; metaphorical — the spiritual reward that "returns" to the believer on the Day of Judgment.
- Root: ف-ت-ر (f-t-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To slacken, weaken, or become languid — a cessation of vigor.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Spiritual lassitude (fatrah) — a period of diminished devotional fervor that afflicts even the righteous.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the cooling of fire or the weakening of a limb; metaphorical — the cooling of one's zeal for worship.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Condition and Consequence (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) — In the phrase "if a man recites and gifts the reward," the conditional clause establishes the permissibility, and the consequence affirms the benefit reaching the deceased.
translation:
I say — may Allah grant us success:

Know that the sixth station of this path concerns the matter of one who has no excellent deed to his credit — then let him at least not fall short of performing a deed that is not futile. 

I was asked about a man who said: "Mercy came to them, and they were dividing it among themselves." So I said: "Why did you not go with them?" He replied: "I have been prevented by what comes to me from my child — from sharing with them in what they have of the Muslims' merit." I said to him: "And what is it that comes to you from your child?" He said: "He recites every day {Qul Huwa Allāhu Aḥad} (Say: He is Allah, the One) ten times, and gifts its reward [to me]."

Shaykh Ibn Ghulbūn mentioned to me that ever since he heard this story, he would recite {Qul Huwa Allāhu Aḥad} every day ten times on behalf of each of his parents — and he continued in this state until Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Khabbāṭ died. Then he began to recite every night {Qul Huwa Allāhu Aḥad} ten times and gift its reward to him. Shaykh Ibn Ghulbūn said: "I continued in this practice, then a lassitude (fatrah) befell me that cut me off from that. Then I saw Abū al-ʿAbbās in a dream, and he said to me: 'O Abā al-Ṭayyib, have you cut off from us that pure honey (sukkar khāliṣ) that you used to send to us?' So I awoke from my sleep and said: 'The pure honey is the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic — and I was only sending the reward of {Qul Huwa Allāhu Aḥad} to him.' So I resumed reciting it on his behalf — may Allah have mercy on him."

And Ibn Rushd said in his commentary: "When a man recites and gifts the reward, that is permissible; the deceased obtains its benefit, and the reciter obtains his own reward." End of his text.

And consider: if the recitation is at the grave — it has already been mentioned that the descent of mercy is the most hopeful means of benefit. And there is another aspect mentioned by the scholars, from the collection (dīwān) of Ibn Yūnus, whose text is: "The souls of the believers specifically ascend to their graves and to the places where their bodies have decayed, going and returning — as an honor from Allah. For this reason, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded the greeting of peace upon the graves and their visitation." End of the transmission from Ibn Yūnus.

And consider the specification of this visitation for the morning of the seventh day after the burial of the deceased — in the "Commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī," from Ibn Ṭāwūs: that the morning visitation (al-taṣbīḥ) was practiced by the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ) — may Allah be pleased with them.

And Ibn Baṭṭāl and al-Qābisī affirmed this, along with imams whose sincerity is verified — and our opinion of their sources is the best of opinions.

title_en: Section 41 — On Visiting Graves and the Conduct of the Rightly Guided in the Station of Virtue
arabic_text:
### | الصفحة 52

96 منهج التدثي/ المقام السادس: إن لم يكن في عمل أنضل فلا اقل من أن يكون في عمل فاضل
من ظننا في مأخذ غيرهم. ولما تكلم أبو عمر في “شرح الموط" على قوله فل حين
خرج إلى القبورء فقال: 'السلام عليكم" ذكر الأثر عن ابن عمر حين قدم من سفرء
فقام على باب عائشة: فقال: السلام عليكم يا رسول الله؛ عليك يا أبا بكر السلام؛
عليك يا أبت؛ قال: وكان عامر إذا خرج إلى القبور يقول: ألا تسلموث: فيردون
عليكم.
قال أبو عمر: وهذا كثير جدًا في الأخبارء وذهب إليه أكثر أهل العلمء
واستدلوا عليه بقوله عليه السلام: "ما أنتم بأسمع منهم”"» ويغير ذلك. وشهر هذا
كثيرًا في "الاستذكار" و" التمهيد'.
وقال ابن العربي: لا بأس بالمشي إلى القبورء وقد ثبت أن النبي وله خرج بأمر
ربه إلى أهل البقيع يستغفر لهمء ولو شاء لاستغفر لهم في مكانه؛ ولكن لله أراد أن
يشرع الإثيان إلى القبور.
وكان محمد بن واسع”' يزور القبور يوم الجمعة؛ فقيل له: لو أخرت إلى يوم
الاثنين؟ قال: بلغني أن الموتى يعلمون بزوارهم يوم الجمعة ويومًا قبله ويوما بعده.
وقال الباجي في "منتقاه": إنما أمرت عائثة أن يمر عليها بجنازة سعدا أرادت أن
الإعام أب محمدالاء
أخذ القابسي القراءة عرضا بمصر عن أبي الفتح بن بَُنء وأقرأ اناس بالقيروان دهراء ثم
أعمل تفسه في الفقه والحديث حتى برع فيهماء وصار إمام العصر؛ أثى عليه بأكثر من هذا
أبو عمرو الداتي.
من تصتيفه: الممهد في الققه؛ أحكام الديانات» المقذ من شه لتاويل؛ المبه للطن عن
غوائل الفتنء ملخص الموطأاء المناسك؛ الاعتقادات؛ رسالة تزكية الشهود وتجريحهم؛
الرسالة المفصلة لاحوال المعلمين والمتعلمين» رسالة الذكر والدعاء. وغيرها من الكتب.
توفي بمديئة اليروا» وبات عند قيره نخلق من الناس؛ ورئته الشعرا.
<1) أخرجه البخاري (462/1» رقم: 1304).
(2) محمد بن واسع بن جابر الأزدي؛ لبو بكر: فقيه ورع؛ من الزهاد. من أهل البصرة. عرض عليه
قضاؤهاء فابى. وهو من ثفات أهل الحديث.
قال الأصمعي: لما صاف قتبية بن مسلم الترك وهاله أمرهم؛ سأل من محمد بن واسع»
ققيل: هو ذاك في الميمنة يتضنض بأصبعه نحو السماءء قال: تلك الاصبع أحب إلي من مائة
آلف سيف!

‎٠‏ عبد له بن إبراهيم ات 392هه - 1001م).

# PageV1P53
anchors:
- Root: ز-و-ر (z-w-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of "visiting" (ziyārah) — intentional approach to a person or place, often with reverence or seeking blessing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological context, visiting graves (ziyārat al-qubūr) is a sanctioned act of remembrance (tadhkirah) of the afterlife, not worship of the dead.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical journey to graves; metaphorical (majāz) — spiritual turning of the heart toward the deceased's state.
- Root: س-ل-م (s-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Greeting of peace (salām) — a prayer for safety and well-being.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, salām upon the dead is a verbal acknowledgment of their sentience in the barzakh, not a mere ritual formula.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — verbal address; metaphorical — the soul's reception of the greeting, as affirmed by prophetic report.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and exception structures (sharṭ wa-jawāb) — "If not in a superior act, then at least in a virtuous one" (law lā... fa-lā aqall), indicating graded obligation and permissibility.
translation:
I say: The sixth station — if one cannot engage in a superior act, then let him not fall short of a virtuous one.

From our supposition regarding the source of others' [practices]. When Abū ʿUmar spoke in his "Sharḥ al-Muwaṭṭa" on his saying — when he went out to the graves — "Peace be upon you," he mentioned the narration from Ibn ʿUmar that when he returned from a journey, he stood at the door of ʿĀʾishah and said: "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah; peace be upon you, O Abū Bakr; peace be upon you, O my father." He said: And ʿĀmir, when he went out to the graves, would say: "Do you not greet them? For they will respond to you."

Abū ʿUmar said: This is very abundant in the reports, and the majority of scholars adopted it, adducing his saying, peace be upon him: "You are not more hearing than they" {«ما أنتم بأسمع منهم»}, and other than that. And he made this well-known extensively in "Al-Istidhkār" and "Al-Tamhīd."

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: There is no harm in walking to the graves, for it is established that the Prophet, peace be upon him, went out by the command of his Lord to the people of Al-Baqīʿ to seek forgiveness for them. Had he wished, he could have sought forgiveness for them from his place; but Allah intended to legislate the coming to graves.

Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ used to visit the graves on Friday. It was said to him: "Would you delay it to Monday?" He said: "It has reached me that the dead know of their visitors on Friday and the day before it and the day after it."

Al-Bājī said in his "Muntaqā": ʿĀʾishah was only commanded that a funeral of Saʿd pass by her — she intended thereby [to affirm] the imam, Abū Muḥammad.

Al-Qābisī took the reading (qirāʾah) by presentation (ʿarḍ) in Egypt from Abū al-Fatḥ ibn Bunn, and he taught people in Qayrawān for a long time. Then he devoted himself to jurisprudence and hadith until he excelled in both, becoming the imam of his age. Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī praised him with more than this.

Among his compositions: "Al-Mumahhid fī al-Fiqh"; "Aḥkām al-Diyānāt"; "Al-Muqniʿ fī Sharḥ al-Taʾwīl"; "Al-Mubih li al-Ṭaʿn ʿan Ghawāʾil al-Fitan"; "Talkhīṣ al-Muwaṭṭa"; "Al-Manāsik"; "Al-Iʿtiqādāt"; "Risālah fī Tazkiyat al-Shuhūd wa-Tajrīḥihim"; "Al-Risālah al-Mufaṣṣalah li-Aḥwāl al-Muʿallimīn wa-al-Mutaʿallimīn"; "Risālah fī al-Dhikr wa-al-Duʿā"; and other books.

He died in the city of Qayrawān, and a multitude of people spent the night at his grave, and the poets eulogized him.

(1) Narrated by Al-Bukhārī (1/462, no. 1304).
(2) Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ ibn Jābir al-Azdī, Abū Bakr: a pious jurist, among the ascetics of Baṣrah. The judgeship was offered to him, and he refused. He is among the trustworthy narrators of hadith. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: When Qutaybah ibn Muslim faced the Turks and their numbers alarmed him, he asked about Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ. It was said: "He is there in the right flank, pointing his finger toward the sky." He said: "That finger is more beloved to me than a hundred thousand swords!"

(3) ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ibrāhīm, died 392 AH (1001 CE).

title_en: Section 42 — On the Recitation of Qur'an for the Deceased and the Visiting of Graves

### | الصفحة 53

منهج التدلي/ المقام السادس: إن لم يكن في عمل أفضل فلا أقل من أن يكون في عمل ناضل___ 397
يحضر لتدعو له بحضرئه؛ لآن مشاهدته تدعو إلى الإشفاق والاجتهاد له ولذلك
يسعى إلى الجنائز؛ ولا يجتزي بما يدعي له في المنزل. اه
ولم يذكر بسن عرفة في ديوانسه الفقهسي إلا استحباب القراءة على
القبور؛ فقال ما نصه: قبل عياض استدلال بعض العلماء على استحباب
القراءة على القبر؛ لحديث الجريدتين. اه.
وقد ورد الأثر عن عبد الله بن عمر أنه أوصى عند موته أن
(البقرة) عند دفته.
وكذلك: "اقرؤوا يس عند موتاكم'. هو خبر مشهور؛ خرجه غير واحد من
الأئمة. وخرجه أبو داود وما ذكر فيه مغمرًا. واستحباب قراءتها عند العلماء مأثور
قال عبد الحق: يحتمل هذه القراءة أن تكون عند الميت في حال موته. ويحتمل أن
.تكون عند قبره. ولم يتقل اللخمي في ديوانه الفقهي إلا استحباب قراءتها؛ ورشح
هذا الاستحباب ابن رشد وابن يونس وغيرهما من الأئمة الأعلام؛ وكلهم تأول
اللفظة الواردة عن الإمام. اتتهت النصوص المالكية.
وأما النصوص الشافعية التي لو كان مذعبنا متفقًا على المنع لوجب من أجلها
أن لا يكون في ذلك حسبة؛ لآن ما اختلف المالكية والشافعية في منعه لا حسبة فيه.
.وخارج عن السنة من يقول: ذلك ضلال أو بدعة.
فسن ذلك نص السيد الإمام مربي المريدين البلالي مسن أئمة الشافعية.
المعتمدين؛ قال: تلفين الميت غير الطفل مهم جدًاء ونحو هذا للإمام محبي الدين
النووي؛ وذكر لفظ التلقين كيف هو.
وقد سثل عنه الإمام ابن الصلاح؛ فقال: تلقين الميت هو الذي نختاره وتعمل
به وقال البلالي: أدب زائر القبور أن يقرأ ويدعو؛ فإنه يصل إليهم دعاءه وصدقته.
نعمء وقسنا عليهما القراءة من وجوه تحسن لمن تأملهاء ورجحها السبكي”" قال:
ذا ثقي الدين السبكي (683 - 756ه - 1284 - 1355م) علي بن عبد الكافي بن علي بن ثمام
السبكي الأنصاري الخزرجي؛ أبو الحسن؛ تقي الدين: شيخ الإسلام في عصره؛ وأحد
الحفاظ المفسرين المناظرين. وهو والد التاج السبكي صاحب الطبقات. ولد في سبك (من
أعمال المنوفية بمصر) والنتقل إلى الفاهرة ثم إلى الشام.

# PageV1P54

### | الصفحة 54

98 منهج التدثي/ المقام السادس: إن لم يكن في عمل أفضل فلا أقل من أن يكون في عمل نال
لهذا أدلة؛ ليس هذا موضع بسطهاء والإشارة كافية؛ وقد ريء كثير من الموتى»
وأخبروا بنفعهم بالقرآن.انتهت نصوص من رأيت تأليفهم من الأئمة الموثوق
بعلمهم من الشافعية؛ وأما أحمد بن حنبل وأبو حنيفة فما رأيت منقولًا عنهماء إلا
أن مذهبهما أن القراءة يصل ثوابها إلى الميث.

وانظر أيضًا مأخذ الإمام شهاب الدين الذي لاا
الا لاف أن بركة القرآن تصل للميت؛ كما قد ثبت أنه يحصل له بركة الرجل
الصالح يدقن بجنبه؛ ييقى النظر في ثواب القراءة: قال: والذي ينبغي ألا تهمل هذه
المسألة؛ فلمل الحق هو الوصول إلى الموتى؛ فإن هذه أمور مغيية عناء وليس
الخلاف فيها في حكم شرعيء إنما هو في أمر واقع: هل هو كذلك أو لا؟ قال:
.وكذلك التهليل الذي عادة الناس يعملونه اليوم الذي يتبغي أن يعمل؛ ويعتمد في
ذلك على فضل الله تعالى ويسره. ويلتمس فضل الله تعالى بكل سيب ممكن ومن
الله الجود والإحسان. هذا هو اللائق بالعبد؛ فقد تحصل مما قررته أن شتان بين من
هو على عمل تحمل عهدئه موثوق بعلمه ودينه وأنه مشروع؛ وبين من هو على
مباح لا قائل: إنه مشروع؛ ولكن قد يصير المباح مكرمة بنسبة كقول مالك: لو
علمت أن قلبي يصلح بالجلوس على كناسة لجلست عليها. ونحن نعلم أنه ليس
اللشرع مقصد في ذلك إلا بالنية؛ وهذا مقام دون المقام الذي هو مختلف في
مشروعيته: فاعدد هذا المقام أنه المقام الخامس.

في صدق مأخذه؛ أنه قال:

.ولي قضاء الشام سنة 739 واهثل فعا إلى القاهرة؛ فتوفي فيهاء من كتبه "الدر النظيم” في
التفسيرء لم يكمله؛ و'مختصر طبقات القفهاء” و'إحياء بالتقوس في صنعة إلقاء الدروس”
و"الاغريض: في الحقيقة والمجاز والكنية والتعريض'

# PageV1P55
anchors:
- Root: ق-ر-أ (q-r-')
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To read, recite, or proclaim; the act of assembling letters and words in ordered sequence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Recitation of the Qur'an as an act of worship (ʿibādah) whose benefit may be conveyed to others, whether living or dead, by divine grace.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — audible recitation; metaphorical (majāz) — the conveyance of reward (īṣāl al-thawāb) to the deceased, a matter of divine dispensation.
- Root: ل-ق-ن (l-q-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To prompt, dictate, or instruct someone in words so they may repeat them.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The post-burial prompting (talqīn) of the deceased with the testimony of faith, a practice of communal merit.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — verbal instruction to the living; metaphorical — addressing the deceased in the grave, whose hearing is affirmed by sound reports.
- Root: ز-ي-ر (z-y-r) / ز-و-ر (z-w-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To visit; the visitor (zā'ir) who repairs to another out of respect or seeking blessing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Visiting graves (ziyārah) as a reminder of the afterlife and an act of supplication for the dead.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical presence at the grave; metaphorical — the spiritual communion with the deceased through prayer and recitation.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Conditional Concession (al-sharṭ al-istithmānī) — "If not... then at least..." (fa-in lam... fa-lā aqall min...) introduces a graded obligation, where the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is a minimum standard, not an optional alternative.
translation:
I say — and success is from God alone:

Know that the sixth station of this path is this: If one cannot attain to the most excellent of deeds, then let him not fall short of a deed that is sound and well-grounded. For the believer should strive to be present at the funeral of his brother so that he may supplicate for him in his very presence; for the very sight of the deceased moves the heart to compassion and earnest prayer on his behalf. For this reason, the pious predecessors would hasten to funerals and would not content themselves with merely praying for the deceased from their homes. This is the end of the matter.

Now, the author of the legal compendium (al-Dīwān al-Fiqhī) did not mention, in the section on the day of ʿArafah, anything beyond the recommendation (istihbāb) of reciting the Qur'an at graves. He said, quoting ʿIyāḍ: "Some scholars have inferred the recommendation of recitation at the grave from the ḥadīth of the two palm-branches (al-jarīdatayn)." This is the end of his quotation.

And there has come down the report (athar) from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar — may God be pleased with him — that he instructed at the time of his death that Sūrat al-Baqarah {«البقرة»} be recited at his burial.

Likewise, the saying of the Prophet — peace and blessings be upon him — "Recite Yā Sīn over your dead" {«اقرؤوا يس على موتاكم»} is a well-known report (khabar mashhūr), transmitted by more than one of the imams. Abū Dāwūd transmitted it, though with some weakness in its chain. The recommendation of its recitation is well-attested (ma'thūr) among the scholars.

ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq said: "This recitation may be understood as taking place at the time of the person's death, or it may be understood as taking place at his grave." And al-Lakhmī, in his legal compendium, mentioned only the recommendation of its recitation. This recommendation was endorsed by Ibn Rushd, Ibn Yūnus, and other eminent imams; and all of them interpreted the wording transmitted from the Imam (Mālik) in this manner. Thus end the Mālikī texts.

As for the Shāfiʿī texts — had our school been unanimously agreed upon prohibition, it would have been incumbent, by virtue of these texts, that there be no element of praiseworthy competition (ḥisbah) in this matter; for where the Mālikīs and Shāfiʿīs differ on permissibility, there is no room for ḥisbah. And whoever says, "That is error or innovation," has departed from the Sunnah.

Among such texts is the saying of the Sayyid Imam, the trainer of seekers (murabbī al-murīdīn), al-Balālī, one of the relied-upon Shāfiʿī imams. He said: "The prompting (talqīn) of the deceased — other than a child — is a matter of great importance." And similar to this is the saying of Imam Muḥyī al-Dīn al-Nawawī; and he mentioned the precise manner of the talqīn.

The Imam Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ was asked about it, and he said: "The prompting of the deceased is what we choose and act upon." And al-Balālī said: "The etiquette of the visitor of graves is that he recite and supplicate; for his supplication and his charity do reach them." Yes, and we have analogized upon these two matters the recitation (of the Qur'an) from several angles, which becomes evident to whoever reflects upon them. And al-Subkī — that is, Taqī al-Dīn al-Subkī (683–756 AH / 1284–1355 CE), ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-Kāfī ibn ʿAlī ibn Tammām al-Subkī al-Anṣārī al-Khazrajī, Abū al-Ḥasan, Taqī al-Dīn: the Shaykh al-Islām of his age, one of the ḥuffāẓ, exegetes, and disputants; he is the father of Tāj al-Subkī, author of al-Ṭabaqāt; born in Subk (in the province of al-Munūfiyyah in Egypt), then moved to Cairo and then to Damascus; he held the judgeship of Damascus in 739 AH, then returned to Cairo and died there; among his books is al-Durr al-Naẓīm in tafsīr, which he did not complete, and Mukhtaṣar Ṭabaqāt al-Fuqahā', and Iḥyā' bi-l-Taqwīs fī Ṣināʿat Ilqāʾ al-Durūs, and al-Ighrīḍ fī al-Ḥaqīqah wa-l-Majāz wa-l-Kināyah wa-l-Taʿrīḍ — this al-Subkī favored it (the recitation at graves).

He said: "For this there are proofs; this is not the place to expand upon them, and the indication suffices. Many of the dead have been seen (in dreams) and have informed of the benefit they received from the Qur'an." Thus end the texts of those whose works I have seen among the trustworthy Shāfiʿī imams. As for Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and Abū Ḥanīfah, I have not seen anything transmitted from them on this specific point, except that their school holds that the reward of recitation does reach the deceased.

And consider also the position of Imam Shihāb al-Dīn — may God have mercy on him — who did not doubt that the blessing (barakah) of the Qur'an reaches the deceased, just as it is established that the deceased benefits from the blessing of a righteous man buried beside him. The only remaining question is concerning the reward (thawāb) of the recitation itself. He said: "What is proper is that this matter should not be neglected; for perhaps the truth is that (the reward) does reach the dead. These are matters hidden from us, and the disagreement therein is not over a legal ruling (ḥukm sharʿī); rather, it is over a matter of fact: is it so or not?" He said: "Likewise, the tahlīl (saying Lā ilāha illā Allāh) which people customarily practice on that day — it is what ought to be done, relying in that upon God's bounty and His ease. And one seeks God's bounty by every possible means; and from God comes generosity and beneficence. This is what befits the servant."

So, from what I have established, you may perceive the vast difference between one who acts upon a practice whose transmission is borne by one trustworthy in knowledge and religion, and which is declared lawful (mashrūʿ), and one who acts upon a merely permissible (mubāḥ) matter, with no one declaring it lawful — though the permissible may become a noble act (makramah) by virtue of intention, as Mālik said: "If I knew that my heart would be set right by sitting upon a dunghill, I would sit upon it." And we know that the Law (al-sharʿ) has no purpose in that except through intention. Yet this station is below the station that is disputed as to its lawfulness. So count this (the recitation at graves) as the fifth station (in the order of merit), not the sixth.

And in confirmation of the soundness of his source, he (al-Subkī) said: "I held the judgeship of Damascus in 739 AH..." — and the rest of his biography as mentioned above.

title_en: The Fifth Station: The Presence of Intention Transforms the Permissible into a Meritorious Act

### | الصفحة 55

المقام الخامس

حضور النية يصير المباح مكرمة

هو من حيث فشوى المفتي مباح؛ ولكنه يصير مكرمة بالنية؛ بل قالوا: من
حضرت له نية في مباح ولم تحضر في فضيلة فالمباح أولى؛ مثل أن تكون له نية في
الأكل والشرب والنوم ليريح نفسه ويتقوى على العبادة في المستقبل؛ وليس تتبعث
انفسه في الحال للصوم والصلاة فالنوم والأكل هو الأفضل له وعندي أن هذا هو
دون هذا المقام الذي قد قصرت الكلام عليه؛ وإتما عنيت بهذا المقام أن يتحرى
من المباحات ما يكسبه رقة في قلبه؛ كزيارة أماكن الصالحين» والشرب من قلدح
البي َك وإيثار سكنى العقيق؛ كما حكى مالك عن نفسه؛ وإدارة ابن عمر ناقته إثر
لة رسول لله يك فهذه كلها مقاصد لذاتها تنتظم في سلك المندوبات: فما من
مباح إلا ويصير مكرمة بسب النية والمعصية هي التي لا تنقلب أبدا مكرمة
إلا أنهم استثنوا من هذا مصلحة شرعية لم تثل إلا بمفسدة دونهاء وأعدد هذا
أيضًا من المقام بعد هذا؛ وهو المقام الرابع.

# PageV1P56

### | الصفحة 56

المقام الرابع

درء الأخس بالخسيس

وأن يقصد بالأمور الخسيسة التوسل بها لمقاصد تضمحل خسة الوسيلة في
جنب المقصد المتوسل إليه؛ وقد تقدم أن المعصية إذا كانت تدرأ معصية أعظم؛
فإنها تفعل؛ كالكذب بالنسبة لنجاة معصوم الدم من القتل؛ أو من أخذ ماله؛ وكذا
.يقول الصوفية: بل وغيرهم؛ كإمامنا مالك بالنسبة لصلاح القلب.

أما مالك فمثل قوله: لو علمت أن قلبي يصلح بالجلوس على كناسة لجلست
عليها. ونقل ابن عباد قال: إذا جاز لمن غص باللقمة من طعام حلال أن يسيغها
بجرعة من الخمر إذا لم يجد غيره؛ مع أن تحريمه مقطوع به ولا تفوته إلا
حياة فانيةء فلان يجوز مثل هذا إذا تعين أولى؛ إذ يفوته بذلك الحياة الباقية والقرب

امن اله

وعنى بمثل هذا ما يستدفع المريد به الدواخل على قلبه؛ قالوا: ولا بد لكل
مريد من معالجة الدواخل بعلم وعمل: أما العلم فمثل قول تاج الدين في" حكمه''
الناس يمدحونك بما يظنون فيك؛ فكن أنت ذامًا لنفسك بما تعلمه منهاء ومن جهل
المريد أن يترك يقين ما عنده لما يظنه الناس. وأما العمل فيما يسقطه من قلوب
الأغيار وسفره أسلم.

وقال سيدي مربي المرهدين: المباحات بلا شره لقصد التقوبة على الطاعة
عبادات: بل تجب نحو نومة بعد سهر مؤثر وأكلة وشربة بعد جوع أو ظمأ مؤثرء

يأفي بسط هذا عند التكلم على هذا المقام نفسه في الترقي.

وقال تاج الدين من "حكمه": ريما وردت عليك الأنوار؛ قوجدت القلب.
محشوًا بصور الآثاره فرغ قليك من الأغيار تملاه بالمعارف والأسرار.

.ومن هذا هو السماع عند القاثلين بهء كان موضعه زمن السلف لحظ الأنفس
الطيب نغمات الغناء في أوقات السرورء وشدد الفقهاء في إنكار هذا. فقال أصبغ: لا

# PageV1P57
anchors:
- Root: ح-ض-ر (ḥ-ḍ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Presence" (ḥuḍūr) as the opposite of absence; the physical and spiritual attendance of something before one.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological terms, "presence of the heart" (ḥuḍūr al-qalb) denotes the soul's attentiveness to God, free from distraction—here, the intentional focus that elevates an act.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for spatial presence; metaphorical (majāz) for the mind's engagement with an intention (niyyah).
- Root: ن-و-ي (n-w-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Intention" (niyyah) from the root meaning "to aim" or "to purpose"; the resolve that directs an action.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, niyyah is the inward determination that distinguishes worship (ʿibādah) from mere habit (ʿādah), and it is the criterion for an act's moral value.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the act of aiming; metaphorical for the spiritual orientation that converts the mundane into the sacred.
- Root: ك-ر-م (k-r-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Generosity" or "nobility" (karāmah); a state of honor and excellence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Quranic lexicon, karāmah signifies divine favor and the elevation of a believer's station; here, it denotes an act's transformation into a praiseworthy deed (mandūb).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for noble lineage; metaphorical for the spiritual worth acquired through intention.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Predication (al-Isnād) — The sentence "al-mubāḥ yaṣīru makramah" (the permissible becomes a meritorious act) employs a verbal predicate (yaṣīru) that indicates transformation (taḥawwul), requiring the subject to retain its essence while acquiring a new attribute through the cause (sabab) of intention.
translation:
I say: The Fifth Station — The presence of intention makes the permissible (mubāḥ) a meritorious act (makramah).

This [act] is, in terms of the fatwa's general ruling, permissible; but it becomes a meritorious deed through intention. Indeed, they said: Whoever has an intention present for a permissible act, while no intention arises for a supererogatory virtue (faḍīlah), then the permissible act takes precedence. For example, if one has the intention in eating, drinking, and sleeping to rest his body and strengthen himself for future worship, and his soul does not presently incline toward fasting or prayer, then sleeping and eating are better for him. In my view, this is below this station, about which I have already curtailed my speech. Rather, I mean by this station that one deliberately seeks out, from among permissible things, that which earns him tenderness (riqqah) in his heart — such as visiting the places of the righteous, drinking from the cup of the blessed water (al-bīr), and preferring to dwell in al-ʿAqīq [a valley near Medina]. This is as Mālik narrated about himself, and as Ibn ʿUmar's turning his she-camel toward the direction of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him. All these are purposes in themselves that are woven into the string of recommended acts (mandūbāt). For there is no permissible act but that it becomes a meritorious deed by virtue of intention; and disobedience (maʿṣiyah) is that which never transforms into a meritorious deed — except that they exempted from this a legal benefit (maṣlaḥah sharʿiyyah) that is not attained except through a lesser harm (mafsadah). And I also count this as belonging to the station after this one, which is the Fourth Station.

I say: The Fourth Station — Repelling the baser by the base (darʾ al-akhass bi-al-khasīs).

This is that one intends, through base matters, to use them as a means to purposes such that the baseness of the means vanishes in comparison to the purpose sought thereby. It has already been stated that if a disobedience repels a greater disobedience, then it is done — like lying for the sake of saving a person whose blood is inviolable (maʿṣūm al-dam) from being killed, or from having his wealth seized. And likewise say the Sufis — indeed, others too — such as our Imam Mālik, regarding the soundness of the heart.

As for Mālik, there is his saying: "If I knew that my heart would be set right by sitting on a dunghill, I would sit upon it." And Ibn ʿAbbād transmitted, saying: "If it is permissible for one who chokes on a morsel of lawful food to wash it down with a gulp of wine when he finds nothing else — even though its prohibition is definitively established (maqṭūʿ bihi) and he loses thereby only a fleeting life — then it is more fitting that such [a concession] be permissible when it is determined [as necessary], since he loses thereby the everlasting life and nearness to God."

By such [examples], what is meant is that by which the seeker (murīd) repels the intrusions (dawākhil) upon his heart. They said: Every seeker must treat the intrusions with knowledge (ʿilm) and action (ʿamal). As for knowledge, it is like the saying of Tāj al-Dīn in his "Wise Sayings" (Ḥikam): "People praise you for what they suppose about you; so be you a blamer of yourself for what you know of it." And from the seeker's ignorance is that he abandons the certainty of what he possesses for what people suppose. As for action, it is in what he casts down from his heart of other-than-God (aghayr), and his journeying is safer.

And my master, the nurturer of the rightly guided (murabbī al-murhidīn), said: "Permissible acts, without greed, for the purpose of strengthening oneself for obedience, are acts of worship — nay, they are obligatory, such as a sleep after a wearisome vigil, and a meal and drink after a hunger or thirst that is wearisome." The elaboration of this will come when discussing this very station in the ascent (al-taraqqī).

And Tāj al-Dīn said in his "Wise Sayings": "Perhaps the lights may come upon you, and you find the heart stuffed with the forms of traces [of other-than-God]. So empty your heart of other-than-God, and it will be filled with gnoses (maʿārif) and secrets (asrār)."

And from this [station] is the audition (samāʿ) according to those who affirm it. Its place in the era of the Salaf was the enjoyment of the soul with pleasant melodies of song at times of joy. The jurists (fuqahāʾ) were severe in rejecting this. Thus Aṣbagh said: "No —"

title_en: Section 44 — The Fourth Station: Warding Off Harm by the Lowest Means; The Permissibility of Singing and Its Conditions

# PageV1P60
anchors:
- Root: غ-ن-ي (gh-n-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of "singing" (ghināʾ) — raising the voice with melodious rhythm; also carries the sense of "self-sufficiency" (istighnāʾ), indicating a state of being free from need.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ghināʾ relates to the soul's inclination toward sensory pleasure; its permissibility hinges on the intent (niyyah) and the context, distinguishing lawful recreation from heedlessness (ghaflah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) refers to vocal melody; metaphorical (majāz) extends to any alluring speech or sound that stirs the heart, whether toward virtue or vice.
- Root: س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Hearing" (samāʿ) — the auditory perception; in this context, it denotes the spiritual audition of song and its effect on the listener's state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Samāʿ as a technical term among the Sufis — the deliberate listening to poetry or melody to evoke spiritual yearning (shawq) or remembrance of God; its ruling depends on the listener's dominant inclination.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal hearing versus the metaphorical "hearing of the heart" — the inner receptivity that translates sound into spiritual or carnal movement.
- Root: د-ف-ع (d-f-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Repelling" (dafʿ) — pushing away harm; the root of the section's title, indicating a defensive measure.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, dafʿ al-ḍarar (repelling harm) is a principle of jurisprudential necessity, prioritizing the lesser evil.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal physical repulsion; metaphorical — the strategic concession to a lesser permissible act to avert a greater prohibited one.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs conditional clauses (e.g., "if the listener's dominant trait is...") and exceptions ("except in weddings") to delineate precise legal boundaries; parsing requires identifying the protasis and apodosis to capture the nuanced rulings.
translation:
I say — may God guide us and you:

Know that singing (ghināʾ) is not permissible except at weddings, and solely for women, with the duff (frame drum) and without accompaniment of stringed instruments or reeds — or [it may be] with the remembrance of God (dhikr), or with His glorification (tasbīḥ), or with His praise (taḥmīd) for His guidance; or with light verse (rajaz) that contains neither indecency nor excessive length.

Ibn Rushd said: There is no difference in this matter between men and women. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: The statement of Aṣbagh — that it is only for women — and the disapproval of its attendance by a man of dignity (dhū al-hayʾah) is corrupt, for the Prophet ﷺ attended the beating of the duff; and it is not sound that a man of dignity be greater than the Prophet ﷺ.

Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ said: Analogous to the wedding are the festivals (aʿyād) of the Muslims and their joyous occasions. Another said: Likewise for the arrival of an absent one, or a birth, or a circumcision, or a boy's completion of the Qurʾān, or a virtuous invitation. Then, when the listener hears the melodies (taghammāt), they may evoke reproach (ʿitāb), or separation (ṣadal), or abandonment (hajr), or nearness (qurb), or distance (buʿd), or yearning for a beloved (talahhuf ʿalā fāʾit), or thirst for an awaited one (taʿaṭṭush ilā mutanaẓẓar), or longing for an approaching one (shawq ilā wārid), or hope (ṭamaʿ), or despair (yaʾs), or solitude (waḥshah), or intimacy (istīʾnās), or fulfillment of a covenant (wafāʾ bi-ʿahd), or breach of a covenant (naqḍ ʿahd), or fear of parting (khawf firāq), or joy of union (faraḥ bi-wiṣāl) — or other such meanings that the term "audition" (samāʿ) encompasses. It is inevitable that some of these will correspond to the listener's state (ḥāl), and thus it runs the course of the fire-stick (qidāḥ) that ignites the flint of his heart; and he finds a vast field for applying the words to his own conditions. If the dominant trait of the listener is a forbidden passion (hawā muḥarram), this audition stirs him to pursue the unlawful; and if the dominant trait is a permissible passion (hawā mubāḥ), the audition stirs him and affects him with the traces of longing, fear of parting, and hope of reunion. Thus, the audition of such a person is permissible (mubāḥ) — even if this listener's audition reminds him of what his states with his Lord require, for he has attained two things: the pleasure of his soul and the attachment to the attributes of his Lord. Yet in this state there is a deficiency, from the aspect of the soul's share (ḥaẓẓ al-nafs) within it. They said concerning this: "Whoever knows what he seeks, what he spends becomes easy for him."

It has thus become clear that audition (samāʿ) is never an end in itself — neither for the Sufis (ṣūfiyyah) nor for the jurists (fuqahāʾ). Is it then a means (wasīlah)? Many scholars are averse to considering it a means to [spiritual] effort (jihād), while all the Sufis and many scholars of God's rulings undertake the responsibility that it is a means.

Al-Qushayrī said in his "Risālah": Indeed, al-Rūdhabārī — may God have mercy on him — was the most knowledgeable of people in the Path (ṭarīqah) among the companions of al-Junayd. He said: "Would that we were delivered from this audition, head for head."

Ibn al-Subkī said: We hold the belief that the path of al-Junayd and his companions is an advanced path; and al-Junayd — may God be pleased with him — said: "Audition is a trial (fitnah) for the one who seeks it, and a relief (rāḥah) for the one who encounters it." And they prohibited its attendance for the common folk (ʿawāmm), for the audition of melodies is enjoyed by the immoral (fāsiq), the foolish (safīh), the child, and the minor. Whoever intends it as a means of approach (tawassul) alongside these listeners, with a share of the soul, the matter is not hidden. And whoever intends mere audition, without another meaning, the scholars of God's rulings and the Imām of the Path, al-Junayd, disavow him — for his saying: "The one who seeks audition purely is among the deluded (maftūnīn)." However, if it is as al-Junayd said — that it gathers a measure [of benefit] and attends to a deed thereby — then there is no objection, except if it is from the rabble of the common folk (ʿāmmah al-ghawghāʾ), for then there is no accountability (ḥisbah) upon him. And this is the third station.

[Footnote: Al-Rūdhabārī — Abū ʿAlī, the shaykh of the Sufis; it is said his name was Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim ibn Manṣūr, and it is said his name was Ḥasan ibn Hārūn. He resided in Egypt; he accompanied al-Junayd, Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Nūrī, Abū Ḥamzah al-Baghdādī, and Ibn al-Jallāʾ. He narrated from Masʿūd al-Ramlī and others. He said: My teacher in jurisprudence (fiqh) was Ibn Surayj; in literature (adab), Thaʿlab; and in ḥadīth, Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī.]

[Footnote: Ibn al-Subkī — ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn ʿAlī al-Shāfiʿī, Tāj al-Dīn al-Subkī, the jurist, muftī, and judge; he excelled in many sciences. Among his works is "Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ" in uṣūl. He was born in Cairo in 727 AH and died in Damascus in 771 AH.]

---

THE THIRD STATION: THE STATION OF THE RABBLE (GHawGHāʾ)

The station of the rabble (ghawghāʾ) — those who have no aspiration (himmah), neither in lawful conduct (ḥill) nor in abstention (ḥurr). It suffices for these that it be said to them: "Beware of stringed instruments (awtār) and reeds (mazāmīr), and there is no accountability (ḥisbah) upon you therein." And by this they attain a certain honor over the negligent (mukhalliṭīn). In sum, the legal opinion (fatwā) necessitates the permissibility of the common folk engaging in what has neither benefit nor harm — even if this is a base acquisition, for the soul that turns toward it is baser still. For if, by abandoning it, they would occupy themselves with what entails a burden of consequence upon them, then dancing (raqṣ) and amusement (lahw) for the rabble — provided they do not abandon an obligatory duty for its sake, nor deem it an act of worship — is better than consuming people's honor (ʿirḍ). Then, below this station is another station — and that is the second station.

title_en: The Second Station and the First: The Confused One Afflicted by Opposition and the One Extravagant Against Himself

المقام الثاني والأول
المخلط الميتلى بالمخالفة والمسرف على نفسه

انفسه؛ وهذا المقام هو أخس مقام.

# PageV1P61

### | الصفحة 61

سس منهج الترقيا؟

المقام الأول
مقام المسرف على نفسه

مقام مسرف على نفسه لم يتمسك إلا بكلمة التوحيد؛ فهذا مخوف عليه؛ إلا
أن مذهب أهل السنة والجماعة أن لا يكفر أحد بذنب من أهل القبلة؛ ويجب علينا
أن نكون معه على حالة لو وزناها بحال كافر أدركنا تفرقة بينهما. فذلك هو الحب
في الله الذي هو فرض ععين؛ وتعلم أن الكافر لا يقبل الله منه صرئًا ولا عدا
بخلاف هذا؛ فإنه لا يخرجه ذنبه وإن عظم عن الإسلام؛ وكل ذرة يفعلها هذا من
اخير يتقبلها لله منه؛ لأن متقي الشرك يتقبل الله منه كل طاعة.

قال ابن عطية”) في "تفسيره': روي عن ابن عباس أن العبد إذا ذكر الله ولم
يؤد فرائضه رد قوله؛ قال ابن عطية: وهذا قول يرده معتقد أهل الحق والسنة» ولا
يصح عن ابن عباس: والح أن العاصي التارك للفراتض إذا ذكر الله وقال كلاما

# PageV1P62
anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ط (khalata)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Mixing, blending, confusion of elements; one whose state is compounded of obedience and disobedience.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The one whose deeds are intermixed—neither wholly obedient nor wholly rebellious; a moral intermediary.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical mixture; Metaphorical: moral confusion of states (akhlaṭa al-amr).
- Root: س-ر-ف (sarafa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Transgression beyond bounds, excess, extravagance against oneself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Exceeding the limit in sin; the one who oppresses his own soul by persisting in disobedience.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: exceeding measure in spending; Metaphorical: exceeding the divine limits in conduct.
- Root: ر-ف-ق (rifq)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Gentleness, kindness, leniency in dealing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The prophetic manner of guidance—gentleness as a means to hearts, contrasted with harsh knowledge.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: softness in touch; Metaphorical: gentleness in spiritual instruction.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Ḥāl (Circumstantial Clause) — The phrase "مخلط مبتلى بالمخالفة" functions as a descriptive state (ḥāl) qualifying the subject, indicating a permanent attribute in the station of moral confusion.
translation:
I say—may Allah grant us success:

The second station, which is also the first [in the ascending order]: the station of the one confused, afflicted by opposition—may Allah protect us—yet he is not at all like the one extravagant against himself. This station is the basest of stations.

I have descended from the highest station to this one—I mean, the station of the one extravagant against himself.

So let us return, by ascending through these stations, to the station from which I began; and with it, Allah willing, I shall conclude. May Allah seal [my end] with it, by His grace and bounty. I have already explained in this descent the intent, in the language of knowledge, briefly. So let us now return to ascending, speaking on these stations at length and with abundance, in the language of the Sacred Law (lisān al-sharīʿah) and the language of Reality (lisān al-ḥaqīqah), and in the tongues of the people of spiritual states (arbāb al-aḥwāl)—for their tongue is more eloquent than the tongue of the people of discourse. [And let us speak] with gentleness (rifq) and with concealing of ecstatic finding (wajd). Everything I transmit is upon my responsibility from the side of the Sacred Law; and I follow in gentleness the master of the Path and the Imam of Reality, al-Junayd—may Allah be pleased with him—who said: "Begin with gentleness, and do not begin with knowledge; for gentleness familiarizes, while knowledge frightens." Because, as Abū Bakr said to ʿUmar: "O ʿUmar, knowledge is heavy, and despite its heaviness, it is bitter."

---

THE METHOD OF ASCENT (MANHAJ AL-TARUQQĪ)

THE FIRST STATION
THE STATION OF THE ONE EXTRAVAGANT AGAINST HIMSELF

The station of one extravagant against himself who has clung to nothing but the word of Divine Unity (kalimat al-tawḥīd)—such a one is feared for [his end]; except that the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah) is that no one among the people of the Qiblah is declared an unbeliever (kāfir) for a sin. And it is obligatory upon us to maintain with him a state such that if we weighed it against the state of an unbeliever, we would perceive a distinction between the two. That is the love for Allah's sake (al-ḥubb fī Allāh), which is an individual obligation (farḍ ʿayn). And you should know that Allah does not accept from the unbeliever either supererogatory (ṣarf) or obligatory (ʿadā) [deeds]—unlike this one [the sinner]; for his sin, however great, does not expel him from Islam. And every atom of good that this one performs, Allah accepts from him; because whoever guards against shirk (ittaqā al-shirk), Allah accepts from him every act of obedience.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said in his Tafsīr: It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that when a servant mentions Allah but does not fulfill his obligatory duties, his words are rejected. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This is a saying rejected by the creed of the people of Truth and the Sunnah, and it is not authentically established from Ibn ʿAbbās. Rather, the disobedient one who abandons obligatory duties—if he mentions Allah and speaks good words, it is written for him and accepted from him; he has his good deeds [credited] and upon him are his evil deeds. And Allah—exalted—accepts from everyone who guards against shirk. Moreover, the good word (al-kalim al-ṭayyib) is itself a righteous deed. Thus ends the text of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah.

And in the Ṣaḥīḥ [al-Bukhārī]: "Whoever misses the ʿAṣr prayer, his deeds have been rendered void." Abū ʿUmar said: This [hadith] is [understood]...

# PageV1P64
anchors:
- Root: س-ر-ف (s-r-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Exceeding proper bounds; squandering; transgression beyond the mean (iʿtidāl).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Moral extravagance—violating the divine limit (ḥadd) in action, distinct from kufr (disbelief) which annuls all deeds.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: exceeding measure in spending; Metaphorical: exceeding in sin while retaining faith (īmān).
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ) — "If your sin grieves you..." (idhā asāʾatka...) marks a protasis-apodosis structure where the apodosis (fa-anta muʾmin) is the logical consequent, not a temporal sequence.
translation:
I say: This is the first station—the station of the one who is extravagant against his own soul. This is in accordance with the meaning of the other hadith: "As if he had lost his family and his wealth" {فَكَأَنَّمَا وَتَرَ أَهْلَهُ وَمَالَهُ}—not that his deed is annulled in other than that. I seek refuge with Allah from such an interpretation, for it is the doctrine of the Khawārij. Rather, only disbelief (kufr) annuls deeds.

He also said in a sixth hadith concerning ʿAbd Allāh: The Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah—and they are the people of jurisprudence (fiqh) and transmitted tradition (athar)—are agreed that no one is expelled from Islam by his sin, however great it may be. The people of innovation (ahl al-bidʿah) opposed them in this.

Then he transmitted by his chain of narration to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ—and Ibn al-Mubārak related it from Abū Umāmah—that a man asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "What is faith (īmān)?" He said: "If your sin grieves you and your good deed delights you, then you are a believer" {إِذَا أَسَاءَتْكَ سَيِّئَتُكَ وَسَرَّتْكَ حَسَنَتُكَ فَأَنْتَ مُؤْمِنٌ}.

Abū ʿUmar said: Would that I knew—why is testifying against someone of disbelief more fitting than testifying for him of faith? And Ibn al-ʿArabī said: Whoever plunges into lust and then reproaches his soul is fearful from one aspect and extravagant from another. And if he disobeys while assuming that he will be forgiven, he is deluded (maghrūr).

Likewise, if he seeks refuge with Allah while he is violating His sanctity (ḥurimah), how can he hope for His protection? Nevertheless, it behooves him to say: "O He in Whose hand is the dominion of all things, and Who grants protection and none can protect against Him—I seek refuge with You from the evil of my soul and from the evil of every creature You seize by its forelock. So grant me refuge." Perhaps he will be answered.

Let him also call to mind in this regard the saying of Tāj al-Dīn in his "Ḥikam": Whoever finds it strange that Allah should rescue him from his lust and bring him out of the existence of his heedlessness has deemed an divine power incapable: {وَكَانَ اللَّهُ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ مُقْتَدِرًا} [Al-Kahf: 45] {«وَكَانَ اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ مُقْتَدِرًا»}. And let the possessor of this station also call to mind the creed of the Ahl al-Ḥaqq that repentance (tawbah) from one sin while leaving another is sound. So let him say to himself: Perhaps Satan overcame me through the dominance of lust in some acts of disobedience—so I did not cast off the reins nor slacken the bridle, but rather I struggle against him in some acts of disobedience. Perhaps I shall overcome him, and my overcoming him in some matters will be an expiation (kaffārah) for some of my sins. Had he not conceived this, he would not conceive of the sinner (fāsiq) praying and fasting. And this is the state of every Muslim, for there is no Muslim who does not combine disobedience and obedience. There is no doubt that the extravagant one, when he is in this state, has departed from extravagance (isrāf). He has mingled with his evil deeds humility (inkisār) and supplication (duʿāʾ)—and all of this is righteous work (ʿamal ṣāliḥ). And this is the second station.
