بالنصيحة كتابا ما اطلع عليه إلا لله والسلام. فكتب إليه مالك: وصل لي كتابك»
فوقع مني موقع النصيحة في الإشفاق والأدب. متعك الله بالتقوى. وجزاك
بالنصيحة خيراء وأما ما ذكرت أني آكل الرقاق وألبس الرقيق وأحتجب وأجلس
على الوطاء؛ فتحن نفعل؛ علم الله ذلك؛ ونستغفر الله عز وجل؛ وقد قال الله ععز
وجل: اف سنح زيكةأثوله مج ليادر. الِبِيَ 4 [الأعراف: 32] الآية.

وإني لأعلم أن ترك ذلك خير من الدخول فيه؛ ولا تدعنا من كتابك؛ قلسنا
ندعك من كتابناء والسلام.

وفي "الموطا”: كان عمر رضي الله عنه يطرح له صاع من تمر فيأكل حتى

قال الباجي: ليس كل الزاهدين زهده في قلة الأكل: قد يكون في التوسط مع
الإقبال على العبادة» وقد يكون بالإنفاق وقلة الاحتكار؛ قال مالك: إن رجلا دخحل
على رجل له قدر وهو يأكل؛ فلم يعرض عليه أن يأكل معه؛ فعاب ذلك عليه؛ فقال:
إن في مستمعها في أمور

وقال أبو الدرداء رضي الله عنه: إن الله يؤتي الرجل العلم ولا يؤتيه الحللم»
ويؤتيه الحلم ولا يؤتيه العملم؛ وإن شداد ببن أوس"" ممن آنا الله العلم والحللم»
وسئل ابن وهب وابن القاسم عن قبالة مصر. فكلاهما قال: لا تجوز فقيل لهما:

(ا) شداد بن أوس بن ثابت الخزرجي الأنصاري أبو يعلى: صحابي» من الأمراء. ولاه عمر
إمارة حمص؛ ولما قثل عثمان اعتزل؛ وعكف على العبادة. كان قصيا حليما حكيقاء قال
أبو الدرداء: لكل أمة فقيه؛ وفقيه هذه الامة شداد بن أوس.
توفي في القدس عن 75 سنة. وله في كتب الحديث 50 حديقً.

# PageV1P100
anchors:
- Root: ف-ت-ح (f-t-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To open, to grant access, to disclose; in divine context, the opening of a door of grace or provision.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine facilitation (fatḥ) of specific acts of worship or worldly means; a sign of divine favor and decree.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: opening a physical door; Metaphorical: God's granting of spiritual or practical opportunities (istiʿmāl majāzī).
- Root: ر-ق-ق (r-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Thinness, softness; fine clothing (raqīq) and thin bread (ruqāq); also servitude (riqq).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Material refinement or luxury; in ascetic discourse, a test of detachment from worldly comforts.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: thinness of fabric or food; Metaphorical: indulgence in ease, contrasted with zuhd (renunciation).
- Root: و-ط-ء (w-ṭ-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To tread, to sit upon; a cushion or soft seating (wiṭāʾ).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Physical comfort as a marker of social status; in Kalam, a neutral worldly matter subject to intention.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: sitting surface; Metaphorical: adopting the trappings of authority or ease.
- Root: ح-ج-ب (ḥ-j-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To veil, to screen; a doorkeeper (ḥājib) who restricts access.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In divine attributes, the veil of majesty; in human conduct, a barrier between the scholar and the people, often criticized as pride.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical screening; Metaphorical: spiritual or social separation from the community.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — In the phrase "وكلانا على خير" (and both of us are upon good), the conjunction coordinates two subjects with a shared predicate, requiring balanced syntactic parallelism; also, the conditional "إن شاء الله" (if God wills) functions as a parenthetical qualifier (iʿtirāḍ) that does not disrupt the main clause's grammatical structure.
translation:
I say — and in this section I convey the conduct of the rightly guided, may God be pleased with them — that one man was opened a door in prayer, and another was opened a door in charity but not in fasting. And you have already known that spreading knowledge and teaching it is among the most excellent acts of righteousness (al-birr). I have been content with what God has opened for me and apportioned to me thereof. And I do not deem that which I am upon to be less than that which you are upon of worship; and both of us are upon good, if God wills.

And Yaḥyā ibn Yazīd also wrote to Mālik [ibn Anas]: "It has reached me that you wear fine garments (al-raqīq), eat thin bread (al-ruqāq), sit upon soft cushions (al-wiṭāʾ), and have a doorkeeper (ḥājib) at your gate — while you have taken the seat of knowledge, and the people have taken you as an imam and are pleased with your word. So fear God, O Mālik, and adhere to humility. I have written this to you as sincere counsel (naṣīḥah), a letter which none but God has seen. And peace." So Mālik wrote back to him: "Your letter reached me, and it fell from me in the position of sincere counsel, in compassion and propriety. May God benefit you with piety, and reward you well for your counsel. As for what you mentioned — that I eat thin bread, wear fine garments, screen myself with a doorkeeper, and sit upon soft cushions — indeed we do this; God knows that, and we seek forgiveness from God, Mighty and Majestic. For God, Mighty and Majestic, has said: {«قُلْ مَنْ حَرَّمَ زِينَةَ اللَّهِ الَّتِي أَخْرَجَ لِعِبَادِهِ وَالطَّيِّبَاتِ مِنَ الرِّزْقِ»} [Al-Aʿrāf: 32] — the verse. And I know that abandoning this is better than entering into it. Do not withhold your letters from us, for we shall not withhold our letters from you. And peace."

And in the Muwaṭṭaʾ: ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, used to have a ṣāʿ of dates thrown before him, and he would eat until...

Al-Bājī said: Not every ascetic (zāhid) has his asceticism in the scarcity of eating; it may be in moderation (tawassuṭ) alongside devotion to worship, and it may be in spending [in charity] and refraining from hoarding (iḥtikār). Mālik said: A man entered upon another man who had food before him and was eating, and he did not invite him to eat with him; so he [the visitor] disapproved of that against him. He said: "Indeed, in its hearing [there is a lesson] in such matters."

And Abū al-Dardāʾ, may God be pleased with him, said: "God gives a man knowledge but does not give him forbearance (ḥilm), and gives him forbearance but does not give him knowledge." And Shaddād ibn Aws — may God be pleased with him — was among those to whom God gave both knowledge and forbearance. And Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qāsim were asked about the tax-farming of Egypt (qibālat Miṣr), and both said: "It is not permissible." So it was said to them: [What is the proof?] — and the discussion continues in the following section.

# PageV1P102
anchors:
- Root: ق-ب-ل (q-b-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To receive, accept, meet face-to-face; acceptance with volition and approbation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Acceptance of that which is lawful (ḥalāl) versus that which is tainted by suspicion (shubhah); theological nuance of permissibility (ibāḥah) versus prohibition (taḥrīm).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical reception; metaphorical (majāz) — acceptance of authority or judgment, as in "accepting" a legal opinion.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs conditional clauses (e.g., "if it were not for this...") and exceptions ("except that...") to delineate legal boundaries; parsing requires attention to the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) and the excepted particle (illā).
translation:
I say — may Allah guide us and you. Know that the scholars have differed concerning the acceptance of gifts from rulers and their presents, and concerning attendance upon them. The basis of this is what has been transmitted from Mālik and his companions.

Ashhab used to accept gifts from rulers. Ibn al-Qāsim said to him: "Do you do what Ashhab does?" And he accepted the congregational mosque [gifts]. Ibn Wahb said: "Give us a ruling like Ashhab's, and we permit him to innovate in our mosque." Ashhab was asked about that, and he forbade it. It was said to him: "You yourself innovate in it?" He replied: "Shall I then bear the burden for myself and for you as well?"

Ibn Abī Zayd said in his Nawādir, in the chapter concerning the oppression of rulers after they have introduced injustice: Mālik said: "Do not accept the wealth of oppressors, whether they be rulers or not rulers, [for] they have taken wealth without right." It was said to him: "Then you would leave your family and your children to be destroyed by your sins?" He said: "And Hārūn [al-Rashīd] granted him three thousand [dirhams]." A man of the ascetics said to him: "O Abā ʿAbdillāh — three thousand dirhams you take from this man?!" As if he deemed it excessive. Mālik said: "When the amount is such that if a just imam had given it, and he had been equitable to the people of probity (ahl al-murūʾah), it would not be tainted by suspicion — I see no harm in it. I only dislike the excessive amount which is not likely that its possessor deserves it."

It was said to al-Fuḍayl: "Sufyān accepts the gifts of the Sultan?" Al-Fuḍayl said: "He takes nothing but what is less than his due." Then he [Sufyān] was alone with him and admonished him. Sufyān said: "O Abā ʿAlī — if I am not among the righteous, verily I love the righteous."

In sum, the scholars have their purposes, as has preceded: either increase of knowledge, or diminution of scrupulousness (waraʿ) if there be no reward [in it]; otherwise there is no sin. It was said to Mālik: "You abandon the congregation and the Friday prayer; but when the Sultan invites you, you hasten to him?!" He said: "O my son, if I did not do this, you would not see in this town a single Sunnah."

My master Ibn Sirāj — may Allah have mercy on him — used to relate to us concerning the righteous al-Zayyāt of Balash, that a certain chief among our Naṣrid kings had a [gift] in his hand. This chief used to come to the circle of the aforementioned Shaykh, and the Shaykh would move aside for him and welcome him. Some of the students felt resentment at that. While that student was coming from a village with a garment of silk in his hand, a policeman seized it from him. The Shaykh came, and he complained to him. The Shaykh ordered a muezzin to go to the chief. It was not long before the chief came as was his custom, and the Shaykh moved aside for him and sat [with him]. Then after the session concluded, and the chief wished to rise, he said to the Shaykh: "You sent for me concerning this?" And he brought out the silk. He said: "Yes, it is for this student." The chief said to the student: "Take, O my beloved, your garment, and depart." Then the Shaykh stood and said to that student: "O you with the defect — it is for the likes of this that such moving aside is done."

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "Whoever is deprived of his share of gentleness (rifq) is deprived of his share of goodness." Among the names of the Prophet — may Allah bless him and grant him peace — is "the gentle one" (al-rafīq). This is the Messenger of Allah — may Allah bless him and grant him peace — and he is as he is, in what does not cease of reports.

ʿĀʾishah — may Allah be pleased with her — said: "I saw the Abyssinians playing in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah — may Allah bless him and grant him peace." She said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, look at them.' He stood me behind him..." — the ḥadīth. And the other ḥadīth: "Two young girls were singing, and Abū Bakr rebuked them, saying: 'A flute of Satan at the Messenger of Allah — may Allah bless him and grant him peace?!' The Messenger of Allah — may Allah bless him and grant him peace — turned to him and said: 'Leave them, O Abā Bakr, for it is the day of ʿĪd.'"

Ibn Baṭṭāl said: "Abū Bakr disapproved of excessive singing and going out to vocal ornamentation (taṭrīb), and therefore he likened it to the flute. Al-Bukhārī responded to him, saying: 'Chapter: Striking the duff [frame drum].'"

Ibn Baṭṭāl said: "In it [is evidence for] the imam and the scholar attending the wedding feast, even if there be in it play and amusement and the like."

Abū ʿUmar said: "In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī: al-Rubayyiʿ said: 'The Prophet — may Allah bless him and grant him peace — came and entered upon me, and sat on my bed; and I had two young girls striking the duff...'" — the ḥadīth.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "Singing is not forbidden, because the Prophet — may Allah bless him and grant him peace — heard it in his house and in the house of others. What has occurred in the Samāʿ of Aṣbagh of disapproval of a person of dignity (dhū al-hayʾah) attending it is corrupt, because the Prophet — may Allah bless him and grant him peace — attended the striking of the duff, and it is not valid that a person of dignity be greater than the Prophet — may Allah bless him and grant him peace." Thus Ibn al-ʿArabī stated. What is in the Samāʿ of Aṣbagh is that singing is only for women specifically, with the duff and the tambourine, or with the remembrance of Allah, or glorification (tasbīḥ), or praise (taḥmīd) upon what guidance [dictates], or with light rajaz poetry, without anything objectionable and without prolongation. Ibn Rushd: "There is no difference between men and women."

ʿIyāḍ transmitted from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam, who said: "My father, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ibn Bukayr..."

### | الصفحة 102

00 من تفي المقاع اثالث مقامالنوفاء
وجماعة من أصحابهم في منزل يوسف بن عمرو في صنيع عرس لهم وكان ثم
الهو ودف؛ فما أنكره واحد منهم.

وعن عكرمة قال: لما خن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما بنيه أرسلني؛ فدعوت
اللعايين؛ فلعبواء فأعطاهم ابن عباس أربعة دراهم. قال أبو عمر في "تمهيده': ما منع
النفسه وعيته يستوي قليله وكثيره؛ إلا أن يكون مضطرًا إليه؛ فيستوي أيضًاء كما قاله
في "الموطا": للمضطر أن يأكل الميتة ويشبع ويتزود.

وانظر تعقب ابن رشد على أصبغ: اختصاص ذلك بالنساء. وكذا تعقب
ابن العربي: كراهة حضوره ذو الهيئة: وما عقب أحد كون ذلك بذكر لله وا
والتحميد. والمذهب أيضًا متفق أن الافتخار عند السيق والانتماء للقبيلة جائز
وكونه بذكر الله أحسن. وقال أبو عمر في "استذكاره' في قول بلالة

ألاليت شعري... اليست

قال أبو عمر: فيه تمشل الصالحين بالشعر؛ ودليل على جواز إنشاده ورفع
العقيرة بهه وهو الغناء الذي يسمى غناء الركبان وغناء العرب. والعقيرة: الصوت»
وقد قال عز الدين بن عبد السلام في "قواعده”: من يغلب عليه هوى مباح كمن
يعشق زوجته أو سريته: فهذا يهيجه السماع؛ ويؤثر فيه آثار الشوق وخوف الفراق
ورجاء الثلاقيء فسماع هذا لا بأس بهد

فانظر إذا كان هذا كله مباحا على البراءة الأصلية؛ وأجمعوا أن المباح قد يصير
مكرمة بالنية؛ فمباح بمياح؛ ينبغي أن يتحرى منهما ما يتخلى به من هواجس نفسه
الردية وأحاديثها الدنية. فعوض ما ينزل السماع على ما يجب ينزله على حال نفسه
في معاملة ربه؛ وقد تقدم ما حكاه الشاطبي عن الإمام الذي شكاء قومه لعمر رضي الله
عنه؛ قالوا له: إنه إذا فرغ من صلاته تغنى؛ فقال له عمر: أوتتمجن في عبادتك؟ فلما
أنشده الأبيات قال له عمر: على هذا فليغن من غنى. وهذا هو المقام الرابع.

(!) هو عكرمة مولى ابن عباس؛ العامة الحافظ المقسرء أب عبد لله القرشي مولاهم؛ المدنيء
البريري الأصل؛ تابعي جليل: توفي سنة 105ه (انظر السير 15/6: 12/5).

### | الصفحة 103

المقام الرايع

درء الأخس بالخسيس

بهذا القصد يصير مكرمة بالنسبة للمقام الثالث؛ تقل القشيري في "رسالته":
أفضل أوقاتك وقت تسلم فيه من هواجس نفسك ويسلم الناس فيه من سوء ظنك.

وقال تاج الدين في "حكمه": ريما وردت عليك الأنوار؛ فوجدت القلب
محشًا بصور الآثارء فارتحلت من حيث نزلت؛ فرغ قلبك من الأغيار تملاء
بالمعارف والأسرار.

ومن كلام سيدي أحمد الزيات من شيوخ شيوخنا: خذ حظوظك من حيث
الأمرء ولا تأخذها من حيث هواك وغاية الطاعة أن توافق أمر مولاك وقد أمرك
بالرفق بنفسك: فإن كلفتها خيف عليك لدخول هواك ونحذ المباح كرسيًا
اللاستراحة عليه؛ إذ لا تزال حمولة التكليف على ظهر العبد: فإذا كل وضعها على
ذلك الكرسي فليا ليستريح وبرد النفس؛ ثم يرجع لحمولة التكليف.

.يبفى النظر في أي المباحات يكون أولى لتجميم النفس؛ فيقول العلماء: بمشل
المزاح؛ وقالت طائفة كثيرة منهم: وبالشطرنج؛ قال ابن عرفة: علق مالك رد الشهاه
بها على الإدمان لا المرة بعد المرة؛ لأنه لا يسلم الانسان من يسير لهو.

قال أبو عمر: هذا كله يدلك على أن اللعب بها ليس بمحرم لنفسه وعيته إذا
الم يقامر به وتسترء لأنه لو كان حراما لاستوى قلبله وكثيره في التحريم؛ إذ
اليس بمضطر إليه؛ ولا مما لا بتفك عنه؛ فبعفى عن اليسير منه. قال: وممن أجاز
اللعب بالشطرنج سعيد بن المسيب» وسعيد بسن جيير”''؛ ومحمد بسن سيرينء

# PageV1P104
anchors:
- Root: خ-س-س (kh-s-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Base, lowly, contemptible; that which is mean in kind or degree.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The lower faculty or pursuit, contrasted with the noble (sharīf) in the scale of religious ends.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: inferiority of substance; metaphorical: the permissible (mubāḥ) as a lesser means to preserve the higher aim of worship.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-bayān (Appositional explicative) — The phrase "the fourth station" explicates the preceding "warding off the base with the baser," showing the station's definitional role.
translation:
I say: Know that the permissibility of these diversions rests upon the original principle of innocence (al-barāʾah al-aṣliyyah). A group of the Companions — may God be pleased with them — were present at a wedding feast in the house of Yūsuf ibn ʿAmr, wherein there was play and drumming, and not one of them disapproved of it.

It is related from ʿIkrimah — the freed slave of Ibn ʿAbbās, the ḥāfiẓ, the mufassir, Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Qurashī, of Berber origin, a noble Tābiʿī who died in 105 AH — who said: When Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, married off his sons, he sent me; so I summoned the singers, and they sang, and Ibn ʿAbbās gave them four dirhams.

Abū ʿUmar said in his "Tamhīd": Nothing prevents the permissibility of that which is not intrinsically forbidden, whether little or much, except that one be compelled to it; then it becomes equal [in permissibility], as he stated in the "Muwaṭṭaʾ": The one compelled may eat carrion, satiate himself, and take provisions.

Consider the critique of Ibn Rushd upon Aṣbagh: that this [permissibility] is specific to women. Likewise, the critique of Ibn al-ʿArabī: the disapproval of the presence of a man of dignified appearance [at such gatherings]. And none critiqued the notion that this be accompanied by the remembrance of God and praise of Him. The school (al-madhhab) is also agreed that boasting at weddings and affiliation to one's tribe is permissible, and that doing so with the remembrance of God is more excellent.

Abū ʿUmar said in his "Istidhkār" regarding the verse of Bilāl:

"Would that I knew... is it not..." — 

Abū ʿUmar said: In this is the emulation of the righteous through poetry, and evidence for the permissibility of reciting it and raising the voice with it — and this is the singing called the singing of riders (ghināʾ al-rukbān) and the singing of the Arabs. Al-ʿAqīrah is the voice.

Indeed, ʿIzz al-Dīn ibn ʿAbd al-Salām said in his "Qawāʿid": Whoever is overcome by a permissible passion — such as one who loves his wife or his concubine — this one is stirred by listening (al-samāʿ), and it affects him with the traces of longing, fear of separation, and hope of reunion. So listening for such a one is not objectionable.

So consider: if all this is permissible upon the original principle of innocence, and they are agreed that the permissible may become a merit (makrumah) through intention, then the permissible is [still] permissible. One ought to seek from among these [permissible things] that which purges oneself of its base whisperings (hawājis) and vile inner discourses. Thus, instead of letting listening descend upon what is obligatory, let it descend upon the state of one's soul in its dealing with its Lord. Already mentioned is what al-Shāṭibī related about the imam whom his people complained of to ʿUmar — may God be pleased with him — saying: "When he finishes his prayer, he sings." ʿUmar said to him: "Do you jest in your worship?" When he recited the verses to him, ʿUmar said: "Upon this, let him sing who sings." And this is the fourth station.

---

**The Fourth Station: Warding Off the Base with the Baser**

With this intention, [the permissible] becomes a merit relative to the third station. Al-Qushayrī said in his "Risālah": The most excellent of your times is a time in which you are safe from the whisperings of your soul, and the people are safe from your ill opinion of them.

Tāj al-Dīn said in his "Ḥikam": Perhaps the lights descend upon you, and you find the heart stuffed with the forms of [worldly] traces; so they depart from where they alighted. Empty your heart of other-than-God (al-aghyār), and it will be filled with gnoses (maʿārif) and secrets.

From the sayings of my master Aḥmad al-Zayyāt, one of the teachers of our teachers: Take your shares from where the command [of God] dictates, and do not take them from where your caprice dictates. The utmost of obedience is to conform to the command of your Master — and He has commanded you to be gentle with yourself. For if you burden it [beyond capacity], you are to be feared for it, due to the entry of caprice. And treat the permissible as a chair upon which to rest; for the load of obligation (ḥumūlat al-taklīf) never leaves the back of the servant. So when he tires, let him place it upon that chair to rest and cool his soul; then return to the load of obligation.

It remains to consider which of the permissible things is most fitting for the refreshment of the soul. The scholars say: such as jesting (muzāḥ). And a large group of them said: and chess. Ibn ʿArafah said: Mālik conditioned the rejection of testimony upon addiction to chess, not upon playing it once in a while — because a person is not free from a little diversion.

Abū ʿUmar said: All this indicates to you that playing it is not forbidden in itself, provided one does not gamble with it or use it to waste [obligations] — for were it forbidden, its little and much would be equal in prohibition, since it is neither something one is compelled to nor something one cannot abstain from; so its little is pardoned. He said: Among those who permitted playing chess are Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr — the Kūfan, the Tābiʿī, one of the most learned of them, trustworthy, devout, a jurist, virtuous, scrupulous, who died in 95 AH — and Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn.

# PageV1P105
anchors:
- Root: و-ق-ي (wa-qā-ya)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Protection, guarding against harm; the act of warding off danger through vigilance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Taqwā as the safeguarding of the soul from spiritual ruin by adhering to divine commands.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical shielding; Metaphorical: the scholar's meticulous care in preserving and transmitting ḥadīth.
- Root: ح-د-ث (ḥ-d-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To narrate, to report an event; ḥadīth as the spoken conveyance of prophetic tradition.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The origination (ḥudūth) of speech; in transmission, the act of bringing forth knowledge from memory.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: new occurrence; Metaphorical: the living chain (isnād) that renews the prophetic past.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The listing of proper names in sequence without explicit conjunctions, each serving as a distinct link in the chain of transmission, requires the reader to parse each as an independent subject of the implicit verb "narrated."
translation:
I say — may Allah guide us and you to the straight path:

Know that the scholars of the past — may Allah be pleased with them — were exceedingly cautious in the matter of narrating ḥadīth, for they understood that they bore the trust of the prophetic legacy. Among those who exemplified this scrupulousness were Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, his son Hishām, Sulaymān ibn Yasār, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Abū Wāʾil, ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit, Sulaymān ibn Mihrān al-Aʿmash, Ḥuṣayn ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and others.

It is reported that Ibn ʿAbbās — may Allah be pleased with him — said to one of his students: "Look how you narrate from me, for you have indeed preserved from me many a ḥadīth." And when Ibn ʿAbbās was stricken with blindness, and the people of Kūfah would come to him asking questions, he would say: "Do you ask me while among you is Ibn Umm al-Daḥmāʾ?" — meaning Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

Now, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr went out with ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ashʿath against ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. When Ibn al-Ashʿath was defeated, Saʿīd fled to Mecca, where its governor Khālid al-Qasrī seized him and sent him to al-Ḥajjāj, who put him to death. He had not yet completed fifty years of age. Imam Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said concerning him: "Al-Ḥajjāj killed Saʿīd, yet there is no one on the face of the earth who is not in need of his knowledge."

As for the biographical notices of those mentioned:

(1) Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Hudayr al-Taymī al-Madanī — the ḥāfiẓ. He narrated from his father, ʿĀʾishah, Abū Hurayrah, Abū Qatādah, Abū Ayyūb, and Jābir. From him narrated Shuʿbah, Mālik, and the two Sufyāns. He was a pious imam. He died in the year 131 AH.

(2) ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām — Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Qurashī al-Asadī. He heard from his father, ʿĀʾishah, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar. From him narrated al-Zuhrī and his son Hishām.

(3) Hishām ibn ʿUrwah (61–146 AH / 681–763 CE) — Hishām ibn ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām. A leading ḥāfiẓ, trustworthy. He was born and lived in Medina, then traveled to Kūfah and died in Baghdad. He narrated from his uncle ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, his father, and his wife Fāṭimah bint al-Mundhir ibn al-Zubayr. Shuʿbah and Mālik narrated from him, as did the two Sufyāns — Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah and Sufyān al-Thawrī — and others. Ibn ʿUmar — may Allah be pleased with them both — wiped over his head and prayed for him. Hishām has nearly 400 ḥadīths, and his narrations are found in the six canonical books and others.

(4) Sulaymān ibn Yasār (34–107 AH / 654–725 CE) — the freed slave of the Mother of the Believers Maymūnah bint al-Ḥārith al-Hilāliyyah. A Medinan, his father was Persian. He narrated from the Mothers of the Believers: Maymūnah bint al-Ḥārith, Umm Salamah, and ʿĀʾishah; and from Zayd ibn Thābit, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, Abū Hurayrah, and other prominent Companions and Followers. From him narrated ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dīnār, Ṣāliḥ ibn Kaysān, Muḥammad ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī, Makḥūl, Nāfiʿ the freed slave of Ibn ʿUmar, Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Anṣārī, and other Followers. Al-Nawawī said: "He was trustworthy, a noble scholar, a jurist, with abundant ḥadīth and abundant knowledge." He was one of the seven jurists of Medina.

(5) Abū Wāʾil (d. 99 AH / 718 CE) — Shaqīq ibn Salamah, Abū Wāʾil al-Asadī al-Kūfī. A mukhaḍram who reached the time of the Messenger of Allah — may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace — but did not see him; though it is said he did see him. A traditionist with abundant ḥadīth. The scholars unanimously affirmed his trustworthiness and knowledge. He narrated from ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, ʿĀʾishah, ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, and others. From him narrated ʿĀmir al-Shaʿbī, ʿĀṣim ibn Bahdalah, Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī, Sulaymān ibn Mihrān al-Aʿmash, Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir, and others. He was among the most knowledgeable of people concerning the ḥadīth of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd. The authors of the six books narrated from him. He died during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

# PageV1P107
anchors:
- Root: س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Auditory perception; the act of hearing with the ear, extended to attentive reception of speech.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the spiritual path, samāʿ denotes the disciplined listening to devotional recitation (dhikr) or poetry that stirs the heart toward God, distinct from mere sensory hearing.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) = acoustic hearing; metaphorical (majāz) = the soul's receptive compliance to divine address, as in {«سَمِعْنَا وَأَطَعْنَا»} (We hear and obey).
- Root: خ-ل-و (kh-l-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Solitude; emptiness of place or company; seclusion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Khalwah as the ascetic practice of withdrawing from creation to focus exclusively on worship and divine contemplation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = physical isolation; metaphorical = the heart's detachment from worldly concerns even amid crowds.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ wa-l-Jawāb) — The particle "law" (if) governs a protasis whose apodosis is often suppressed or implied, as in the author's conditional framing of the weak soul's need for samāʿ.
translation:
I say — and God grants success:

Know that the people of the spiritual path (al-ṣūfiyyah) hold that the attainment of this station is achieved by combining inner ease (irtiyāḥ) with steadfast adherence to the demands of servitude (ʿubūdiyyah), so that the soul does not slip away from the requirements of worship and thereby forget the very meaning of devotion (taʿabbud). Thus, they gather their souls together through communal engagement in certain vocal acts of remembrance (dhikr) and audition (samāʿ) — concerning which the author of *al-Mudawwanah* said: "I disapprove of hiring oneself out to teach singing (nawḥ)."

Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ said: "This refers to the chanting of the Sufis, known as *taghyīr* (emotional alteration)." It has already been established that the object of disapproval is the *hiring* for such performance, not the *listening* to it.

The author of *al-Risālah* said: "Absolute solitude (infirād) can only be sustained by the spiritually strong; for those like us, communal gathering is more beneficial — so that each of us may look upon the other (for mutual support)."

They also explicitly stated — may God be pleased with them — that they never relied upon this kind of gathering as their fundamental support; rather, it is a state they deem undesirable and a form of idleness relative to their true goal. And whenever the soul takes its share from such audition, the listener returns to the continuation of his seclusion (khalwah) and the repose of his worship.

Ibn al-Bannāʾ — may God have mercy on him — said, with reference to the spiritual master (al-shaykh) and the office of shaykhdom:

> "The folk are but travelers to the Holy Presence, and we are their followers."

[Footnote: Ibn al-Bannāʾ is Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān al-Azdī al-Marrākushī (654–721 AH / 1256–1334 CE), known as Ibn al-Bannāʾ because his father was a builder. He was a Mālikī jurist, uṣūlī, theologian, astronomer, mathematician, and man of letters; he excelled in the sciences and was renowned for righteousness and piety. He was beloved among scholars and saints. Among those who transmitted from him were Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm Ibn al-Ḥājj, Abū Zayd al-Bajāʾī, and Abū Jaʿfar ibn Ṣafwān. His works include: *al-Iqtiḍāb*, *al-Taqrīb li-l-Ṭālib al-Labīb* (a gloss on *al-Kashshāf*), *Muntahā al-Sūl fī ʿIlm al-Uṣūl*, *Tanbīh al-Fuhūm ʿalā Idrāk al-ʿUlūm*, a commentary on *Tanqīḥ al-Fuṣūl* of al-Qarāfī, *Marāsim al-Ṭarīqah fī ʿIlm al-Ḥaqīqah*, *al-Farrān* (an epitome on arithmetic), *al-Kulliyyāt fī ʿIlm al-Manṭiq*, *al-Jadal*, *Kulliyyāt fī al-ʿArabiyyah*, *al-Rawḍ al-Murīʿ fī Ṣināʿat al-Badīʿ*, *al-Makāyīl al-Sharʿiyyah*, *al-Misāḥāt*, *Minhāj al-Ṭālib fī Taʿdīl al-Kawākib*, and a treatise on the principal and subsidiary directions (jihāt).]

[Footnote: See *al-Baḥr al-Madīd* 1/113 and *Īqāẓ al-Himam* 1/206. It is also cited in *Laṭāʾif al-Minan*: "Whoever has no master to connect him to the chain of followers and to unveil to his heart the annihilation (fanāʾ), he is in this matter like one who has no father — nay, like one who has no son. For if he possesses a light, the prevailing influence of the (spiritual) state overcomes him; and what dominates him is his standing with what comes to him from God — the discipline of training and refinement has not satisfied him, nor has the gain of upbringing and drilling sufficed him."]

---

Then I say — and upon God I rely:

The fourth station of ascent: it is the station of the weak one, who is overpowered by the sun (of spiritual reality).

They (the Sufis) divided the ranks of wayfarers into degrees: between a walker, a rider, and one who is carried.

And when the bodies grew weary, one of them said: "O camel-driver of the herds — O singer of the caravan — sing for the sake of the men!"

And another said: "None needs the audition (samāʿ) except the brother of weakness, short of reach."

And another said: "It is a path stretched out among them, traversed by the finder and the destitute alike. No word may deviate from it, nor any distraction, nor any 'lā ilāha' (negation) without 'illā Allāh' (affirmation)."

And the novices (aḥdāth) are prevented from attending it — for if that occurs, it is a defect in its manifestation.

They also commanded the closing of doors during it — and that is only for the sake of those veiled (from true perception).

Nor was it (the audition) ever a condition, nor a means of approach (wasīlah) upon which they relied.

Nor was communal gathering held for its sake, nor was there any connection to it in their firm resolve.

Ibn al-Bannāʾ — may God have mercy on him — said: "It is by this (principle) that seekers of knowledge ought to gather, and (likewise) for the sake of admonition (tashnīʿ)."

I had already explained this meaning in a treatise issued from me — namely, that most of the scholars of God's judgments disapproved of the innovation of Sufi lodges (zawāyā), and held that the endowments (awqāf) upon them were diverted from their proper purpose. Among them were those who sided with the Sufis and approved of establishing such lodges, holding that in gathering therein there is a collective blessing derived from the inner states of the past masters — because of the repentance (tawbah) that arises therein and the tenderness of heart (riqqah) that attaches to it.

The report has come: "Seek supplication at moments of tenderness, for it is a mercy." [Footnote: Recorded by al-Daylamī via Ibn Shāhīn, as in *al-Madāwī* of al-Khumārī (2/37), and by al-Qudāʿī (1/402, no. 692). Al-Munāwī said (2/16): "In it is ʿUmar ibn Aḥmad Abū Ḥafṣ ibn Shāhīn — al-Dhahabī said that al-Dāraquṭnī declared: 'He errs but is trustworthy'; and Shabābah ibn Sawwār — al-Kāshif states: 'He is a Murjiʾ, but ṣadūq (truthful).'"]

And the folk (the Sufis) explicitly stated — may God be pleased with them — that they never made this gathering their reliance; rather, it is a state they deem undesirable and a form of idleness relative to their true goal. And whenever the soul takes its share from that, the listener returns to the continuation of his seclusion and the repose of his worship.

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz — his age was one hundred years.

# PageV1P109
anchors:
- Root: ع-ز-ل (ʿ-z-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Separation, withdrawal, setting apart from others; al-ʿazl is the act of isolating oneself from a group.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the spiritual path, ʿuzlah signifies the soul's disengagement from worldly attachments to attain divine proximity (qurb), a prerequisite for the station of uns (intimate familiarity with God).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) meaning is physical separation; metaphorical (majāz) usage denotes the heart's detachment from created things while the body remains among them.
- Root: خ-ل-و (kh-l-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Emptiness, solitude; a place devoid of others; khalwah is the state of being alone.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Khalwah is the higher stage of ʿuzlah—the soul's complete absorption in divine contemplation (mushāhadah), where the seeker (murīd) attains true intimacy (uns) with God.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical emptiness of a place; metaphorical: the heart's emptiness of all thoughts save God.
- Root: س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Hearing, listening; samāʿ in the Sufi lexicon refers to auditory spiritual audition (often with music or chant).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Samāʿ is a trial (fitnah) for the seeker unless it leads to increased fear of God and remembrance; its permissibility depends on intention and context.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: the physical act of hearing; metaphorical: the heart's attentive listening to divine truths.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs conditional clauses (e.g., "if he is from the common folk...") and exceptive phrases (e.g., "unless it be for...") to delineate precise legal and spiritual rulings, requiring careful parsing of protasis and apodosis.
translation:
I say—may God guide us and you to the straight path:

Know that the people of this path (al-qawm) have made the conduct of travel (ādāb al-safar) a station of their spiritual striving (mujāhadah), just as they have made seclusion (ʿuzlah) and solitude (khalwah) pillars of their way. For they said: "The one who travels for the sake of God, leaving behind his homeland and his habits, is like the one who secludes himself from creation—both are exercises in breaking the soul's attachments."

As for the one who enters the spiritual retreats (zawāyā) with this description—being righteous (ṣāliḥ) and wholly devoted (mutajarrid)—then he has undertaken the covenant (ʿuhdah) of those whose belief in their path is obligatory, as has been established by al-Shāṭibī, al-Subkī, and ʿIzz al-Dīn, among others.

But as for the one who enters them from among the common folk (al-ʿāmmah), it has already been stated that the legal ruling (fatwā) permits the common people to engage in matters that are neither beneficial nor harmful, so long as they do not abandon an obligatory act of obedience for its sake, nor consider it an act of worship. Consider then, if the matter is one whose permissibility or prohibition is disputed, and there is no accountability (ḥisbah) upon such people—how much more so is it permissible? For no one is held to account over such persons; rather, by holding them to account, these self-appointed censors establish for themselves a station. For necessarily, they are better than those who are worse than them, upon whom no accountability is placed. So if this censor (muḥtasib) claims a relative merit and says: "A night spent with the rebuker (al-muzammir) is better than a night with these people," then it is more fitting that they limit themselves to a relative merit. And they say: "Never has it been thus."

My master Ibn Sirāj—may God have mercy on him—used to say: "This is the innovation of misguidance (bidʿat al-ḍalāl)—to judge the permissible (mubāḥ) as either disliked (makrūh) or recommended (mustaḥabb)." And the Sufis say: "Whoever mixes for you a cup of remembrance (al-dhikr)..." And they say: "Every knower (ʿārif) who does not annihilate his own existence before his disciple (murīd), nor strip himself of the traces of his human attributes, no disciple will ever reach God at his hands."

And as for the one who comes to these retreats from among the students of sacred knowledge (ṭullāb al-ʿilm) but is not righteous nor wholly devoted, then the way of the censuring scholars (al-mutakarrirīn) of God's rulings is to disavow him. And on the way of the people (al-qawm), they do not undertake his covenant, nor do they include him in their ranks—especially if his intention is only to hear the spiritual audition (al-samāʿ). For the Imam, the leader, the model (al-qudwah) al-Junayd said: "The audition is a trial (fitnah) for the one who seeks it." However, if the audition coincides with a gathering of spiritual presence (ḥuḍūr) like attending a Friday prayer or similar, then there is no harm in it, as has come from Saḥnūn and others. For this was its subject during the time of the Companions—may God be pleased with them.

And consider also: just as the Sufis have established a chapter on audition, they have also established a chapter on travel. It is said in "al-Risālah" (of al-Qushayrī): "Many of this sect chose travel."

For this reason, we have devoted a separate chapter to travel, because it is among the greatest of their concerns.

It is related that a jurist (faqīh) said to al-Kattānī: "Give me an exhortation." He said: "Strive to be a guest every night, and die only between two dwellings—a mosque and a grave." And Ruwaym was asked about the etiquette of travel; he said: "That his aspiration (himmah) not exceed his footstep, and wherever his heart stops, there is his dwelling."

It is said: A young man came to Abū ʿAlī al-Rūdhbārī, and when he wanted to leave, the Shaykh said: "The young men used not to gather without an appointment, nor part without consultation."

Know that the people (al-qawm) attached the rulings of travel to their spiritual striving (mujāhadah) and discipline of the soul (riyāḍah), when they brought it out of the realm of known things and carried it upon separation from familiar associations—so that they might live with God without attachment or intermediary. Thus they did not abandon any of their daily litanies (awrād) during their travels. And they said: "Legal concession (tarakhkhuṣ) is for the one whose travel is a necessity; but we have no occupation nor necessity in our travels upon us." Ibn al-Bannāʾ—may God have mercy on him—said:

*Their travels were a roaming through the lands,*
*A circle of the elders and the brethren,*
*Seeking the transmission of knowledge and traditions (āthār),*
*Or for reflection (iʿtibār),*
*Or for obscurity, or for seeking provision, or for the Messenger, or for God's sake.*
*And their travels were not for leisure, but rather they were for the sake of abandoning leisure.*

And he said:
*They disliked wasting their litanies,*
*How could they not, when they had come for increase?*

And likewise, they established a chapter on seclusion (ʿuzlah). ʿUmar—may God be pleased with him—said: "Take your share of seclusion." It is said in "al-Risālah": "Solitude (khalwah) is the choicest of the choicest people (ṣafwat al-ṣafwah), and seclusion (ʿuzlah) is among the signs of connection (wiṣlah)." The disciple (murīd) at the beginning of his state must have seclusion from his fellow beings; then at its end, he must have solitude (khalwah) to realize his intimacy (uns) with God. And let him believe, by his withdrawal from creation, that he seeks the safety of people from his own evil—not his own safety from the evil of creation. For the first of these two divisions is the result of deeming himself small (istiṣghār nafsihi); the second is the witnessing of his own superiority over creation. Whoever deems himself small is humble (mutawāḍiʿ); and whoever sees for himself any merit over another is arrogant (mutakabbir).

It is related that one of the monks was seen, and it was said to him: "Are you a monk?" He said: "No, I am a guard of a dog. My soul (nafs) is a dog that bites creation; I have brought it out from among them so that they might be safe from it." Then he said in "al-Risālah": Indeed...

title_en: On the Need for the Soul's Recreation and the Permissibility of Light Diversion for the Righteous
arabic_text:
### | الصفحة 109

منهج اترقي/ المقا لايع درء الأعس بالخسيس نا
هذا كله للأقوياء. وأما لغيرهم فالاجتماع أنقع أن يعمل بعضهم على رؤية بعضء
ومع ذلك إنما هو عندهم تجميم؛ وبالجملة فقد قالوا: عامل البر وطالب العلم
كلاهما لا بد له أن يجمم نفسه. وورد في الأثر: طالب العلم وعامل البر كآكل
الطعام؛ إن أخذ القوت عصمه وإن أسرف أبشمه.

وقال علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه: سلوا هذه التفوس ساعة بعد ساعة؛
فإنها تصدأ كما يصدأ الحديد.

وكان ابن عباس يقول: إذا أفاض من عنده في الحديث بعد القرآن والتفسير:
أحمضوا إذا مللتم من الحديث والفقه: فخذوا في الشعر وأخبار العرب كالإبل إذا
ملت ما حلا رعت الحمض: وهو ما ملح منه.

وقال الزهري: هاتوا من أشعاركم؛ فإن الأذن مجاجة: وللنفس حمضة؛ أي:
تشتهي الشيء بعد الشيء كما تفعل الابل. وقال أبو الدردء: إني لاستجمم نفسي
ببعض اللهو؛ ليكون ذلك عونًا لي على الحق. عن علي رضي الله عنه: القلب إذا
أكره عمي.

وروى ابن المبارك: أن عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه كان يأخذ بهم في
العلمء فإذا ملوا أخذوا في غيره حتى يذكر الغراس.

وفال أبو عمر في حديث بيرحاء أن رسول اله و كان يأنبها ويشرب من ماء
فيها طيب؛ فقال فيها: لا تقيصة على فاضل في حبه الماء. وفيه إباحة دخول
الفضلاء للجنات طلبا للراحة والفرح والنظر إلى ما يسلي النفس وما يوجب شكر
الله تعالى على نعمه؛ وقال ابن مسعود: إن لهذ النفوس شهرة وإقبالا وإن لها نفورا
وإدباراء فخذوها عند شهرتها وإقبالهاء وذروها عند نفورها وإدبارها. وقال
أبو حامد: الحاذق بالطب قد يعالج المجذوم باللحم مع حرارته؛ ويستبعده القاصر
في الطبء وإنما يبغي به أن يعيد ألا قوته إليه؛ ليحتمل المعالجة بالضد. والحاذق
ِبالشطرنج ينزل عن الرخم والفرس مجائا؛ ليتوصل به إلى الغلية: والضعيف البصيرة
قد يضحك به ويتعجب منه؛ والخبير بالفتال قد يعمل الهزيمة ويولي العدو دبره
ويستجره إلى مضيق فيكر عليه؛ فكذلك سلوك طريق اله كله قتال مع العدو الشيطان
ومعالجة للقلب: والبصير الموفق يقف فيها على لطائف من الحيل يستبعدها
الضعفاء.

# PageV1P110
anchors:
- Root: ج-م-م (j-m-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To rest, to grant respite; the act of refreshing oneself after exertion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The soul's need for periodic relief from sustained devotional rigor, akin to the body's need for sleep.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in reference to animals resting; metaphorical here for the spiritual self's recuperation.
- Root: ح-م-ض (ḥ-m-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sour or saline pasture (ḥamḍ) that camels graze after sweet herbage (khalā); a change of diet.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A metaphor for shifting intellectual focus to poetry and Arab lore when the heart tires of jurisprudence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Majāz (metaphor) — the soul's palate, like a camel's, craves variety to restore appetite for serious study.
- Root: ص-د-أ (ṣ-d-')
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Rust (ṣada') on iron; corrosion from disuse.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The heart's spiritual dullness when neglected, requiring the polish of remembrance and varied worship.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for metal; metaphorical for the soul's susceptibility to moral erosion.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The phrase "أي: تشتهي الشيء بعد الشيء" explicates the preceding metaphor, a common device in prophetic and scholarly discourse.
translation:
All of this [strict discipline] is for the strong. As for others, the more beneficial approach is that they work while observing one another's condition. Even so, for them it is merely recreation (tajmīm). In sum, they have said: The man of righteous deeds and the seeker of knowledge — both must necessarily grant their souls recreation. It is reported in the tradition (athar): "The seeker of knowledge and the man of righteous deeds are like one who eats food; if he takes the sustaining portion, it preserves him, but if he overindulges, it chokes him."

And ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, said: "Ask these souls [for exertion] hour after hour, for they rust just as iron rusts."

Ibn ʿAbbās used to say, when he had poured forth from his store of ḥadīth after [expounding] the Qurʾān and its interpretation: "Give them sour pasture (aḥmiḍū) when you tire of ḥadīth and jurisprudence — take up poetry and the reports of the Arabs, just as camels, when they tire of sweet herbage, graze on ḥamḍ — that which is saline."

Al-Zuhrī said: "Bring forth from your poetry, for the ear grows weary, and the soul has a craving for sourness (ḥamḍah)" — that is, it desires one thing after another, as camels do. Abū al-Dardāʾ said: "I grant my soul recreation with a measure of light diversion, so that it may be an aid to me in [pursuing] the truth." From ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him: "The heart, when compelled, goes blind."

Ibn al-Mubārak related that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, would engage them in knowledge; when they grew weary, they would turn to other matters until they mentioned [even] planting.

Abū ʿUmar said, in the ḥadīth of Bīr Ḥāʾ (the Well of Ḥāʾ), that the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, used to visit it and drink from its pleasant water, and he said concerning it: "No reproach falls upon the excellent man for his love of water." In this is the permissibility of the virtuous entering gardens seeking rest, joy, and the contemplation of what delights the soul and necessitates gratitude to God the Exalted for His blessings. Ibn Masʿūd said: "These souls have a craving and an inclination, and they have an aversion and a turning away. So take them at their craving and inclination, and leave them at their aversion and turning away."

Abū Ḥāmid said: The skilled physician may treat the leper with meat despite its heat, while the deficient in medicine deems this far-fetched — he only intends thereby to restore his strength, so that he may endure treatment by the opposite. The skilled chess player sacrifices the rook and the knight as a gift, to thereby attain victory; the weak-sighted one laughs at it and marvels. The expert in warfare may feign defeat, turn his back to the enemy, and lure him into a narrow pass, then wheel upon him. Likewise, traversing the path of God is entirely combat against the enemy, Satan, and treatment of the heart; the insightful and divinely aided one perceives therein subtle stratagems that the weak deem far-fetched.

title_en: On Gentleness in Spiritual Training and the Physician's Method
arabic_text:
### | الصفحة 110

154 منهج انوي المفاء الرلع: ددء الاعس بالضيس

ثم قال: وهذه حقاتق لا يعرفها إلا سماسرة العلماء دون الحشوية منهم؛ قال: ومن
الطائف الرياضة أن النفس إذا كانت لا تسخو بترك الرعونة رأشا أو ترك صفة أخرى
ولم تسمح بضدهاء فينبغي أن تنقل من خلق مذموم إلى مذموم آخر أخف منه؛ كالذي
يغسل الدم بالبول إذا كان الماء لا يزيل الدم. وكما أن الطييب لا يعائج العييل ما لم
يعرف أن العلة من حرارة أو ضدها أو يعرف درجتها من ضعيفة أو قوية: فإذا عرف
ذلك التفت إلى أحوال البدن والزمان وصناعة المريض وسنه وسائر أحواله. فكذلك
الشيخ الذي يطب تفوس المريدين ويعالج قلوب المسترشدين؛ ينبغي أن لا يهجم
عليهم بالتكاليف في فن مخصوص ما لم يعرف أخلافهم وأمراضهم: كما أن اليب
لو عالج جميع المرضى بعلاج واحد قثل أكثرهم؛ كذلك الشيخ لو أشار على المريدين
بنمط واحد من الرياضة أهلكهم وأمات قلوبهم؛ بل ينبغي أن ينظر في مرض المريد
وحاله وسته ومزاجه وما تحتمله نفسه؛ فيني على ذلك رياضته.

وتقدم قول صاحب كتاب "عوارف المعارف”: وما دام المريد لا يتخطى حريم
الرخصة فهو بخيرء ثم إذا يت يتدرج برفق إلى أوطان العزيمة. قال: وانقطع شاب
إلى الصوفية؛ وكان لأييه نعمة؛ وصحب أبا أحمد الغلانسي فريما كان يقع بيد
الشيخ شيء من الدراهم؛ فكان يشتري للشاب الحلوى: ويقول: هذا خرج من
الدنياء وتعود النعمة؛ فيجب أن يرفق به؛ وقد قال سيد الطريقة أبو القاسم الجنيد:
إذا لقيت المريد فابدأه بالرفق؛ ولا تبدأه بالعلم؛ فإن العلم يوحشه والرفق يؤنسه.
قال: وكل من هو أكمل وأوفر علما كان أكثر رفقًا بالمبتدئ السالك. وفي الصحيح:
كان رسول اله يتخولنا بالموعظة مخافة السآمة علينا. ونقل أبو عمر في
"تمهيده": أن عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه قال: أيها الناس؛ لا تبغضوا الله إلى
عباده؛ فقال قائل منهم: وكيف ذلك؟ قال: يكون الرجل إماما بالناس يصلي بهم فلا
يزال يطول عليهم حتى يبغض إليهم ما هم فيه.

وانظر وصية الخضر لموسى عليه السلام: يا طالب العلم: إن القائل أقل ملالة
من المستمع؛ فلا تمل جلساءك إذا حدثتهم؛ وأعرض عن الجهال؛ واحلم عن
السفهاء؛ فإن ذلك فعل الحكماء ورأي العلماء وإذا أسمعك الجاهل كلمة تغيظك
فأعرض عنه حلتماء وجانبه حزما؛ فإن ما بقي من جهله عليك وشتمه إياك أغيظ
وأكثر.

# PageV1P111
anchors:
- Root: ر-ف-ق (r-f-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Gentleness, kindness, leniency; the opposite of harshness (ʿunf). Also "companionship" (rifāq) and "provision" (rafīq).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the spiritual path, rifq is the prophetic virtue of gradual, compassionate guidance that preserves the novice's capacity, mirroring divine gentleness (rifq Allāh) in creation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: softness in handling objects or persons. Metaphorical: the method of the spiritual physician who treats souls according to their tolerance, not by rigid uniformity.
- Root: م-ر-ض (m-r-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sickness, disease; bodily ailment. Also "to be soft" (marīḍ) in the sense of weak.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Spiritual diseases (amrāḍ al-qulūb) — vices like pride, envy, and avarice — which require the physician of hearts to diagnose before prescribing.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical illness. Metaphorical: moral corruption of the soul, as in {«فِي قُلُوبِهِم مَّرَضٌ»} (Q 2:10).
- Sībawayh Rule: Condition-Clause (Jawāb al-Sharṭ) — The conditional "if... then" (fa-... in) structures the analogy between the physician's diagnosis and the shaykh's method, requiring the apodosis to be semantically parallel to the protasis.
translation:
Then he said: These are realities known only to the elite of the scholars (samāsirat al-ʿulamāʾ), not to the vulgar traditionalists (ḥashwiyyah) among them. He said: Among the subtleties of spiritual discipline (riyāḍah) is this: when the soul does not willingly abandon vanity (ruʿūnah) or another blameworthy trait, and does not yield its opposite, then one should transfer it from one blameworthy character trait to another that is lighter than it — like one who washes blood with urine when water does not remove the blood. And just as the physician does not treat the sick until he knows whether the ailment is from heat or its opposite, or knows its degree whether weak or strong — and when he knows that, he attends to the states of the body, the season, the patient's occupation, age, and all his other circumstances — so likewise the shaykh who treats the souls of disciples (murīdīn) and heals the hearts of seekers (mustarshidīn) should not rush upon them with obligations in a particular discipline until he knows their temperaments and their diseases. For if the physician treated all the sick with a single remedy, he would kill most of them. Likewise, if the shaykh prescribed to the disciples a single pattern of discipline, he would destroy them and kill their hearts. Rather, he should examine the disciple's disease, his state, his age, his constitution (mizāj), and what his soul can bear, and build his discipline upon that.

And the saying of the author of the book "ʿAwārif al-Maʿārif" has preceded: "As long as the disciple does not overstep the sanctuary of concession (rukhaṣ), he is in good state." Then, if he becomes strong, he should be gradually advanced with gentleness to the abodes of resolve (ʿazīmah). He said: A young man attached himself to the Sufis, and his father had wealth. He accompanied Abū Aḥmad al-Ghilānī, and sometimes some dirhams would fall into the shaykh's hand, so he would buy sweets for the young man and say: "This came from the world, and he is accustomed to comfort; so one must be gentle with him." And the master of the path, Abū al-Qāsim al-Junayd, said: "When you meet a disciple, begin with gentleness, and do not begin with knowledge; for knowledge makes him feel estranged (yūḥishuh), while gentleness makes him feel at home (yuʾnisuh)." He said: And whoever is more complete and more abundant in knowledge is more gentle with the beginner on the path. And in the Ṣaḥīḥ: The Messenger of Allah {ﷺ} used to space out his exhortations to us, fearing weariness (al-sāʾam) upon us. And Abū ʿUmar transmitted in his "Tamhīd" that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O people, do not make Allah hateful to His servants." Someone among them said: "How is that?" He said: "A man becomes an imam for the people, leading them in prayer, and he keeps prolonging it over them until he makes them hate what they are engaged in."

And consider the counsel of al-Khaḍir to Moses, peace be upon him: "O seeker of knowledge: verily the speaker is less prone to boredom than the listener. So do not weary your companions when you speak to them. Turn away from the ignorant, and be forbearing with the foolish; for that is the conduct of the wise and the opinion of the scholars. And when the ignorant makes you hear a word that angers you, turn away from him with clemency and avoid him with prudence; for what remains of his ignorance against you and his insulting of you is more angering and more abundant."

title_en: Section 83 — On the Impermissibility of Prolonging Prayer and the Obligation of Brevity for the Imam
arabic_text:
### | الصفحة 111

منهج اترقي/ المقا لايع درء الأعس بالخسيس كر

ومن "الموافقات” الربائي الذي يربي بصغار العلم قبل كباره. قال: وعمن
أبي رجاء العطاردي”' قال: قلت للزيير بن العوام: ما لي أراكم يا أصحاب
محمد فق من أخف الناس صلاة؟ قال: نبادر الوسواس مع أن التطويل مستحب»

وفي البخاري: أن رجلا قال: يا رسول الله إننا نتأخر عن الصلاة في الفجر
مما يطيل بنا فلان» قغنضب رسول الله يلو ما رأ
منه يومثذه ثم قال: "أها الناسء إن متكم متفرين» فمن أم الناس فليتجوز ”0

"فلولا صليت بدسبح اسم ريك الأعلى) ووالشمس وضحاها) و(والليل إذا يفش"
وذلك في العشاء قال أبو عمر: ينبغي لكل إمام أن يخفف جهده إذا أكمل الركوع
والسجود. ولا يجوز له التطويل؛ وإن علم قدرة من خلفه فإنه لا يدري ما يحدث

الصلب والاعتدال من الطمأنينة والمكث قليلا؛ فليس من الواجب ولكنه من
الكمال والعمل في الأئمة التخفيف لا يختلفون في ذلك.

وقال في "التمهيد”: التخفيف لكل إمام أمر مجمع عليه. إلا أن ذلك إنما هو
أقل الكمال» وأما الحذف والنقصان فلا؛ لأن رسول الله يك نهى عن نقر الغراب؛ ثم

غضب في موعظة كان أشاد

# PageV1P112
anchors:
- Root: خ-ف-ف (khafafa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Lightness and diminution of weight; to make something light and swift.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In ritual acts, denotes reducing the quantity of actions while preserving their essential pillars (arkān) and conditions (shurūṭ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in physical weight; metaphorical (majāz) in prayer, meaning to shorten recitation and postures without violating completeness.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ) — The phrase "if he completes the bowing and prostration" (idhā akmala al-rukūʿ wa al-sujūd) establishes a conditional restriction, indicating that brevity is permissible only when the obligatory elements are fulfilled.
translation:
I say — and from the book "Al-Muwāfaqāt" of the noble scholar who nurtures with the lesser knowledge before the greater: He related from Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿAṭāridī — may God have mercy on him — who said: I said to al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām: "Why is it that I see you, O companions of Muhammad ﷺ, among the lightest of people in prayer?" He replied: "We hasten against the whisperer (al-waswās), even though prolongation is recommended (mustaḥabb), but something has come to oppose it."

And in al-Bukhārī: That a man said: "O Messenger of God, we delay the dawn prayer because of one who prolongs it for us." The Messenger of God ﷺ became so angry that day that his anger was visible upon his face, then he said: {«O people, verily among you are those who repel (others). Whoever leads the people in prayer, let him be brief»}.

And likewise, the Messenger of God ﷺ said to Muʿādh — three times — "Would you not have prayed with {«Glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most High»} and {«By the sun and its brightness»} and {«By the night when it covers»}?" — and that was in the night prayer (al-ʿishāʾ).

Abū ʿUmar said: It behooves every imam to be brief to the extent of his effort, when he completes the bowing and prostration. And it is not permissible for him to prolong, even if he knows the capability of those behind him, for he does not know what may befall them of sudden events, occupations, obstacles, needs, hadath (ritual impurity), urine, and other things. He said: And as for what is beyond the standing of the spine and the moderation (iʿtidāl) of tranquility (ṭumaʾnīnah) and a brief pause — that is not obligatory, but it is of perfection (kamāl). And the practice among the imams is brevity; they do not differ in that.

And he said in "Al-Tamhīd": Brevity for every imam is a matter of consensus (mujmaʿ ʿalayh). However, that is only the lesser of perfection. As for omission and deficiency — no, for the Messenger of God ﷺ forbade the pecking of the crow (naqr al-ghurāb). Then I know of no disagreement among the people of knowledge regarding the recommendation of brevity for whoever leads a people in an obligatory or supererogatory prayer, except the eclipse prayer (ṣalāt al-kusūf). He said: And ʿUmar — may God be pleased with him — said: "O people, do not..."

title_en: Section 84 — On Gentleness in Religious Rulings and the Conduct of the Righteous Predecessors
arabic_text:
### | الصفحة 112

بده منهج الترفي / المقام الرايع: هرء الاعس بالخيسٍ
اتبغضوا الله لعباده؛ وقال يق لمعاذ: "اتريد أن تكون فتانا””'؛ لما أطال بالناس في
الصلاة.
وانظر في هذا المعنى ما وقيع لابن العربي في "مواصمه": ينبغي للفقبه
المجتهد إذا جاءه من وقع في الورطة من يمين أن يخلصه بمسألة ظاهرة بين
الصحابة والتابعين إذا رأى أنه إن لم يخلصه بها وقع في أشد منها؛ وهو أن يستهين
بالمسألة ويقتحم فيها ما لا يجوزء فالأفضل للمفتي أن يفتح له بابًا ويمشي به على
اطريق: فإنه إن سد عليه باب الشرع فتح هو إلى الحنث بابًا يقتحمه؛ وأخذ في طريق
من المعصية يسلكه؛ ويرى أنه قد وقع في ورطة فلا يبالي ما صنع بعد ذلك.

ثم قال بعد ذلك: فهذه سيرة العلماء المتقدمين: كمالك مع المغيرة وابن
القاسم مع ابنه خاف إن كلفه المشي أن لا يفعل؛ فيستهين بمسألة في الدين» فيكون
ذلك طريقًا إلى غيرهاء فيستهين أيضًا بهاء فأراد أن يخرجه عنها. فال ابن رشد: على
اقوة الخلاف تقوى مراعاته. وقال ابن العربي أيضًا: وجزء من الفدوى عظيم أن
يركب المتفق عليه على المختلف فيه؛ وهذا أمر خفي على علمائنا فافهموء.

وفي حكمة آل داود: ينبغي للعاقل المميز أن لا يخلي نفسه من واحدة من

يفسده؛ أو لذة في غير محرم يستعين بها على الحالات الثلاث.

وقد تقدم قول تاج الدين: ريما وردت عليك الأنوار: فوجدت القلب محشوًا

# PageV1P113
anchors:
- Root: خ-ف-ف (kh-f-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Lightness, ease, alleviation of burden; opposite of heaviness (thiqal).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological context, denotes the principle of facilitation (takhfīf) in rulings, reflecting divine mercy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical lightness; Metaphorical: easing a legal difficulty for one in distress.
- Root: و-ر-ط (w-r-ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A pitfall, a treacherous place; a predicament from which escape is difficult.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Moral-spiritual crisis; a state of sin or legal entanglement requiring rescue.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a snare or trap; Metaphorical: a situation of religious or ethical peril.
- Root: ف-ت-ن (f-t-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Trial, tribulation, seduction; to cause discord or excessive burden.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In prophetic hadith, refers to causing spiritual harm or overburdening the congregation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: refining gold by fire; Metaphorical: testing believers through hardship.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Condition and Exception (al-sharṭ wa al-jazāʾ) — The conditional clause "if he sees that..." governs the apodosis, requiring careful parsing of the muftī's discretionary action.
translation:
I say — may Allah guide us and you: Know that the Prophet ﷺ commanded gentleness (al-rifq) toward Allah's servants; and he said to Muʿādh: "Do you wish to be a cause of trial (fattān)?" — when he prolonged the prayer with the people.

Consider in this meaning what occurred with Ibn al-ʿArabī in his "Muʿāṣim": It behooves the diligent jurist (al-faqīh al-mujtahid), when one who has fallen into a predicament (warṭah) by an oath comes to him, to extricate him by means of a manifest issue (masʾalah ẓāhirah) agreed upon among the Companions and the Followers — if he sees that were he not to extricate him thereby, he would fall into something more severe; namely, that he would treat the matter lightly and plunge into what is not permissible. Thus, it is preferable for the muftī to open a door for him and walk him along the path; for if he closes the door of the Sacred Law upon him, he (the oath-taker) will open for himself a door toward perjury and plunge through it, and take a path of disobedience and traverse it — and he will see that he has fallen into a predicament, so he will no longer care what he does afterward.

Then he said after that: Such is the conduct (sīrah) of the early scholars: like Mālik with al-Mughīrah, and Ibn al-Qāsim with his son — he feared that if he burdened him with walking (the strict path), he would not do it, and would then treat a matter of religion lightly, and that would become a path to other matters, and he would also treat them lightly — so he desired to extricate him from it. Ibn Rushd said: The stronger the disagreement (khilāf), the stronger the observance (murāʿāh) of it. Ibn al-ʿArabī also said: A great part of fatwā is to mount the agreed-upon (al-muttafaq ʿalayh) upon the disagreed-upon (al-mukhtalaf fīh); and this is a subtle matter hidden from our scholars — so understand it.

And in the Wisdom of the Family of Dāwūd: It behooves the discerning rational person (al-ʿāqil al-mumayyiz) not to leave himself devoid of one of four things: a going forth for his final return (maʿād), or a rectification of his livelihood (maʿāsh), or a reflection (fikr) by which he discerns what benefits him from what corrupts him, or a permissible pleasure (ladhdhah fī ghayr muḥarram) by which he aids himself in the other three states.

And the saying of Tāj al-Dīn has preceded: "Perhaps the lights (anwār) may come upon you, and you find the heart stuffed with the forms of traces (āthār)." Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh said: The worst of sins is the whispering of the self (ḥadīth al-nafs); and likewise, according to the people of wisdom, it is the affliction of the intellect (āfat al-dhihn). Al-Ḥajjāj said to Ibn al-Qirriyyah: "You claim that the Arabs hold that everything has an..." — [the text continues with the hadith of prolonging prayer, as cited from Ibn Mājah, Muslim, al-Nasāʾī, and Abū ʿAwānah].

title_en: Section 85 — On Warding Off the Base with the Baser, and the Ailments of the Intellect, Worship, and Knowledge
arabic_text:

أمور ذكرها. وكذلك الأطباء أيضًا قالوا؛ حديث النفس ميشدأ المالخوليا؛ وقال
جالينوس: يحدث من النظر في العلم من الهم والغيرة والفكرة أمراض كثيرة. وقال

# PageV1P114
anchors:
- Root: د-ر-أ (d-r-')
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To repel, push away, or ward off (a harm or attacker); the act of deflecting an evil before it strikes.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, the defensive repulsion of moral or spiritual corruption (fasād) by a countermeasure, even if the countermeasure is of a lower order — a principle of lesser-evil jurisprudence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in physical combat; metaphorical (majāz) in ethical therapy — warding off a spiritual ailment by an allowable, though inferior, remedy.
- Root: خ-س-س (kh-s-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The low, the vile, the contemptible; that which is base in rank or worth.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The lesser of two evils; the permissible but inferior means chosen to avert a greater harm.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in market-value; metaphorical in moral valuation — the "baser" as the lesser sin or the licit distraction.
- Root: ف-ت-ر (f-t-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Languor, slackness, intermission after exertion; the cooling of zeal.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The spiritual torpor that follows devotional intensity — a recognized ailment of worship ('ibādah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for bodily fatigue; metaphorical for the weakening of religious resolve.
- Root: ن-س-ي (n-s-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Forgetfulness, the erasure of what was once retained.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ailment of knowledge ('ilm) — the loss of sacred learning through neglect, as opposed to deliberate abandonment.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for memory-loss; metaphorical for the soul's heedlessness (ghaflah) of divine truths.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of 'Aṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — In the phrase "آفة العبادة الفترة" and its parallels, the predicate is a simple nominal annexation (iḍāfah) without copula, requiring the translator to render the implicit "is" while preserving the aphoristic brevity of the original.
translation:
I say — and success is with God:

Know that the physicians of the bodies and the physicians of the hearts are agreed that the remedy for every ailment is its opposite, and that the base is warded off by the baser. For they have said: The ailment of the intellect is the whispering of the self (ḥadīth al-nafs); the ailment of worship is languor (fatrah); and the ailment of knowledge is forgetfulness (nisyān) — along with other matters they have mentioned. Likewise, the physicians also have said: The whispering of the self is the beginning of melancholia (mālikhūliyā). And Galen said: From excessive contemplation in the pursuit of knowledge arise many diseases of anxiety, envy, and obsessive thought. And he said in his book *Kāmil al-Ṣināʿah* (The Complete Art): "It behooves a man not to persist in nor multiply reflection, for all of that alters the temperament of the body, aids in its wasting, and weakens the innate heat (al-ḥarārah al-gharīziyyah). And whoever has a hot temperament, these symptoms generate in him something akin to the fever of consumption (ḥummā al-diq), the ulcer of tuberculosis (qarḥat al-sill), and what runs in this course." He said: "For this reason, a man ought to avoid all psychic disturbances (al-aʿrāḍ al-nafsāniyyah), and to divert himself with joy (surūr), for it strengthens the innate heat, moves it to the surface of the body, increases vigor, and fortifies the soul." — End of the quotation from *Kāmil al-Ṣināʿah*.

And consider his saying: "to divert himself with joy" — for the jurists (fuqahāʾ) say [this is achieved] by jesting (mizāḥ), and the Sufis say by audition (ghināʾ). And it has already preceded in the station before this one that both are permissible.

And ʿIyāḍ — may God have mercy on him — was acquainted with Ibn Waḍḍāḥ, and he said: Through him and through Baqī ibn Makhlad, al-Andalus became an abode of ḥadīth. He said: Ibn Waḍḍāḥ was the teacher of the people of al-Andalus in knowledge and asceticism (zuhd). His tongue was detained [from speaking the truth], so he said: "O God, if in the release [of my tongue] there is [some good]..." — and he was threatened with the fire [of punishment]. He said: "Then grant me relief, for I feel its heat!" So he commanded that his neck be struck. And when he [the ruler] saw him reciting [the Qurʾān], he said: "Had we left him, we would have heard from his speech!" And his accounts are many.

title_en: Section 86 — On the Permissibility of Recreation and Easing the Soul for the Student of Knowledge

# PageV1P115
anchors:
- Root: ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To breathe, to expand; relief from distress; the soul's vital breath.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Spiritual refreshment (tarwīḥ) as a means to restore the heart's receptivity to worship and knowledge.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: releasing wind from a sail; metaphorical: easing the soul's burden (istirwāḥ) — here used in the latter sense.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The phrase "فأطلق الله لسانه" (so God loosened his tongue) is an explanatory appositive to the preceding supplication, showing cause and effect.
translation:
I say: Among the paths of the rightly guided is the beginning of one's affair with gentleness toward oneself. The Shaykh (may God have mercy on him) sought to spread this knowledge, so he released it; thus God released his tongue, and through him God revived the people of al-Andalus.

He mentioned for him (i.e., the Shaykh) miracles (karāmāt). He said: And his final state weakened; so the physicians advised him to give his soul respite (yurawwiḥ nafsahu); so he would jest and laugh. And he had eighty days in which he occupied himself with nothing: forty in extreme heat and forty in extreme cold. The physicians have explicitly stated regarding the elderly, and they mentioned from their regimen that they should adhere to rest and ease, and abandon exertion and fatigue — matters they detailed, saying: This is so that withering is repelled from them and their bodies do not break down quickly, God willing.

And consider, regarding the jurist (faqīh): Whoever fears an illness, or its increase, or delayed recovery due to fasting Ramaḍān or due to the major ablution (ghusl al-janābah), then he abandons the obligatory act and eats and performs dry ablution (tayammum). So a fortiori, he should abandon the supererogatory. From this same meaning, the authors of legal rulings (ahl kutub al-aḥkām) have stated regarding the judge: He should not exhaust himself all day; he said in the narration (al-riwāyah): "I fear that if he does much, he will err." And he should set specific hours for his sitting, and he should not judge while angry or in a similar state.

And he said in "al-Iḥyā’" (The Revival): Recreation (lahw) is a refreshment for the heart and lightens from it the weariness of thought; and that is an aid to seriousness. He said: So the one who perseveres in jurisprudence (tafaqquh) should take a day off, so that his vigor may surge in other days. And if he tires of worship, and his vigor subsides, and he knows that were he to relax for an hour with some recreation, his vigor would return — then recreation is better for him. As Ibn Masʿūd said: "I indeed refresh my soul with some recreation, so that it may be an aid for me upon the truth."

And al-Maqqarī has the following text: The reality is: the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammārah) is not subdued except by subtle stratagems, and the tranquil soul (al-muṭma’innah) is tractable and does not slip away except from one who is heedless. {وَكَذَٰلِكَ مَكَّنَّا لِيُوسُفَ فِي الْأَرْضِ} [Yūsuf: 21] — "And thus We established Joseph in the land."

A subtle point (raqīqah): The piercing of the ship was a display of a miracle (karāmah) for its manager — {أَمَّا السَّفِينَةُ فَكَانَتْ لِمَسَاكِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ فِي الْبَحْرِ} [al-Kahf: 79] — "As for the ship, it belonged to poor people working in the sea." And perhaps bodies are healed by intellect. End quote. And consider this principle as well. The jurists said: When the benefit (maṣlaḥah) is greater than the harm (mafsadah), we secure the benefit while enduring the harm — as is done in ransoming captives, and for the oppressor, paying to ward off transgression. And by consensus, when two harms meet, the lesser is borne for the greater.

And consider: The enormity of lying dissolves in comparison to reconciling between people (iṣlāḥ dhāt al-bayn). In sum, the seeker of the Hereafter — if he perceives from himself that were he to commit a base act in which there is no sin, he would thereby be relieved of his inner obsessions (hawājis), and he finds afterward his heart with his Lord — then let him not disdain it; perhaps he will stand and pray immediately after that.

title_en: The Method of Ascent / The Fourth Station: Repelling the Base with the Vile — The Permissible (Mubāḥ) While Present of Mind and Collected of Heart
arabic_text:
### | الصفحة 115

منهج الترقي/ المفام الرابع: درء الاعس بالخسيس ‏ ور
المباح مستحضرًا الذهن مجتمع البال. ولاشك أن القيام للصلاة كذلك فرض
منعين عليه. قال سبحانه وتعالى: طيَج مثا ادر المحلو أن شكرى
حَقٍ تَلّمُوأمَانَمُوُونَ © [النساء: 43].

قال في "الاحياء": وهب أن المراد من الآية ظاهرهاء ففيه تنبيه على سكر
الدنيا؛ إذ بين سبحانه العلة» فقال: (إحقٌ ُو نووت 4 فانظر ريما تجد أحدنا
اقد رفع همته عن هذه المآخذ العلاجية وارتكب وقارًا يربي على وقار الصحابة
فضا عن غيرهم. بحيث لو كلف أن يلبس ثويًا تستتقصه به العامة وذلك الثوب قد
البسه السلف وأجازوه؛ أو طلب منه أن يحضر لهوًا مما قعل مثله في السلف
وحضروه؛ لكان ذلك عنده بمنزلة الربح تمر به يقوم يصلي فلا يدري ما يقرأء أنت
ترا ظاهرا على أعلى غابة من الوقار والسكينة والخضوع؛ وهو في الحقيقة قائم بين
يدي شهوة من شهواته قرد ييصبص أو كلب ينبح أو ختزير يشره. قالوا: وهبه الله نية
صالحة في وقاره لأجل صون عرضه وحفظ مروءته فقد فاته الصدق يسبب
هواجس النفس» قال سهل بن عبد اله: أول خيانة الصديقين حديثهم مع أنفسهمء
وقالوا: إذا ظهر على المرء الوقار أكثر مما في باطنه فهو غير صادق في وقاره» وإن
الم يكن ملتفنا إلى الخلق ولا مراتيا إياهم.

ولهنا قالوا: مخالفة الظاهر للباطن إن كان عن قصد فهو الرياء؛ وإن كان ععن
غير قصد فقد فاته به الصدق؛ وهذا معنى الأئر: اللهم اجعل سريرتي خيرًا من
علانيتي؛ واجعل علانيتي خالصة لوجهك الكريم. وكان بعضهم يتسع في بعض

# PageV1P116
anchors:
- Root: د-ر-أ (d-r-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To repel, push away, ward off (deflection of harm).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Repelling spiritual harm by engaging the lower permissible — a means (wasīlah) not an end.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical repulsion; Metaphorical: diverting the soul’s distraction from worship.
- Root: خ-س-س (kh-s-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Base, vile, contemptible (the lower of two things).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The permissible (mubāḥ) as the “vile” relative to the excellence of worship.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: lowliness of rank; Metaphorical: the soul’s inclination to what is beneath it.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ) — “If the outward contradicts the inward, then…” (governing the apodosis by the protasis, as in the author’s “if it was by intent, then it is riyāʾ”).
translation:
I say — and success is with God:

Know that the fourth station of ascent is the repelling of the base (al-khasīs) by the vile (al-khasīs), meaning: the permissible (mubāḥ) — while keeping the mind present and the heart collected. And there is no doubt that standing for prayer is likewise an obligation incumbent upon him. He, glorified and exalted, said: {«يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا تَقْرَبُوا الصَّلَاةَ وَأَنتُمْ سُكَارَىٰ حَتَّىٰ تَعْلَمُوا مَا تَقُولُونَ»} [Al-Nisāʾ 4:43].

He said in the Iḥyāʾ: “Even if one grants that the apparent meaning of the verse is intended, still therein is a warning against the intoxication of this world; for He, glorified, clarified the cause, saying: {«حَتَّىٰ تَعْلَمُوا مَا تَقُولُونَ»} — so reflect: how often do we find one of us who has raised his aspiration above these remedial means (al-māʾākhidh al-ʿilājiyyah), and has adopted a solemnity (waqār) exceeding the solemnity of the Companions — let alone others — such that if he were asked to wear a garment that the common folk would deem shameful, while that very garment had been worn and permitted by the Salaf; or if he were asked to attend a permissible amusement that the Salaf had done and attended; that would be in his view tantamount to a disgrace (dhanm) — [yet] he stands in prayer and does not know what he recites. You see him outwardly at the highest pitch of solemnity, tranquility, and humility; but in reality he stands before one of his lusts like a monkey grimacing, or a dog barking, or a pig grunting. They said: Even if God granted him a sound intention in his solemnity, for the sake of guarding his honor and preserving his manliness (murūʾah), still he has missed truthfulness (ṣidq) because of the whisperings of the soul. Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh said: “The first betrayal of the truthful ones is their conversing with themselves.” And they said: “When solemnity appears on a man more than what is in his inward, he is not truthful in his solemnity — even if he is not turning to the creatures nor showing off to them.”

Hence they said: The contradiction of the outward to the inward — if it is by intent, it is ostentation (riyāʾ); and if it is without intent, then truthfulness has escaped him thereby. And this is the meaning of the supplication: “O God, make my secret better than my public, and make my public purely for Your noble Face.” And some of them would expand [his freedom] in certain permissible things, and was reproached for that; so he said: “Has any of you ever had a thought of lust cross his mind while standing before God?” They said: “That does befall us.” He said: “If I were content, in my whole life, with your state, I would not have expanded [my freedom]; but no thought ever crossed me that distracted me from my state, except that I repelled it, so as to rest from it and return to my occupation.”

And in the Risālah: “The truthful one is he who wishes to die and would not be ashamed of his secret if it were exposed.” God, glorified, said: {«قُلْ إِن كَانَتْ لَكُمُ الدَّارُ الْآخِرَةُ عِندَ اللَّهِ خَالِصَةً مِّن دُونِ النَّاسِ فَتَمَنَّوُا الْمَوْتَ إِن كُنتُمْ صَادِقِينَ»} [Al-Baqarah 2:94].

And ʿIyāḍ said: While Ashab was with his companions, he heard a man announcing a thief; so he rose, took his weapon, and went out pursuing him. It was said to him: “Someone like you should not do this.” He said: “I would not adopt a character other than what [I truly am].”

title_en: On the Station of Sincerity (Ikhlaṣ) and the Conduct of the Righteous in Adorning Themselves
