### | الصفحة 116

16 منهج التوفي/ المقام الرايع: هرء الاعس بالخصيس
جبلني الله عليه ولما نقل عياض هذه الحكاية قال عن بعضهم: رحم الله أشهب؛ ما
كان أصدقه وأخوفه لله. قال: وقال له ابن عبد الحكم يوما: لو أمسكت قليلًا؛ قال:
قد علمت الذي تقول؛ ولو فعلت لكنت أجل في أعبين الناس؛ ولكين ولله لا أعمل
شيئًا أبدا إلا أريد به اله اه من عياض.

وعرف أيضًا بمحمد بن عيسى من الفقهاء الم الثقات وكانت له
وجاهة في العلم مع فضل وورع؛ وروى عن ابن القاسم وأشهب وابن وهب
وغيرهم؛ عوتب في كثرة دعابته» فقال: علي بن أبي طالب لم يتركها للخلافة
أتركها أنا للشهادة والعدالة؟ وقال الشيخ أبو مدين: ترك الدنيا للدنيا شر من أخخذها.

الآن ألقى الله بجميع المعاصي أحب إلي من أن ألقاه بذرة من التصنع.

دخل يسار البصرة؛ فبينما هو يصلي. وكان حسن الصلاة؛ وعليه ثياب جياد..
فرآه مالك بن دينارء فجلس إليه؛ فسلم يسار؛ فقال مالك: هذه الصلاة وهذه
الثياب» فقال له يسار: ثيابي هذه ترفعني عندك أو تضعني؟ قال: تضعك؛ قال: هذا

تنزلك من الله فبكى مالك وقال له: أنت يسار؟ قال: نعم؛ فعائقه مالك؛ وقعد بين

ونقل أبو عمر في 'تمهيده' عن مسلم بن يسار قال: إذا لبست ثوبًا فظندت أنك

أكثر الفضلاء يشوشون ظواهرهم بما يستبشعه الناس ويكرهه الشرع؛ لأن قصارى
أمره إن لم يثب على تركه فلا يعاقب على فعله؛ وهذا كما اعتذر به بعض الفضلاء»
فقال: زيادة علم أو نقصان ورع إن لم يكن ثواب, وإلا فلا حرج. ويقيسونه يمن

مقطوع به؛ ولا يفوته بتركه إلا فلآن يجوز ما يحكى عن هؤلاء الفضلاء
أولى وأحرى؛ إذ يفوت إن لم يتعالج بمثلها القرب من الله؛ ويقولون: من عرف ما
يطلب هان عليه ما يبذل. ويقولون: ريما صحت الأجسام بالعلل.

ونقل عياض عن ابن مهدي قال: سمعت مالكنًا يقول: لو علمت أن قلبي
يصلح بالجلوس على كناسة لجلست عليها.

# PageV1P117
anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ص (khalasa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Purity, clarity, and freedom from admixture; the essence of a thing when stripped of all foreign elements.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Sincerity (ikhlāṣ) as the purification of intention (niyyah) from all motives save the Divine Countenance—the very axis of accepted deeds.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) purity of gold from dross; metaphorically (majāz), the heart's cleansing from ostentation (riyāʾ).
- Root: ز-ي-ن (zayyana)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Adornment, beautification, and outward embellishment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The Quranic contrast between the adornment of worldly life (zīnat al-ḥayāh al-dunyā) and the enduring good deeds (al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥāt).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal physical ornamentation; metaphorically, the deliberate display of piety for social elevation—condemned as hypocrisy (nifāq).
- Sībawayh Rule: The Conditional Clause with Inna-mā (الحصر بالقصر) — Restriction via "innamā" to affirm exclusive intent in action, as in "I do nothing ever except desiring God thereby."
translation:
I say—may God establish me upon what He has habituated me—and when ʿIyāḍ transmitted this anecdote, he said concerning one of them: "God have mercy on Asbagh; how truthful he was, and how fearful of God!" He said: Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam said to him one day: "Would that you had restrained yourself a little." He replied: "I know what you mean; and had I done so, I would have been more august in people's eyes. But by God, I will never do anything at all except desiring God thereby." This is from ʿIyāḍ.

He was also known—Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, one of the trustworthy jurists—and he held prestige in knowledge along with virtue and scrupulousness (waraʿ). He transmitted from Ibn al-Qāsim, Asbagh, Ibn Wahb, and others. He was reproached for his frequent jesting, and he said: "ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib did not abandon it for the caliphate; shall I abandon it for testimony and probity?" And Shaykh Abū Madyan said: "Abandoning the world for the sake of the world is worse than taking it."

And from the *Risālah*: "Whoever adorns himself before people with what is not in him falls in God's sight." And also from it: "That I should meet God with all sins is dearer to me than that I should meet Him with a speck of affectation (taṣannuʿ)."

Yasār entered Baṣrah; and while he was praying—and he prayed beautifully, wearing fine garments—Mālik ibn Dīnār saw him, sat beside him, and greeted him. Yasār returned the greeting. Mālik said: "This prayer, and these garments!" Yasār said to him: "Do these garments of mine raise me in your estimation, or lower me?" He said: "They lower you." He said: "That is what I intended." Then he said: "O Mālik, I think these two garments of yours have brought you down in your own sight to a degree that God has not brought you down." Mālik wept and said to him: "Are you Yasār?" He said: "Yes." So Mālik embraced him and sat before him.

Abū ʿUmar transmitted in his *Tamhīd* from Muslim ibn Yasār, who said: "If you don a garment and think that you are better in it than in another, then wretched is that garment for you." Some of them said: "Out of fear of this very thing, most of the virtuous used to dishevel their outward appearances with what people find repugnant and the Law dislikes—because the utmost consequence of it is that if one is not rewarded for abandoning it, one is not punished for doing it." This is like the excuse offered by one of the virtuous, who said: "Increased knowledge or decreased scrupulousness—if there is no reward, then no harm." And they analogize this to one who chokes on food: he may wash it down with a gulp of wine if he finds nothing else—even though its prohibition is definitively established, and by abandoning it he loses nothing except that. So how much more fitting and proper is it to permit what is narrated of these virtuous ones, since by not treating oneself with its like, one loses nearness to God? And they say: "Whoever knows what he seeks, what he spends becomes light upon him." And they say: "How often bodies are healed by ailments."

And ʿIyāḍ transmitted from Ibn Mahdī, who said: "I heard Mālik say: 'If I knew that my heart would be set right by sitting on a dunghill, I would sit upon it.'"

title_en: Section 89 — On the Treatment of Hidden Riya' (Show) and Concealed Desires, and the Conduct of the Righteous in Guarding Their Hearts
arabic_text:

منهج الوقي/ لعفم الايع: ده الس بالخيس ل
ونقل ابن المبارك وغيره عن وهب بن منبه؛ قال: كان رجل من أفضل أهل
زماته؛ قال: خرجنا من الدنيا مخافة الطغيان: فنخاف أن نكون قد دخعل علينا في
أمرنا هذا من الطفيان أكثر مما دخخل على أهل الأموال في أموالهم؛ أرانا نحب أن
نقضي حوائجنا ونحترم لمكان ديتناء وإن اشترينا
ديناء فبلغ الملك دين هذا الرجل: فركب في موكيه؛ فجاءه وسلم عليه؛ والرجل قلد

وهذا من سهل فعل كبير وتواضع:
وعرف عياض بأبي العباس الأبياني؛ قال: كان عالم إفريقيا غير مدافع»
أشخص الوالي فيه ليوليه القضاء؛ فسبق أبو العباس إلى السلطان من ينقصه عندهء
اثم دخمل إليه أبو العباس في زي بدوي حاف ونعلاه في يدهء فلما رآه السلطان
صدق ما قاله القائل؛ فعرض عليه القضاء فعافاه. ويقول أهل الحقيقة في مثل هذا:

# PageV1P118
anchors:
- Root: ع-ل-ج (ʿ-l-j)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To treat, remedy, or set right a malady; to manage a matter with skill and diligence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The therapeutic discipline of the soul (ʿilāj al-qalb) — restoring the heart's soundness (ṣiḥḥah) against spiritual diseases like riyā' and hawā.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: medical treatment of the body. Metaphorical (majāz): the rectification of inward states through spiritual means — here, deliberately lowering oneself in people's eyes to sever the root of show.
- Root: ر-ي-ء (r-y-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To see, to show; riyā' — performing acts for the sight of others, not for God.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A branch of shirk al-khafī (hidden polytheism); the heart's inclination toward creatures' approval over the Creator's.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: visual perception. Metaphorical: the act of "displaying" piety — the disease of the self that seeks witness from creation.
- Root: خ-ف-ي (kh-f-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be hidden, concealed; khafīyah — the subtle, inward dimension of sin.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The hidden (al-khafī) versus the manifest (al-ẓāhir) — the battleground of the heart where true sincerity (ikhlāṣ) is tested.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: what is veiled from sight. Metaphorical: the secret motives that corrupt worship — the "hidden shirk" that scholars must root out.
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-ʿAṭf ʿalā al-Sabab (Coordination on the Cause) — When two clauses are joined by "fa" (ف), the second is the consequence or cause of the first, as in "فنخاف أن نكون قد دخل علينا" — the fear is the direct result of having left the world for fear of tyranny.
translation:
I say — may God guide us and you to the straight path:

Know that the treatment of the hidden diseases of the heart is among the most subtle of the stations of religion, and the rightly guided (al-muhtadūn) have trodden in it paths of wisdom that confound the heedless.

It has been transmitted from Ibn al-Mubārak and others, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: There was a man among the most virtuous of his time. He said: "We departed from the world out of fear of tyranny (ṭughyān). Now we fear that more tyranny has entered upon us in our affair than entered upon the people of wealth in their wealth. It seems we love to have our needs fulfilled and to be honored for the sake of our religion — even if we have purchased our religion with it."

When the king learned of this man's piety, he rode out in his procession, came to him, and greeted him. The man was gathering wild greens and olives, collecting the greens into a large morsel, dipping it in oil, and stuffing his mouth. The king said to him: "How are you?" He replied: "I am well." The king said to those with him: "There is no good in this man." And he turned away from him. Then the man said: "Praise be to God who turned him away from me, while He is for me — not against me."

It has been stated in the Iḥyā' (al-Ghazālī's Iḥyā' ʿUlūm al-Dīn) that the treatment of the heart by such means is sought after. The expression of the Master al-Bilālī is: "The treatment of riyā' and hidden desire is by knowledge and by action." Then he said: "As for action — it is by that which casts one down from the hearts of others, such as a man eating in public before someone he fears for himself, so that the other turns away from him."

And ʿIyāḍ transmitted in his Madārik that a man said to Sahl al-Tustarī: "It has reached me that you walk on water — pray for me." He said: "I will not pray for you until you go to the boatman so-and-so and ask him about my affair on such-and-such a day." So the man went and asked him. The boatman said: "He climbed up there to perform ablution, slipped, and fell into the water, thrashing about. I threw myself upon him and pulled him out — he had nearly perished. We grabbed him and much water poured out of him." The man returned to Sahl and informed him. Sahl said: "After this, I will pray for you." And he prayed for him. ʿIyāḍ said: "This was from Sahl a great deed and an act of humility."

And ʿIyāḍ reported on the authority of Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Abyānī, who said: He was the scholar of Ifrīqiya without dispute. The governor summoned him to appoint him to the judgeship. Before Abū al-ʿAbbās arrived, someone had already gone to the sultan to diminish him in his sight. Then Abū al-ʿAbbās entered upon the sultan in the garb of a Bedouin, barefoot, with his sandals in his hand. When the sultan saw him, he confirmed what the detractor had said. He offered him the judgeship, but he declined it and was spared.

The people of reality (ahl al-ḥaqīqah) say concerning such matters: "Whoever knows what he seeks, what he gives becomes easy to him." The scholars of God's rulings say: "Eating in the market is a degradation." It was said to one of them: "Enter the mosque." He replied: "I am ashamed before my Lord to enter His house [while my heart is attached to the market]."

And the story of the butcher with Ibn al-Mubārak follows in the ninth station after this. He said in the Iḥyā': "Our saying concerning the blameworthy attributes of the inward — 'dog,' 'pig,' 'monkey,' and the like — is not meant except as an indication of the meaning. There is a difference between changing the outward appearances into the inward, and between alerting the inward by mentioning the outward while affirming the outward. By this subtle distinction we part from the Bāṭiniyyah (esotericists), for this is the path [of the Sunnah]."

We love that concession be granted to us for the sake of our religion — and if we have purchased our religion [with it], then the king's turning away is a mercy.

الاعتبارء وهو مسلك العلماء والأبرار؛ إذ معنى الاعتبار أن تعير مما ذكر إلى غ/
ولا تقتصر عليه؛ كما يرى العاقل مصيبة بغيره فيكون له عبرة بأن يعبر بها إلى
النبيه؛ لكوته أيضًا عرضة للمصائب؛ وكون الدنيا بصدد الانقلاب: فعبوره من غيره
إلى نفسه ومن نفسه إلى أصل الدنيا عبرة محمودة» فاعبر أنت من الكلب الذي ذم
الصفته لاالصورته؛ وهو ما فيه من سبعية إلى روح الكلبية؛ فتعلم أن القلب
المشحون بالغضب والحرص على تمزيق الأعراض كلب في المعنى: وقلب في
الصورة؛ ونور البصيرة يلاحظ المعاني دون الصور؛ والصور في هذا العالم غالبة
على المعاني؛ والمعائي باطئة فيهاء وفي الآخرة تتبع الصور للمعاني؛ وتغلب
المعاتي؛ فلذلك ورد أن كل شخص يحشر على صورته المعنوية؛ وقد رشح
الشاطبي هذا المعنى واستدل باستشهاد عمر رضي الله عنه على الذي رآه يشتري
الحنا أبن تذهب بحكم هذه الآبة: َعَم لبوق ايديا 4 [الأحقاف: 20]:
والآية إنما نزلت في الكفارء فلم يمنع عمر إنزالها في الكفار من الاستشهاد بها في
مواضع اعتباًا يما تقدم؛ وهو أصل شرعي. اه من "الموافقات”. وانظر من هذا

تون الأ َكَاطتَِمُيتَام آأمعالمْ4 [الأنعام: 38]؛ قال: أثبت سبحانه
المماثلة؛ ومعلوم أنهم لم يماثلونا في خلقنا وأشكالنا وعقولناء فلا تبقى الممائلة إلا
في الأخلاقء فلا أحد إلا وفيه خلق من خلق البهائم: فإذا رأيت إنسانًا فيه خلق

فانظر بالنسبة إليه لما تقتضيه أخوة الإيمان؛ يقول النبي يقة: “لا يؤمن أحدكم حتى

النصح نفسك الأمارةء فلا تقل له في حال غضبه: اذكر الله أو صل على رسول الله كل

الفسقه؛ والأصل في الأمر بالمعروف تقليل الشر بخلاف الجهاد: وتأمل قول الله

# PageV1P119
anchors:
- Root: ع-ب-ر (ʿ-b-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cross over, traverse from one state to another; to interpret a dream by passing from its image to its meaning.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Iʿtibār is the act of transiting from the observed (shāhid) to the unseen (ghāʾib), drawing a moral lesson by analogy — a hallmark of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal crossing (ʿubūr) over a physical bridge vs. metaphorical crossing of the mind from one consideration to another; here, the metaphorical sense dominates.
- Root: س-ب-ع (s-b-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Predatory ferocity (sabuʿiyyah); the nature of a beast of prey.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The animal soul (nafs ammārah) characterized by anger (ghaḍab) and predatory lust — a spiritual not physical attribute.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal beast (sabuʿ) vs. metaphorical beastliness of the heart; the latter is the intended meaning in this passage.
- Root: م-ث-ل (m-th-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Likeness, similarity, equivalence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The Quranic principle of takāfuʾ (moral correspondence) between human and animal traits, as in {«إِن كُلٌّ إِلَّا بَلَغَ الْحُدُودَ»} — here, the similitude is in character (akhlāq), not form.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal resemblance in shape vs. metaphorical resemblance in conduct; the latter is the operative sense.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-Maḥdhūf (Ellipsis Restoration) — The phrase "فاعبر أنت من الكلب" requires supplying the implied object (min ṣifatihi) to complete the syntactic sense; likewise, the conditional "فإذا رأيت" governs an implied apodosis of action.
translation:
I say — may Allah guide us and you to the path of the rightly guided, and cause us to die upon the way of the people of truth and certainty:

Know that the path of elevation (al-taraqqī) from the station of taking heed (iʿtibār) is the way of the scholars and the righteous. For the meaning of iʿtibār is that you cross over (taʿbir) from what is mentioned to something else, and do not restrict yourself to it alone. Thus, the intelligent person sees a calamity befalling another, and it becomes for him a lesson (ʿibrah) — that he crosses over by it to himself, because he too is exposed to calamities, and because this world is on the verge of overturning. So his crossing from another to himself, and from himself to the very origin of this world, is a praiseworthy lesson. Therefore, you too must take warning (iʿtabir) from the dog — not from its form, but from the attribute that is blamed in it, namely the ferocity (sabuʿiyyah) within it — and cross over to the reality of dog-likeness (rūḥ al-kalbiyyah). Then you will know that the heart filled with anger and greed for tearing apart reputations (aʿrāḍ) is a dog in meaning (maʿnā), though a heart in form (ṣūrah). The light of insight (nūr al-baṣīrah) observes meanings, not forms. In this world, forms dominate over meanings, and meanings are hidden within them; but in the Hereafter, forms will follow meanings, and meanings will prevail. For this reason, it has been reported that every person will be resurrected according to his spiritual form (ṣūratihi al-maʿnawiyyah).

Al-Shāṭibī (may Allah have mercy on him) elaborated this meaning and cited as evidence the testimony of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) regarding the man he saw buying a date-stone (al-ḥannāʾ) — that he went on to invoke the ruling of this verse: {«يَوْمَ يُعْرَضُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا عَلَى النَّارِ أَذْهَبْتُمْ طَيِّبَاتِكُمْ فِي حَيَاتِكُمُ الدُّنْيَا»} [al-Aḥqāf: 20]. Although the verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers, ʿUmar’s use of it as testimony in other contexts was not prevented by its original occasion of revelation, because he drew a lesson (iʿtibāran) from what had preceded — and this is a sound legal principle (aṣl sharʿī). This concludes the quotation from al-Muwāfaqāt.

Consider also, from this same meaning, what is found in the thirty-fifth chapter of al-Ṭurṭūshī’s Sirāj, regarding His saying (Exalted is He): {«إِن كُلٌّ إِلَّا بَلَغَ الْحُدُودَ»} [al-Anʿām: 38]. He (al-Ṭurṭūshī) said: Allah (Glory be to Him) affirmed the similitude (al-mumāthalah). It is known that the beasts do not resemble us in our creation, forms, or intellects. So the similitude remains only in character (akhlāq). There is no one who does not possess some trait from the traits of the beasts. So when you see a person in whom there is a trait that departs from moderation, look at which trait of the beasts that trait resembles, attach him to it, and deal with him as you would deal with that beast — then you will be relieved from contention, and companionship will endure. This concludes his quotation.

This is with respect to yourself. But with respect to him, consider what the brotherhood of faith requires. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: “None of you truly believes until he loves for his believing brother what he loves for himself.” So you must contrive to counsel his commanding soul (nafsuhu al-ammārah) just as you contrive to counsel your own commanding soul. Do not say to him in a state of anger: “Remember Allah” or “Send blessings upon the Messenger of Allah,” for fear that anger might drive him to increase his disobedience. This was stated by al-Nawawī, and something similar was said by ʿIzz al-Dīn, who said: For this reason, the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ) abandoned rebuking the wicked and the oppressors, because they knew it would not avail. And among them, when one is told “Fear Allah,” pride seizes him in sin, and he increases in oppression upon his oppression and in transgression upon his transgression. The fundamental principle in commanding good (al-amr bi-l-maʿrūf) is the reduction of evil — unlike jihad. And ponder the saying of Allah (Exalted is He): {«وَلَا تَسُبُّوا الَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ فَيَسُبُّوا اللَّهَ عَدْوًا بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ»} [al-Anʿām: 108] — for He prohibited what is itself an act of obedience (cursing the idols) because it leads to a greater disobedience (cursing Allah). This is the very essence of the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dharāʾiʿ).

# PageV1P120
anchors:
- Root: د-ر-أ (d-r-')
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To repel, ward off, or push away with force; to avert harm by interposing a shield or countermeasure.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, the act of repelling evil (dar' al-mafsadah) by a lesser means, prioritizing the lesser harm to prevent the greater — a principle of juristic preference (taṣarruf bi-al-akhaff).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical repulsion (e.g., pushing back an attacker). Metaphorical: employing a stratagem (ḥīlah) or lesser concession to avert a graver spiritual or moral corruption.
- Root: خ-س-س (kh-s-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The low, the vile, the contemptible; that which is base in rank or worth.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In ethical discourse, the base (khasīs) stands opposed to the noble (sharīf); here it denotes the permissible but lowly means (e.g., amatory prelude) used to attain a higher end.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: inferiority in substance or value. Metaphorical: a rhetorical device of lesser dignity employed as a vehicle for a nobler purpose.
- Root: ح-ي-ل (ḥ-y-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Cunning, stratagem, artful management; the power to devise means.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, ḥīlah carries a dual valence: blameworthy trickery (makr) when used for falsehood, and praiseworthy prudence (tawassul) when used to attain truth or repel corruption.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: turning and twisting (taḥawwul). Metaphorical: the subtle maneuvering of the soul against its own passions, or of the poet against the listener's inattention.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taqdīm wa-Ta'sīr (Fronting and Deferring) — The preposed element (here, the amatory prelude) is not the grammatical subject of intent but a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) preparing the hearer for the deferred main clause (the panegyric or true purpose), mirroring the syntactic principle that fronting signals emphasis or preparatory function.
translation:
I say — and God grants success:

Know that the path of God, all of it, is a warfare against the devil and a treatment of the heart, as Abū Ḥāmid (al-Ghazālī) has already stated. Thus the insightful and divinely aided one proceeds upon it by way of the subtle devices (al-ḥiyal) that are permissible.

And al-Maqqarī has already stated in his "Realities" (Ḥaqāʾiq): The commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammārah) is not subdued except by the subtle devices of stratagem (laṭāʾif al-ḥiyal).

Consider, then, the habit of the poets — how they advance amatory preludes (al-taghazzul wa-al-tashbīb) before their true intent, until al-Mutanabbī denied that this prelude was itself the aim, saying in the meter Ṭawīl:

"If praise be the goal, then the amatory prelude comes first — for every eloquent man who speaks verse is a lover."

He thereby indicated that this prelude is but a stirring of the soul and an alerting of the listener to lend ear to what follows it — even as another poet said, namely Mālik ibn al-Muraḥḥal, in the meter of the returning ode (qafr al-ʿawdah):

"The lovers have perished, save a poet who is amorous — the panegyric raises him by the prelude through successive states."

[Footnote on al-Mutanabbī:] He is Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAbd al-Ṣamad al-Juʿfī al-Kindī al-Kūfī, Abū al-Ṭayyib — the philosopher-poet and one of the glories of Arabic letters; his proverbs and wisdom sayings are proverbial. He was born in Kūfah in a quarter called Kindah, to which he is attributed; he grew up in Syria, then roamed the desert seeking literature, Arabic philology, and the days of the Arabs. He composed poetry while still young and wandered in the desert of al-Samāwah between Kūfah and Syria; many followed him, and before his affair grew strong, Luʾluʾ, the governor of Ḥimṣ and deputy of al-Ikhshīd, went out against him, seized him, and imprisoned him until he repented and recanted his claim. He then came to Sayf al-Dawlah ibn Ḥamdān, lord of Aleppo, praised him, and found favor with him. He went to Egypt and praised Kāfūr al-Ikhshīdī, seeking appointment from him; but Kāfūr did not appoint him, so Abū al-Ṭayyib grew angry and departed, satirizing him. He made for Iraq and Persia, and praised ʿAḍud al-Dawlah ibn Būyah al-Daylamī in Shīrāz. Returning, he intended Baghdad and Kūfah, when Fātik ibn Abī Jahl al-Asadī confronted him on the road with a company of his followers — and al-Mutanabbī had a company with him as well; the two parties clashed. Abū al-Ṭayyib was killed, along with his son Muḥassad and his servant Mufliḥ, at al-Nuʿmāniyyah near Dayr al-ʿĀqūl on the near side of the Sawād of Baghdad. This Fātik is the maternal uncle of Ḍabbah ibn Yazīd al-Asadī al-ʿAynī, whom al-Mutanabbī satirized in his famous poem in the bāʾ-rhyme — one of al-Mutanabbī's lapses.

[Footnote on sources:] See: al-ʿUmdah fī Maḥāsin al-Shiʿr 1/76; al-Mathal al-Sāʾir 1/237; al-Wisāṭah bayn al-Mutanabbī wa-Khuṣūmihi 46; Qirāḍ al-Ḍayf 1/217; Yatīmat al-Dahr 1/54; al-Ḥilal fī Sharḥ abyāt al-Jumal 1/130; al-Ṣubḥ al-Munabbī ʿan Ḥaythiyyat al-Mutanabbī 1/102; Sharḥ al-Mushkil min Shiʿr al-Mutanabbī 1/598.

title_en: Section 92 — The Station of Repelling the Base with the Vile (Dar' al-Akhass bi al-Khasis)
arabic_text:
### | الصفحة 120

الله منهج التوفي/ المقام الرايع: هرء الاعس بالخصيس
لا يذكر الحب إلا في مدائجه دعوى ليمع أسماعا وأبنصارا
كناقر العود وشى فيه توشية- ويعدذلك غنى فيه أشعارا
وقد قصد صاحب البردة التبرك بمدح رسول الله يه وقد بدأها بالتشيب»

وكذلك حسان بن ثابت”' في قصيدته التي قال فيها©:

# PageV1P122
anchors:
- Root: د-ر-أ (d-r-')
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To repel, push away, or ward off with force; to parry an attack.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The deliberate deflection of harm or falsehood by a counter-measure, often employing a lesser or apparent evil to preserve a greater good.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in physical combat; metaphorical here as a rhetorical and pedagogical strategy — using obscurity or delay to provoke longing and attention.
- Root: خ-ص-ي-س (kh-s-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Base, vile, contemptible; that which is lowly or of little worth.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the moral context, that which is deemed inferior or repugnant to the soul, yet may be employed as a means to a noble end.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally "the vile"; metaphorically, the initial unattractive or puzzling elements (like the disjointed letters of the Qur'an) used to captivate and draw the listener toward the sublime.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taqdīm wa Ta'khīr (Fronting and Delaying) — The deliberate postponement of clarification (ibhām) followed by elucidation (tawḍīḥ) to heighten rhetorical effect and psychological engagement.
translation:
I say — may Allah grant success — this is the fourth station: repelling the base with the vile.

The lover does not mention the Beloved except in his praises — a claim that deafens ears and blinds eyes — like a lute-player who adorns his instrument with ornamentation, and after that, enriches it with melodies.

The author of the Burdah (al-Būṣīrī) sought blessing by praising the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, yet he began it with the amatory prelude (al-tashbīb). Likewise, Ḥassān ibn Thābit — may Allah be pleased with him — in his ode in which he said, beginning with the amatory prelude and love-talk:

[al-Wāfir meter]
"Effaced are the abodes of Dhāt al-Aṣābi' and al-Jiwā', / to ʿAsas-darā', whose dwelling has become desolate."

And al-Fakhr (al-Rāzī) said in his commentary (al-Tafsīr): The strongest of the sayings concerning the openings of the Sūrahs (al-fawātiḥ) is what we have narrated from Qutrub — that the polytheists said to one another: {«لَا تَسْمَعُوا لِهَٰذَا الْقُرْآنِ وَالْغَوْا فِيهِ»} [Fussilat: 26] ("Do not listen to this Qur'an and make noise therein"). So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would speak at the beginnings of the Sūrahs with these letters (like Alif-Lām-Mīm), and they would understand nothing from them. And man is eager for what is withheld from him; thus they would incline their ears to the Qur'an and reflect upon it, hoping that perhaps there would be speech that would interpret that which was obscure and clarify that which was problematic. So that became a means by which they would become listeners to the Qur'an.

And from this same meaning is the descent of revelation at the beginning of al-Bukhārī's chapters (Abwāb), where he (the Prophet ﷺ) said: "Recite!" He (Jibrīl) replied: "I am not one who recites." And it also came that he (the Prophet ﷺ) was seized in the manner of the ringing of a bell — and the worlds gather to listen. Consider also what is in al-Bukhārī, when he said: "Do you know what is the right of Allah upon His servants?" And likewise in al-Bukhārī, when Muʿādh was riding behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the saddle; the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Muʿādh ibn Jabal!" He said: "At your service, O Messenger of Allah, and at your pleasure." He said: "O Muʿādh ibn Jabal" — three times — then: "Do you know what is the right of Allah upon His servants?" — see the end of the chapters on knowledge (Abwāb al-ʿIlm). And similar is the ḥadīth of Abū Dharr, and similar is in al-Ṣaḥīḥ according to what al-Tirmidhī mentioned, when he ﷺ said: "Say!" — and I said nothing. He said the third time: "Say: {«قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ»} and the Muʿawwidhatayn (the two chapters of refuge) when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, three times."

And in the Muwaṭṭaʾ, when he ﷺ said to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "Indeed, I hope that you will not leave the mosque until you learn a Sūrah the like of which has not been revealed in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Psalms." Ubayy said: "So I began to slow my walking, hoping for that." Then I said: "O Messenger of Allah, the Sūrah which you promised me?" So I recited {«الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ»} to its end. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It is this one, and it is the Seven Oft-Repeated (al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī)."

So consider: the Sūrah was already in Ubayy ibn Kaʿb's memory. Yet despite that, the Prophet ﷺ kept it obscure to him. Then, with the obscurity, he remained silent toward him until Ubayy's motives for longing to know it were fully gathered, so that it would fall in the station of merit that it deserved.

Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ said: A group of scholars and imitators of the Ummah have enumerated many aspects of the inimitability (iʿjāz) of the Qur'an. Among them: that its reciter never tires of it, and its listener never loathes it; one delights in it in solitude, and finds comfort in its recitation in times of distress. And other books do not contain this — until their authors introduced melodies and tunes (alḥān wa ṭuruq) by which they sought to stimulate their enthusiasm for reading them.

Consider the saying of ʿIyāḍ: that melodies stimulate enthusiasm. And Ibn al-ʿArabī said: There is no disagreement that the law of those before us is a law for us (sharʿu man qablanā sharʿun lanā).

# PageV1P123
anchors:
- Root: ح-س-ن (ḥ-s-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Beauty, excellence, goodness in form and quality; ḥusn al-ṣawt = melodiousness of voice.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥusn as moral and aesthetic perfection; in recitation, it signifies the outward manifestation of inward reverence (khushūʿ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical beauty of voice; metaphorical (majāz) for spiritual beauty that moves the heart toward God.
- Root: ط-ر-ب (ṭ-r-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Joy, agitation, or emotional stirring; taṭrīb = vocal modulation that induces emotional rapture.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In worship, taṭrīb is permissible only if it enhances khushūʿ, not if it becomes a worldly performance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: musical cadence; metaphorical: excessive ornamentation that may distract from the meaning.
- Root: ل-ح-ن (l-ḥ-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Melody, tune; also deviation from correct speech (laḥn al-qawl).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Talḥīn in recitation = applying melodic patterns; permissible if it preserves the Quranic text's integrity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: singing; metaphorical: reciting with a pleasing voice that aids reflection.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-bayān (Appositional clarification) — The phrase "wa-lam yara li-man yaʾkhuḏu ʿalā al-talḥīn..." uses apposition to clarify the object of dislike, showing the juristic nuance between prohibition and mere disapproval (karāhah).
translation:
I say — and this is from the section on Mālikī legal questions — he (the author) said: Mālik disapproved of vocal modulation (taṭrīb) in the call to prayer (adhān). And he did not permit that one who takes payment for melodic recitation (talḥīn) in Ramadan receive wages or reward, because he disapproved of it. That is because the intention of worldly gain enters into it, and it is as if he is merely selling his voice. Now, payment for prayer (ṣalāh) is permissible in our school; and recitation with melody (talḥīn) is Sunnah; and hearing it increases faith in the Quran and gladness, and it instills fear (khashyah) in the heart.

He said: It has been established through every path (ṭarīq) that Abū Mūsā (al-Ashʿarī) said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Had I known that you were listening to me, I would have beautified it for you with a most beautiful modulation (taḥbīr)." Ibn Mughaffal said: I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ on the Day of Conquest (of Mecca) reciting Sūrat al-Fatḥ {«إِنَّا فَتَحْنَا لَكَ فَتْحًا مُبِينًا»} — and he said: he modulated it (tarajjaʿa fīhā). Then he recited, and he (the narrator) imitated the Prophet's recitation. It was asked: How was his modulation? He said: "Āʾ āʾ āʾ" — three times.

Ibn Baṭṭāl said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and others permitted recitation with melody (talḥīn).

And it was heard from Ibn al-Qāsim: Mālik disapproved that one say to a man with a beautiful voice: "Recite for us." It was said: What do you think of what ʿUmar said to Abū Mūsā: "Remind us of our Lord"? He (Ibn al-Qāsim) said: By God, I have never heard this before this gathering. He said: And I do not love that one act upon it. Then Ibn Rushd interpreted Mālik's words, and he (Ibn Rushd) disapproved of that (i.e., requesting recitation) if they say it to him seeking tenderness of their hearts by hearing his beautiful recitation. And ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, when he saw Abū Mūsā, would say: "Remind us of our Lord," so he would recite to him, and he had a beautiful voice. He (Ibn Rushd) said: And there is no harm in this if it is verified from the doer that it is on this basis (i.e., sincere spiritual seeking). This ends the quotation of some of Ibn Rushd's words.

And he (the author) said in another place: And a beautiful voice with the Quran is a gift (mawhibah) from God and a bestowal upon its possessor, because a beautiful voice with it is among the things that necessitate humility (khushūʿ) and tenderness of heart, and it calls to goodness. He said: And it has been said concerning His statement, the Exalted: {«يَزِيدُ فِي الْخَلْقِ مَا يَشَاءُ»} [Sūrat Fāṭir: 1] — that it means beautiful voice. And the Messenger of God ﷺ said to Abū Mūsā, congratulating him for what God had given him of beautiful voice: "You have indeed been given a flute (mizmār) from the flutes of the family of Dāwūd." And he ﷺ said: "God has not listened to anything as He listens to a Prophet who recites the Quran with a melodious voice (yataghannā bi-al-Qurʾān)" — meaning: He has not listened to a Prophet who beautifies his voice with the Quran, seeking tenderness of heart thereby. He said: And it seems best to me that the meaning of "He is not of us who does not recite the Quran with melody (yataghannā bi-al-Qurʾān)" is: whoever does not seek to make his heart tender thereby (i.e., by beautifying his voice in recitation).

لبا منهج اوفي/ لعفا الريع: هد الأعس بالضييس
من هؤلاء؟ ومن معلمهم؟ فوالله ما رأيت قط أنبل من هؤلاء وما صحب هؤلاء
رجل إلا نبلوه؛ فقالوا: أصحاب سحتون فقال: والله قد رأيت أصحاب العلماء
عندنا في المشرق» فواله ما رأيت مثل هؤلاء.
قال عياض: وكان حمديس ينكر على هؤلاء الذين يجتمعون للتغيير ويدقون
صدورهمء قال: وهو الذي صلى على ابن معتب؛ قال: وكان ابن معتب هذا ثقة
عالما بالحديث صحيح اليقين بله وكان فيه رقة؛ مر في طريقه إلى مسجد السبت
بدار قسمع فيها غناء؛ ققرع الباب» فخرج إليه صاحب الدارء فاستأذنه في الدخوله
فاستحيا صاحب الدارء واعتفرء فقال: لا بد.
فدخل صاحب الدار قبله وغيب ما كان بين أيديهم؛ ثم أذن له. ودخل فسلمه
وقال: من المتكلم؟ قالوا: هذا. فقال: سألتك بالل إلا أعدت ما سمعت منك؛ فقال
العفو أولى لمن كانت له القدر لا سيما عن مقر ليس يتنصر
أقر بالذنب إجلالا لسيده وقام بين يديه وهويعتذر

فبكى ابن معتب وحن وأن وردد مرارًا وانتحب؛ وقام؛ وقال: تاب الله عليكم
وخرج فتاب صاحب الدارء وسار أحمد إلى مسجد السيث:

بكاء ونوح؛ وكان القراء إذا علموا به تحركوا فقرؤوا وغبروا وأخذوا في تغير":
ماديا بسن جهل الشزاا ‏ قَقذ حير الث لَهَاوَعاا

# PageV1P125
anchors:
- Root: ر-ق-ق (r-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Softness, thinness, delicacy; a heart that is tender and easily moved.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The heart’s receptivity to divine admonition, a state of spiritual vulnerability before the truth.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical thinness; Metaphorical: emotional tenderness and humility in worship.
- Root: خ-ش-ع (kh-sh-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Submissiveness, humility, lowering oneself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The soul’s abasement before God, manifesting in bodily stillness and tearful devotion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: lowering the gaze and voice; Metaphorical: inner awe and reverence.
- Root: غ-ن-ي (gh-n-y) — used in the text as "ghinā’" (singing)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Singing, melodious recitation; also wealth (from a different sense of the root).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Not a theological term; here used in its common lexical sense of song.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: vocal music; Metaphorical: the pleasure of the ear, contrasted with the spiritual delight of Qur’anic recitation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — When a noun is followed by another that clarifies it without a conjunction, as in "Sahnūn, the imam of the people," the second noun is in apposition, providing a defining attribute.
translation:
I say — may God guide us and you — the path of the rightly guided in repelling the base with the baser is through hearing the recitation of the Qur’an, due to the tenderness of their hearts; just as the people of error delight in hearing their songstresses. This is part of the speech of Ibn Rushd.

And we relate from ʿIyāḍ, from Saḥnūn, that he said to a man: "Recite to me: {«وَتَهَوْم مِنْ آدْعُوكْمْ إل الت»} [Ghāfir: 41]." So he recited it, and when the reciter reached the verse: {«مَسْكِذُكْيُوتَ مَآ أَقُولُ لَكُمْ»} [Ghāfir: 44], he (Saḥnūn) said: "Enough for you," while he was weeping.

ʿIyāḍ said: Saḥnūn was tender-hearted, outwardly devout, the ascetic of this community; and there was none between Mālik and Saḥnūn more learned in jurisprudence (fiqh) than Saḥnūn. Al-Qābisī said: "I find within myself regarding Saḥnūn’s disagreement with Mālik what I do not find regarding Ibn al-Qāsim’s disagreement with Mālik." And Ibn Ḥārith said: "Saḥnūn was the imam of the people; he made the Sunnah manifest and extinguished innovation (bidʿah); he dispersed the people of innovation from the mosque; and he was severe against them. Those who attended his gathering from the worshippers were more numerous than those who attended from the students of knowledge." ʿIyāḍ said: Saḥnūn, Ibn Rashīd, and Ibn al-Ṣamādaḥī went out to al-Munastīr, and with them was one who would recite with a plaintive voice (yughabbir). The narrator said: "I looked at Saḥnūn as his tears flowed onto his beard; then the young man fell silent, and Saḥnūn said: 'He hopes to raise his voice if there were one to say to him — and he refused to say to him.'"

ʿIyāḍ said, concerning the aforementioned Ibn al-Ṣamādaḥī, that he heard from Ibn al-Qāsim; he said: "And Saḥnūn heard from him." He said: "He was among the people of knowledge and religion, distinct from the people of innovation." Saḥnūn said: "No one has sat for thirty years more deserving of issuing legal rulings (fatwā) than Ibn al-Ṣamādaḥī." And ʿIyāḍ said, concerning the aforementioned Ibn Rashīd: "He is trustworthy, among the people of knowledge and jurisprudence; he narrated from Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qāsim."

And from some of Saḥnūn’s companions, he said: "I married, and on the night of my wedding I invited a group of our companions, among whom was a man from the East, one of the companions of Ibn Ḥanbal, who had come to us, and we used to hear from him. Our companions were at the beginning of the night in plaintive recitation (taghbīr) and humility; then after that they took up questions of knowledge; then after that they hastened to the corners of the house to pray their devotional portions (aḥzāb). The Shaykh said: 'Who are these people? And who is their teacher? By God, I have never seen anyone more noble than these, and no man has accompanied them but that they ennobled him.' They said: 'They are the companions of Saḥnūn.' He said: 'By God, I have seen the companions of the scholars among us in the East, and by God, I have not seen the like of these.'"

ʿIyāḍ said: And Ḥamdīs used to disapprove of those who gathered for plaintive recitation (taghbīr) and beat their chests. He said: "And he (Ḥamdīs) was the one who prayed over Ibn Muʿattib." He said: "This Ibn Muʿattib was trustworthy, learned in ḥadīth, sound in certainty, and there was in him tenderness. He passed on his way to the Saturday mosque by a house in which singing (ghinā’) was heard. He knocked on the door, and the owner of the house came out to him. He asked his permission to enter, and the owner of the house was ashamed and made excuses, but he said: 'It must be.' So the owner of the house entered before him and concealed what was before them; then he gave him permission. He entered, greeted him, and said: 'Who is the speaker?' They said: 'This one.' He said: 'I ask you by God, but that you repeat what I heard from you.' So he (the singer) said:

'Pardon is more fitting for one who has the power — especially from one who confesses, not one who seeks victory.
He confessed the sin out of reverence for his master, and stood before him while excusing himself.'

Then Ibn Muʿattib wept, and moaned, and repeated it many times, and sobbed; then he stood and said: 'God has turned in forgiveness upon you.' And he went out, and the owner of the house repented. And Aḥmad proceeded to the Saturday mosque."

Ibn al-Liyād said: "I attended the gathering of remembrance on Saturday, and Ibn Muʿattib was present, and he had weeping and lamentation. When the reciters knew of him, they were moved, and they recited, and made plaintive recitation (taghbīr), and took up the plaintive mode (taghbīr):

'They have been tried by the ignorance of the times — indeed, the heart has been bewildered by its distractions.'

Then he said:

'O my heart, you are consumed by sorrow, and the night is folded over our griefs.'

He was moved and wept. Then he recited: {«يَتَيبْ لَاحَن لِيكَ ايُّؤمْ لَا أَنْتَزْ خَرُؤت»} [al-Zukhruf: 68] — the three verses — and he cried out with a severe cry, then fell on his face, and remained for an hour. A man lifted him to his chest, and spoke to him, but he did not speak; and he had closed his eyes. Then he vomited something..."

title_en: Section 95 — The Death of Ibn Muʿattib, the Testimony of Ibn al-Labbād, Ibn al-Tabbān, Ibn Masarra, Aḥmad ibn Ayyūb, and Abū Bakr al-Shiblī

أخضر» فلما انقضى المجلس ختم بالدعاء؛ أردنا أن نحمله على دابة فلم نستطع؛ إذ
لا يثبت. فجئنا بمحمل على جمل؛ فحمل؛ وأخذ من في المسجد ييكي؛ كأنه مأتم؛
وحمل في شق المحمل؛ وزامله ابن عم له؛ ثم أنى به داره؛ فققاء شيئًا أخضرء ولم
يتكلم وتركناه لنساته؛ فلما كان بعد العشاء الأخيرة توفي رحمه الله وغلقت
الحوانيت كأنه يوم عيد.

قال ابن اللباد: وحضرت غسله وقد كسي نورًا وضياء بدنء وصلى عليه
حمديس؛ ونودي على جنازته: أيها الناس» لا تفتكم جنازة ابن معتب؛ شهيد القرآ:

وعرف عياض بابن اللباد هذاء قال: كان كثير الاتباع للسنن؛ أحد شيوخ وققهه
ففيهاء مفنئاء مجاب الدعوة؛ عول الشيخ أبو محمد عليه وعلى المميسي؛ قال: وكان
يحضر مجلس السبت؛ ويقول: هو يغيظ بني عبيد. وقال عياض: عن هذا المسجد
كان يجتمع إليه جماعة من أهل الفقه والصلاح والرقة؛ ويقرأ القرآن» وينشد أشعار
الزهد.

.وكذا حكى عياض عن ابن التبان قال: هو الففيه الامام؛ من العلماء الراسخين
والفقهاء المبرزين: قال: ضربت إليه أكباد الإبل من الأمصار؛ لعلمه بالذب عن
مذهب مالك؛ قال: وكان مستجاب الدعوة؛ يميل إلى الرقة؛ يسمع التغيير؛ ويرق
الهذه المعاتيء سأله الخراط يوا وقد وجد عنده مغبرّاء فقال: أليس التغيير بدعة؟
قال له: والاجتماع أيضًا على المسائل بدعة. فش هذا الكلام على السائل.

انظر نص العلماء والسلف أبي بن كعب وزيد وغيرهماء كانوا يكرهون
السؤال في العلم عما لم يتزل. وقال مالك أيضًاء أدركت أهل هذه البلدة وما عند
أحدهم علم غير الكتاب والسئة: فإذا نزلت نازلة جمع الأمير من حضر من العلماء»
فما اتفقوا عليه أنفذه؛ وأنئم تكثرون المسائل ورسول الله يل قد نهى عنها. اه نص
مالك

وقال عياض: لما مات ابن التبان المذكور؛ قال القابسي: رحمك الله لقد كنث
تغار على المذهب؛ وتذب عن الشريعة.

وعرف عياض بابن المسرة من العلماء المالكية: قال: وكان صالمًا ناسكاء
يسمع التغيير وربما حرك منه؛ فيكي ويقيم أي لا يتفع به.

وعرف عياض بأبي بكر الشبلي: فقال: هو شيخ الصوفية. وإمام أهل العلم
الباطن وذوي الأنباء البديعة: أحد المتصرفين في علوم الشريعة؛ كان عالمًا فقيها

والنفس ميلا وقبولاء فإن كان منغما انتهى ذلك بتقدير الحركات والسكنات منه
وترديد الأنقاس عليه وذلك التحبير في الكلام والتنغيم في الغناء» وقد مات قوم

ولما أنشد في "راج"
ليس التصوف لبس الصوف ترقعه ولا بكاؤك إن غنى المغنونا

ولا صياح ولا رقص ولااطرب ولا تغاش كأن قد صرت مجنونا
بل التصوف أن تصفو بلا كدر وتتبع الححق والقسرآن والسدينا
وأن تسرى خاشعاله مكتبا على ذنوبك طول الدهر محزونا

قال: وقد رأيت في هذه الطائفة أعيانًا يفخر بهم على سائر الملل أهل هذه
الملة علمًا وخشية وكرامات كثيرة وإن كان فيهم مثل هذا الوصف المذموم؛ فإنهم

# PageV1P127
anchors:
- Root: خ-ت-م (khatama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To seal, conclude, stamp; the final act of a gathering or ritual.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The concluding supplication (duʿāʾ) as the seal of a spiritual assembly, marking its completion and blessing.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sealing of a document; metaphorically, the closing of a session with prayer.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The use of appositives to specify and elaborate on a preceding noun, as in "Ibn al-Labbād" being identified with further descriptors.
translation:
I say: When the session concluded, it was sealed with supplication. We desired to mount him upon a beast, but we were unable, for he could not remain steady. So we brought a litter upon a camel, and he was carried; and those in the mosque began to weep, as if it were a day of mourning. He was borne in one side of the litter, and a cousin of his accompanied him. Then he was brought to his house, and he vomited something green, and did not speak; we left him to his womenfolk. Then, after the final night prayer (al-ʿishāʾ al-ākhirah), he died — may God have mercy on him — and the shops were closed as if it were a festival day.

Ibn al-Labbād said: I attended his washing, and his body was clothed in light and radiance. Prayer was offered over him by Ḥamdīs, and a crier called out over his bier: "O people, do not let the funeral of Ibn Muʿattib, the martyr of the Qurʾān, escape you!"

Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ identified this Ibn al-Labbād, saying: He was one who greatly followed the Prophetic practices (sunan), one of the leading jurists of his time, a legal authority (muftī), and one whose supplication was answered. Shaykh Abū Muḥammad relied upon him and upon al-Mumayyisī. He said: He used to attend the Saturday session and would say: "It enrages the Banū ʿUbayd." ʿIyāḍ also said: Around this mosque would gather a group of people of jurisprudence, righteousness, and tenderness of heart; they would recite the Qurʾān and chant ascetic poetry.

Likewise, ʿIyāḍ related from Ibn al-Tabbān, saying: He is the jurist, the imam, among the deeply rooted scholars and the distinguished jurists. He said: Camels' livers were struck toward him from the distant provinces (amṣār) for his knowledge in defending the school of Mālik. He said: His supplication was answered; he inclined toward tenderness, would hear the admonition (al-taghayyur), and would soften at these meanings. A turner (al-Kharrāṭ) once asked him a question, finding him with a dusty appearance, and said: "Is not admonition (al-taghayyur) an innovation (bidʿah)?" He replied: "And is not gathering together over questions also an innovation?" This speech silenced the questioner.

Consider the text of the scholars and the Salaf — Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Zayd, and others — they disliked asking questions in knowledge about what had not yet occurred. Mālik also said: I reached the people of this town, and none of them possessed knowledge other than the Book and the Sunnah. When a calamity befell, the governor would gather those scholars present, and whatever they agreed upon, he would implement. But you multiply questions, while the Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — forbade them. This is the end of Mālik's text.

ʿIyāḍ said: When the aforementioned Ibn al-Tabbān died, al-Qābisī said: "May God have mercy on you; you were indeed zealous for the school (madhhab) and defended the Sacred Law (Sharīʿah)."

ʿIyāḍ identified Ibn Masarra among the Mālikī scholars, saying: He was a righteous, devout man; he would hear the admonition and sometimes be moved by it, weeping and remaining — that is, not being benefited by it.

ʿIyāḍ identified Aḥmad ibn Ayyūb, saying: He read under al-Qābisī and adhered to Ibn Abī Zamanīn. He said: He was present in knowledge, and preaching and remembrance (dhikrā) dominated him; he was prolific in poetry, and among the people he had ascetic poems and exaltations (takābīr) that the admonishing chanters circulated. He died in Cordoba in his session in the mosque suddenly, and the common people were agitated with an agitation never heard of its like. People attended his funeral until Cordoba was emptied, and the authorities needed to control it and guard its gates until his affair was finished. His bier did not reach his grave until late afternoon.

ʿIyāḍ identified Abū Bakr al-Shiblī, saying: He is the shaykh of the Sufis and the imam of the people of inner knowledge and those of wondrous insights; one of those who operated within the sciences of the Sacred Law. He was a scholar and jurist upon the school of Mālik. He said: He was asked about listening to music (al-samāʿ); he said: "Its outward aspect is temptation (fitnah), and its inward aspect is a lesson (ʿibrah). Whoever understands the allusion, listening to the lesson is lawful for him." Among the rulings of Ibn al-ʿArabī: Many jurists of the provinces deemed beautiful the recitation with melodies and vocal modulation (al-alḥān wa-l-tarjīʿ), but Mālik disapproved of that; yet it is permissible, and what he said in his "Sirāj" has preceded. He said: "The heart humbles before a beautiful voice just as it humbles before a handsome face; and what hearts are affected by in piety is greater in reward." He said in his "ʿĀriḍah": "The voice has a great effect upon the soul. If the speech is gentle, delicate in its edges, it widens the ear in hearing, and the soul in inclination and acceptance. If it is melodious, that reaches its end by the proportioning of its movements and pauses, and the repetition of breaths upon it — and that is the embellishment in speech and the melodiousness in song. People have died among the poor (fuqarāʾ) in listening to the truth, and many of the idle have died in listening to the passion of love." And when it was recited in his "Rāj":

"Tasawwuf is not the wearing of wool, patched, nor your weeping when the singers sing,
Nor shouting, nor dancing, nor excitement, nor swooning as if you had become mad.
Rather, tasawwuf is that you be pure without blemish, and follow the Truth, the Qurʾān, and the religion,
And that you walk humbly, weeping over your sins all the days, sorrowful."

He said: I have seen in this group eminent persons by whom the people of this religion boast over all other creeds — in knowledge, godliness, and abundant miracles (karāmāt) — even if among them there is such blameworthy description as this; for they are...

فلترجع لما اخترته من نصوص أثمة الصوفية وأختم هذا المقام بكلام الأمام
المتفق على علمه ودينه: قال ابن عرفة: ولا يتعقد للمسلمين إجماع بدونه؛ وهو: عز
الدين بن عبد السلام؛ رويت رسالة القشيري عن شيخي المنتوري من طريقين.
وفال ابن خلكان فيه ما نصه: كان القشيري علامة في الفقه والتغسير والحديث
والأصول؛ عرف الإسفرائيني محله من العلم؛ وقال القاضي ابن العربي في الاسم
الثالث والعشرين والمائة من سراجه: إنه الأستاذ الإمام؛ قال: وكتابه التحيير من
الكتب المفيدة؛ وقال محيي النووي في "المنهاج”: قال السيد الجليل أبو القاسم
القشيري؛ وعرف ابن خلكان أيضًا بالاستاذ أبي علي الدقاق» قال: إمام وقنه؛ فقال
الاستاذ أبو القاسم القشيري المذكور: سألت الأستاذ أبا علي غير مرة شبه طلب
رخصة في السماع؛ وكان يجيبني إلى ما يوجب الإمساك عنه؛ ثم بعد طول المعاودة
: إن المشائخ قالوا: ما أجمع قلبك إلى الله فلا بأس به.

وقيل لابن سالم: كيف تنكر السماع وقد كان الجنيد وسري وذو النون

وغيرهم يسمعون؟ قال: كيف أنكره وقد أجازه من هو خير مني؟

ورويت كتاب القوت عن شيخي المنتوري من طريقين» قال فيه: إن أنكرنا
السماع أنكرنا على سبعين صديفًا من خيار هذه الأمة؛ قال: وإن كنا تعلم أن الإتكار
أقرب إلى قلوب القراء؛ إلا أن لا نفعل؛ لأنا نعلم ما لا يعلمونء وسمعنا من السلف
والأصحاب ما لا يسمعون. قال في 'عوارف المعارف”: قول الشيخ أبي طالب هذا
معتير؛ لوفور علمه؛ وكمال حاله؛ ومعرفته بأحوال السلف: ومكان تقواه: وورعه
وتحريه للأصوب والأولى. اف

ورويت أيضًا هذا الكتاب؛ يعني "عوارف المعارف”؛ عن شيخي المتوري من
طريقين» قال شيخي المنتوري فيه: هو الإمام. وقال عنه ابن خلكان: إنه كان شيخ
ا مشائخ عصرء يكتبون إليه يسألون.

# PageV1P129
anchors:
- Root: س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Auditory perception; the act of hearing with the ear, whether of sound or speech.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, samāʿ denotes the receptive hearing of divine address or spiritual truths; here, it is the technical term for listening to devotional poetry or music.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) = physical hearing; metaphorical (majāz) = the heart's attentive reception of spiritual meanings.
- Root: ق-و-ت (q-w-t)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Nourishment, sustenance; that which sustains life.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Spiritual sustenance for the soul, as in the title Qūt al-Qulūb (Nourishment of Hearts).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = bodily food; metaphorical = that which sustains the inner life of faith.
- Root: و-ر-ع (w-r-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Piety, scrupulous abstention from doubtful matters.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The virtue of cautious avoidance of anything that might compromise one's religious integrity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = protective caution; metaphorical = the soul's guarding against spiritual harm.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa-l-istithnāʾ) — The text employs conditional clauses (e.g., "if the heart is gathered to God") and exceptions to qualify rulings, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis.
translation:
I say — and this concludes what I have gathered from the texts of the Mālikī imams on the matter of spiritual audition (samāʿ). Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ testified that they were righteous, exemplary imams of the Sunnah. Thus, a person finds in himself that they are truthful, due to confidence in them and in their words, upon the original soundness [of their transmission] — just as one believes of their innovator that he is a man with an agenda, and one does not hold that same good opinion of him.

So let us return to what I have selected from the texts of the imams of the Sufis, and conclude this station with the words of the imam whose knowledge and religion are unanimously agreed upon — he said: Ibn ʿArafah said: "No consensus of the Muslims is held valid without him" — namely, ʿIzz al-Dīn ibn ʿAbd al-Salām. I have transmitted the *Risālah* of al-Qushayrī from my shaykh al-Muntūrī through two chains. Ibn Khallikān said of him, verbatim: "Al-Qushayrī was a scholar of the highest rank in jurisprudence (fiqh), exegesis (tafsīr), hadith, and the principles of religion (uṣūl)." Al-Isfarāʾīnī acknowledged his standing in knowledge. And Qāḍī Ibn al-ʿArabī said, in the one hundred and twenty-third name of his book *al-Sirāj*: "He is the master imam (al-ustādh al-imām)." He said: "His book *al-Taḥbīr* is among the most beneficial of books." And Muḥyī al-Nawawī said in *al-Minhāj*: "The noble master Abū al-Qāsim al-Qushayrī said..." Ibn Khallikān also identified him with the master Abū ʿAlī al-Daqqāq, saying: "He was the imam of his time." The aforementioned master Abū al-Qāsim al-Qushayrī said: "I asked the master Abū ʿAlī more than once, seeking a dispensation (rukḥṣah) regarding spiritual audition, and he would answer me with what necessitated refraining from it. Then, after prolonged persistence, he said: 'The shaykhs have said: Whatever your heart is gathered toward God in, there is no harm in it.'"

And it was said to Ibn Sālim: "How do you deny spiritual audition, when al-Junayd, Sarī, and Dhū al-Nūn and others used to listen?" He said: "How could I deny it, when one better than me has permitted it?"

I also transmitted the book *al-Qūt* from my shaykh al-Muntūrī through two chains. In it he said: "If we deny spiritual audition, we would be denying seventy righteous companions from the best of this ummah." He said: "Even though we know that denial is closer to the hearts of the reciters (qurrāʾ), we do not do so, for we know what they do not know, and we have heard from the predecessors (salaf) and the companions what they have not heard." He said in *ʿAwārif al-Maʿārif*: "The statement of Shaykh Abū Ṭālib [al-Makkī] is authoritative, due to the abundance of his knowledge, the perfection of his state, his acquaintance with the conditions of the predecessors, his degree of piety (taqwā), his scrupulousness (waraʿ), and his striving for what is most correct and most fitting."

I also transmitted this book — meaning *ʿAwārif al-Maʿārif* — from my shaykh al-Muntūrī through two chains. My shaykh al-Muntūrī said of it: "It is [the work of] the imam." And Ibn Khallikān said of him [al-Suhrawardī]: "He was the shaykh of the shaykhs of his age; they would write to him seeking [his counsel]."

And from *al-Risālah*, on the authority of some of the shaykhs: "Spiritual audition has three aspects. One aspect is for the beginning seekers (murīdūn), who thereby invoke noble spiritual states (aḥwāl)." And Ibn al-Bannāʾ said:

"When bodies were too heavy to move,  
One of them said: 'O driver of the camels!'"

Then he said:

"It is a path stretched out before them,  
Made easy for the finder and the destitute."

Al-Ghazālī elaborated on this in *al-Iḥyāʾ*, saying: "They apply what they hear to their own states in their dealings with God, and their states overcome them. For the seeker inevitably has a goal — namely, knowledge of God and arrival at Him. So when he hears mention of address or rebuke, acceptance or rejection, union or separation, proximity or distance, yearning for what is lost, thirst for what is awaited, longing for what approaches, hope or despair, solitude or intimacy, fulfillment of a covenant or breaking of a covenant, fear of parting or joy of meeting, mention of the Beloved's gaze, repelling the watchful, the flowing of tears, the succession of regrets, the length of separation, or the difficulty of union — or anything else that poetry contains — it must necessarily correspond to the seeker's state in his quest. Thus it runs the course of the fire-stick that strikes a spark from his heart, so its flames ignite, the stirring of longing is strengthened and agitated, and there rush upon him, by God's will, states contrary to his habit. And he has a wide field in applying the words to his own conditions. So spiritual audition stirs up longing if longing already exists; and if no longing exists, audition brings it about. For effort (kasb) has a role in attracting spiritual states; and for this reason the report came commanding the one who does not weep to feign weeping (tabākā)."

"For these states may have their beginnings undertaken with effort. And just as it is permissible for a preacher to compose his speech in exhortation, adorn it with rhymed prose (sajʿ), and stir people's longing for the proofs, so too is it permissible for another to do the same through the composition of poetry. For when taste (dhawq) is joined to rhymed prose, the speech becomes more impactful upon the heart. And when a beautiful voice and pleasant, measured melodies are added to it, its impact increases." End of the quotation from *al-Iḥyāʾ*. I have also transmitted it from my shaykh al-Muntūrī through two chains. And the account of Ibn Muʿnib has already preceded, when he heard singing at a house, and their singer was saying:

"Pardon is more fitting for one who has the power [to punish]..."

# PageV1P131
anchors:
- Root: س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Auditory perception; the physical act of hearing, distinct from mere sound reception.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, hearing (samāʿ) denotes the heart's attentive reception of divine truth, often contrasted with mere sensual listening.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) hearing is physical; metaphorical (majāz) hearing is the soul's comprehension of spiritual meanings embedded in sound.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ) — The narrative uses "idhā" (when) to introduce contingent events, governing the sequence of actions with precise temporal subordination.
translation:
I say: Know that the station of hearing the call through the base (al-khasīs) is among the subtle paths of the rightly guided. Its reality is that the sincere listener, when struck by a divine reminder in an unexpected or lowly setting, is moved to transformation. Consider what was related in the "Risālah" (of al-Qushayrī) from al-Sarrāj, who said: I and Ibn al-Fawʿatī were passing along the Tigris between Basra and al-Ubullah, when behold, a beautiful palace appeared, upon which sat a man, and before him a slave-girl singing, saying: «...» (a verse of poetry).

Then, a young man beneath the archway, holding a water-skin and wearing a patched cloak, was listening. He called out: "O slave-girl, by the sanctity of your Master, repeat it!" She repeated it, and the poor man said: "By God, this is a trial with the Truth!" Then he gave a gasp that expelled his soul. The palace-owner said: "You are free for the sake of God." And the people of Basra went out and finished burying him and praying over him. Then the palace-owner stood and said: "Do you not know me? I make you witnesses that everything I own is in the path of God."

So observe the repentance of these two men through the sincerity of the listeners. Likewise, they said: The Sufi is like the earth—every ugly thing is cast upon it, yet from it emerges every beautiful thing. They do not cast their stones upon people, but rather they pour their lights upon them.

He said in "al-Taḥbīr": There is nothing between him (the Sufi) and anyone that does not become either truth or falsehood. And ʿIzz al-Dīn ibn ʿAbd al-Salām said: The path to rectifying hearts is by everything that draws near to God—from states of fear, hope, and trust. These states may be elicited by recollection, so one remembers these cognitions (maʿārif), and from them arise their fitting states. Among people, some do not have these cognitions present except through an external cause, and they have ranks: some have them present upon hearing the Qurʾān—these are the best of the listeners; some have them present at preaching and reminding; some have them present at chants and hymns—and in this there is deficiency from the share of the soul; and some have these cognitions present upon hearing melodies whose permissibility is disputed, such as the drum and flutes. For such a one, if he believes that is forbidden, he is wrong in his listening but right in what he attains of cognitions and the states arising from them. Refer to the end of his "Qawāʿid."

He said in his "Qawāʿid": Whoever commits a corruption thinking it a benefit bears no sin; and whoever does an act, then it becomes clear it is forbidden, is rewarded for his intention. He said: Listening (samāʿ) is from the Truth, exalted be He, as a gift. For this reason, the prophets did not occupy themselves with listening to instruments and singing, but confined themselves to their states. He said: Whoever is possessed by whisperings and overcome by self-talk cannot achieve good listening. Then, listening to good speech with melodies is suited to souls and delights them, so it dispels their self-talk; the spirit becomes pure, and wisdom falls into its proper place because the soul is occupied with its familiar thing. The spirit aims at the spirits of meanings hidden in melodies, while the soul aims at the existence of melodies. Already the sayyid, the Mufti of Tunis, al-Burzulī, has stated: I have seen many of my teachers for whom this is not their path—they do not disapprove of these people. Nor is it permissible to use as evidence against such people the saying of the Exalted: {«...those who think they are doing good»} [al-Kahf: 104].

And in "al-Tamhīd": "Whoever is pleased by his good deed and displeased by his evil deed"—he said, peace be upon him: "That one is a believer." So whoever is such, from where would he have testimony without faith? He said: A group has gone astray, opposing the People of the Sunnah and the Community, by adducing the apparent meanings of the saying of the Exalted: {«...those whose efforts are lost in this worldly life»} [al-Kahf: 104]. Consider: if a good deed were permissible from this angle, it would have been for ʿUmar, since he said, peace be upon him: "If there were in my nation any Muhaddithūn..." — the hadith. Yet when Muʿāwiyah met him in his great procession, he said: "This is the Kisrā of the Arabs." Then he asked him about that, and Muʿāwiyah said: "We are in the land of the enemy, and spies are many there, so we wanted to display the might of the Sultan to frighten them." ʿUmar said: "I have not asked you about anything except that you left us in a state like the gaps of a molar." Muʿāwiyah said: "If you forbid me, I will desist." ʿUmar said: "I neither command you nor forbid you. Indeed, this..."

منهج الترقي/ المفام الرابع: درء الاعس بالخسيس ‏ لهذا
كان ما تقوله حمًا إنه لرأي أريب؛ وإن كان باطلا إنه لخدعة أديب.

ورويت عن شيخي المنتوري عن جدي ابن بفي عن شيعخه الأستاذ المقري
أنه قال: حقيقة الشطح كناية؛ والكرامة عناية؛ والاعتراض جنابة؛ إباك إن عرفت
فاتبع؛ وإن جهلت فسلم. وفي "التمهيد” نظر ابن عمر إلى الكمبة وقال: والله إن لك
الحرمة؛ ولكن المؤمن أعظم منك حرمة؛ حرم الله عرضه وماله ودمه: وأن لا يظن به
إلا خير. وانظر في الاسم الخامس عشر المجاهد من سراج ابن العربي قال: نكتة
بديعة؛ وهي: أن النفس تميل إلى اللهوء وتسرع إلى الغزل؛ فينشد المرء الأشعار
الغزلية تأنيَا بهاء ويقصد بها الحقائق الإلهية والشمائل النبوية تحقيقًا معها. وانظر
تمام كلامه في الاسم المذكور: وقد ورد: 'إذا حضر الغداء والصلاة فابدؤوا
بالقداء»

قال في "عوارف المعارف”: وكان الراسبي يشغل أصحابه بالسماع؛ وينعزل
عنهم يصلي: فقد تطرق النغمات مشل هذا المصلي: وتنزل إليها النفس متتعمة
بذلك؛ فيزداد مورد الروح من الإنسان صفاء إلى كلام ذكره؛ ولهذا قيل: السماع
القوم كالدواء. اه

وعلى هذا المأخذ بينت هذا المقام: أن يقصد المرء بالسماع التخلي؛ ولاشك
أن ما يكسب الإنسان تخليًا أولى؛ وهذا هو المقام الخامس.

# PageV1P133
anchors:
- Root: د-ر-أ (d-r-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To repel, push away, or ward off (deflection of harm).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Repelling spiritual corruption by employing a lesser means, akin to averting evil with a permissible counter.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical repulsion; Metaphorical: employing a lowly instrument to safeguard higher religious aims.
- Root: خ-س-س (kh-s-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Baseness, lowness, or vileness in rank or worth.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The worldly or sensory as opposed to the spiritual; that which is contemptible in the scale of divine proximity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: lowly physical position; Metaphorical: moral or religious insignificance.
- Root: ن-و-ي (n-w-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intent, purpose, or resolve.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The inward orientation that transforms acts from mere habit into worship (ʿibādah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: aim; Metaphorical: the spiritual currency that elevates the permissible (mubāḥ) to the rank of merit (makrumah).
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — Governing the nuanced parsing of "لو كان... لاضمحلت" (if it were... it would vanish) to express hypothetical consequence.
translation:
I say: This is why what you utter — if it be true, it is a penetrating opinion; and if it be false, it is a deception of an eloquent one.

And I have related from my shaykh al-Muntūrī, from my grandfather Ibn Bufī, from his shaykh, the master al-Maqqarī, that he said: The reality of ecstatic utterance (shaṭḥ) is an allusion; and the miracle-favor (karāmah) is a divine solicitude; and the objection (iʿtirāḍ) is a defilement. Beware — if you recognize, then follow; and if you are ignorant, then submit. And in "al-Tamhīd": Ibn ʿUmar looked at the Kaʿbah and said: By Allah, you possess sanctity; but the believer is greater in sanctity than you — Allah has made sacred his honor, his wealth, and his blood, and that no thought be held of him but good. And consider the fifteenth Name, "The Striver" (al-Mujāhid), from Sirāj Ibn al-ʿArabī, who said: A wondrous subtlety — namely, that the soul inclines to leisure and hastens to amorous verse; so one recites love-poems to refine his bearing, and thereby intends the divine realities and the prophetic virtues, achieving harmony with them. And see the completion of his words under that mentioned Name: And it has been reported: "When the midday meal and the prayer are both present, begin with the meal."

He said in "ʿAwārif al-Maʿārif": And al-Rāsibī used to occupy his companions with listening (samāʿ), while he withdrew from them to pray. For melodies may intrude upon such a praying one, and the soul descends to them, taking delight therein; so the influx of the spirit from the human being increases in purity — up to words he mentioned. For this reason it was said: The listening of the folk is like medicine. End.

And upon this basis I have clarified this station: that one intends by listening the attainment of solitude (takhallī); and undoubtedly, whatever earns a person greater solitude is more worthy. And this is the fifth station.

THE FIFTH STATION: The Presence of Intention Making the Permissible a Noble Deed

And there has preceded the transmission of ʿIyāḍ from Mālik that he said: If I knew that my heart would be rectified by sitting upon a dunghill, I would sit upon it. And there is no doubt that there is no religious purpose in sitting upon a dunghill; rather, it is a base permissible act. But the Imām informed of himself that if that were to lead him to the rectification of his heart, its baseness would vanish in his sight beside the rectification of his heart. And there is no doubt that from this very basis came al-Shāṭibī's approval of the Imām's deed who committed himself to a poem he would recite after every prayer, as has preceded.

And this is akin to what has preceded from the shaykhs: Whatever gathers your heart to Allah, there is no harm in it. And al-Muḥāsibī said: The truthful one is he who cares not if all his standing in the hearts of creation were lost for the sake of rectifying his heart.

And Ibn al-Jawzī said: Among the deceptions of Iblīs upon the jurists is that he makes attractive to them the disparagement of preaching, and they say: "He is a storyteller." And Iblīs's intent is that they not attend a place where the heart softens and humbles. He, Glorified and Exalted, said: {And all that We relate to you of the accounts of the messengers is that whereby We make firm your heart} [Hūd: 120]. It was said to ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak: We find admonitions in books. He said: No harm; and if you find an admonition upon a wall, then look into it and benefit.

And Ibn al-ʿArabī said: If you hear wisdom, take it — even if it be from the tongue of a false one; and extract benefit from it, even if he be burned by it. For He, Glorified and Exalted, has informed that wisdom is given to whom He wills, and none remembers it save those of understanding. And in [the book]... they imprisoned him, though its use is not permissible — for in its imprisonment there is a benefit: by it one is reminded of the ancient covenant, and through it one shows compassion for those who have passed of the noble predecessors. And consider the scholars' words upon Allah's saying: {We seized them with punishment} [al-Aʿrāf: 130]; they said: Because the states of hardship soften the hearts. And the hadith has been reported: "Seek supplication at times of softness, for it is..." — and in [another narration]: There was a bell with the family of ʿUmar; Ibn Rushdah said: It was only...

# PageV1P134
anchors:
- Root: ق-د-و (q-d-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To follow, to imitate, to take as a model; the act of tracing someone's path.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological terms, al-iqtidā' (following) is the emulation of prophetic practice (sunnah) as an act of devotional obedience.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical tracking of footsteps; metaphorical (majāz) — spiritual emulation of conduct.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The phrase "من باب أولى" (by even stronger reason) functions as an elative construction requiring the reader to infer the comparative syllogism from the preceding clause.
translation:
I say — and this is the fifth station of the noble path: the presence of the sacred trace by which the permissible becomes recommended.

And mercy be upon him. Ibn Yūnus and al-Māzarī and others have deemed commendable the approval of the scholars of Medina regarding the going forth of Mūsā ibn Nuṣayr to the prayer for rain with beasts and children — for this softens the hearts. And there is no doubt that the approval of al-Māzarī and Ibn Yūnus for that is evident, just as Ibn ʿArafah said: The recourse of Saḥnūn, after the explicit text (naṣṣ) of Ibn al-Qāsim, to the action of ʿUmar is a leaning from him toward the saying of ʿUmar. Likewise, he said: It appears from Abū ʿUmar a leaning toward the permissibility of plunder (al-nuhbah), given what he mentioned that contradicts the prohibition.

And likewise, my master Ibn Sirāj — may God have mercy on him — used to say: Ibn Abī Zayd leaned toward the permissibility of the embrace (al-muʿānaqah), for he said in "al-Risālah": And Mālik disapproved of the embrace.

It is more fitting to attribute to Mālik the approval of Ibn ʿUmar's turning his she-camel in the place where he saw the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — on his she-camel. And he said: "If only my she-camel would tread upon the very spot where the mount of the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — trod."

And when Ibn Rushd commented on this narration from Mālik, he endorsed it and said: This is the utmost from Ibn ʿUmar in seeking blessing (tabarruk) from the trace of the Prophet — peace be upon him.

And when Abū ʿUmar transmitted this report in his "Tamhīd," he said: This from Ibn ʿUmar is the extreme in following and emulating the Messenger of God — peace be upon him. And Mālik said: I love the supererogatory prayer at the prayer-place of the Prophet — peace be upon him. Ibn Rushd said: Mālik deemed it commendable for the blessing of the place where the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — prayed. And ʿItbān said: O Messenger of God, pray in my house in a place that I may take as a prayer-place. Ibn Rushd said: Mālik deemed it commendable — for he intended thereby to draw down blessing.

And Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah permitted it. And from this category: if a place where the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — prayed once is better than the rest of the house, then by even stronger reason a place where the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — used to persevere in prayer. And Abū ʿUmar said regarding the ḥadīth of ʿItbān: The seeking of blessing from the places which the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — trod and stood upon. And he said: In it is evidence of what the people were upon of the soundness of sincere faith.

And in "Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī": That Sālim used to seek out places on the road and pray in them, because he saw the Prophet — peace be upon him — praying in those places. And in al-Bukhārī also, from Ibn ʿUbayd, he said: ...

### | الصفحة 134

منهج الترقي/ المفام المدامس: حضور النية يصير المباح مكرمة.

آتي مع سلمة بن الأكوع؛ فيصلي عند الأسطوانة التي عند المصحف؛ فقلت:
يا أبا مسلمء أراك تتحرى الصلاة عند هذه الأسطوانة: قال: فإني رأيت رسول الله ل
يتحرى الصلاة عندها. قال عياض: من إعظام رسول الله يق وإكباره إعظام جميع
أسبابه وإكرام مشاهده وأماكنه وما لمسه وك أو عرف به؛ قبل لمالك: لم تنزل
العقيق؟ فإنه يش بعده من المسجد؛ فقال: بلغني أن النبي يك كان يحبه ويأتيه.

وفي "صحيح البخاري": أن النبي م قال: "بواد أناني الليلة آت من ربيء
فقال: صل في هذا الوادي المبارك”"'؛ وكان مالك لا يركب بالمدينة دابة؛ ويقولة
أستحبي من الله أن أطأ تربة فيها رسول اله يق بحافر دابة. ونقل عياض من هذا
المعنى كثيرا. ومن ذلك أن أبا محذورة كان له قصة في مقدم رأسه إذا قعد وأرسلها
أصابت الأرض: فقيل: ألا تحلقها؟ فقال: لم أكن بالذي أحلقها وقد مسها
رصول الله مرة بيده.

وقال: كان في قلنسوة خالد بن الوليد شعرات من شعر رسول اله يف
فسقطت فلنسوته في بعض حرويه؛ فشد عليها شدة أنكر عليه أصحاب النبي 84
كثرة من قتل فيهاء قال: لم أفعل لسبب الفلنسوة» بل لما تضمنته من شعر رسول الله 1946
الثلا أسلب بركتهاء وتقع بيد المشركين. وفي البخاري: عمن ابن سرين: قلت لعبدة:
عندنا من شعر النبي و قال: لآن تكون عندي شعرة منه أحب إلي من الدنيا وما
فبها. وفيه أيضًا: لما حلق رسول الله يق رأسه كان أبو طلحة أول من أخذ شعره.
وفي البخاري أيضًا: اتخذ النبي يك خاتما من ورق؛ وكان في يده؛ ثم كان بعد
في يد عثمان؛ فسقط له بيشر أريس؛ قال الراوي: فاختلفنا ثلائة أيام مع عثمان
تنزح البشرء فلم نجده. قال ابن بطال: في هذا استعمال آثار الصالحين ولياس
ملابسهم على جهة التبرك؛ قال: ونحو ذلك ابتدار الصحابة رضوان الله عليهم
وضوء رسول اله كه ومن لم يصبه منه شيء أخذ من بلل يد صاحبه. ويب
