# PageV1P201

### | الصفحة 201

منهج ني تفن طم على املد م لمكن م تر كا لوقت يجيد في تسر الأرات الاضة.__ 345
مستحب؛ وليس ثقيضه بمكروه؛ وإنما هو مباح؛ فلذلك يصومه من نذره.

وباقي أيام السنة مقتضى التعبد أن تسرمد الصوم كما قاله الشاطبي عن السلف
الصالح.

.وقد تقدم أن آخر كلمة ختم بها ابن بونس ديوانه الفقهي: أخذ القليل خير من
ترك الجميع.

.وقد تقدم أن كل مؤمن راغب في العبادة إلا أن الغفلة تستهويه والشهوة تغلبه
وبالتأسي والاقتداء يقوى نشاطه.

وقد تقدم تقل ابن بشكوال: من بلغه فضل في عمل فعمل به أعطاه الله ذلك
الثواب؛ وإن لم يكن ما بلغه حقا.

وقد تقدم قول محبي الدين النووي: اعمل به ولو مرة.

وتقدم قول عياض: كل ما بلغني من التعبد عملته حتى بلغني عن رجل أنه
ختم القرآن وجامع عياله؛ فاقنديت به. وهذا ليس مقصد شرعي؛ ولا نية؛ إنما ذلك
مجرد غبطة. وقد تقدم قول الشاطبي في التزام الذكر الذي رآه الكتاتي في النوم.

فخصص أنت أيها المريد إن لم تقدر أن تسرمد؛ وصم الأيام التي لها بركة
على الخصوص كستة أيام من شوال: قال ابن رشد: لا يكره لأحد صيامهاء هذا
نصه وتأول اللفظة الواردة عن الإمام عكس الشاطبين الذين جعلوها أصلا وقاسوا
عليها صيام النصف من شعبان.

وعبارة ابن يونس في ديوانه الفقهي الذي هو مصحف المذهب قال ما نصه:
فصل: صيام يوم عاشوراء مرغب فيه ثم قال: وفيه تكسى الكعبة كل عام؛ وقد
» أن من لم بيت صومه حتى أصبح أن له أن يصومه أو باقيه إن أكلء
وروي ذلك عن رسول الله كك عن غير واحد من السلف.

وكان ابن عباس يوالي صوم اليومين؛ خوفًا أن يفوته؛ وكان يصومه في السفر
وفمله ابن شهاب. ثم قال: فصل: وروي أن النبي يقل صام الأشهر الحرم؛ وهي المحرم
ورجب وذو القعدة وذو الحجة. ورغب أيضًا في صيام سبعة وعشرين من رجب؛ فيه
بعث النبي ف ويوم خمسة وعشرين من ذي القعدة؛ وفيه أثزلت الكعبة ومعها
الرحمة؛ وقد رغب في صيام شعبان؛ إذ كان رسول الله كك يصوم فيه أكثر من غيره.

# PageV1P202
anchors:
- Root: ع-و-ل (ʿ-w-l) / ع-ض-ل (ʿ-ḍ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: عول denotes turning, inclining, or deviating from a course; عضل signifies constriction, prevention, or withholding.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the theological sense, ʿawal implies a moral deviation from the straight path of worship (ṣirāṭ), while ʿaḍl is the divine attribute of justice—here, the servant's own neglect becomes a self-imposed injustice.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage refers to physical obstruction; metaphorically, it denotes the soul's inclination toward ease (dʿa) that obstructs the performance of supererogatory acts.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ) — The construction "in lam aṣduq" (if I had not been truthful) governs a hypothetical past, requiring the apodosis to be understood as a suppressed regret, following the pattern of law + māḍī for unreal conditions.
translation:
I say: Know that the one who abandons the regular voluntary devotion (al-wird) entirely, and does not make it up, has exposed himself to loss. For I have seen many a man who, when he misses his accustomed prayers, says, "I shall perform two rakʿahs without emulation (taʾsī) and without following an imam," as my master al-Mutawallī (may God have mercy on him) used to say: "Hearken to God, not to the self."

And it appeared in what Muḥibb al-Dīn (al-Nawawī) said: Whoever does not persist in the regular devotion (al-waẓīfah) exposes himself to its abandonment. He said: It is incumbent upon him to make it up at another time. For if he is lax in making it up, it becomes easy for him to waste it entirely at its proper time. Likewise, he said in the "Iḥyāʾ": Whoever is hindered by an obstacle from his regular devotion (wird) should not permit himself to abandon making it up; rather, he should make it up at another time, so that his soul does not incline toward idleness and comfort. And making it up is commendable as a form of striving against the self (mujāhadah), not because it is an obligatory duty (farḍ lāzim). Then I came upon the text of al-Ḥāwī, upon which the legal opinion (fatwā) rests in the Shāfiʿī school: The time-bound supererogatory prayers (al-muʾaqqatah min al-nawāfil) are made up forever, except those tied to a cause, such as the eclipse prayer.

Would that I, O man, in these six rakʿahs had followed Ibn Abī Zayd in his Risālah, and had emulated my shaykh Ibn Sirāj therein; or that I had committed myself to making them up according to what Muḥibb al-Dīn said—if I had not been truthful in believing that they equal the worship of twelve years. And also, I would have been as though I had prayed them, since the one who hindered me was an obstacle. For in the Ṣaḥīḥ: {«If a servant falls ill or travels, there is written for him what he used to do while healthy and resident»} (Bukhārī, no. 2996). And likewise the other report: {«Whoever had a night prayer and his eyes overcame him, his prayer is written for him, and his sleep is a charity for him»} (Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, al-Tamhīd, 19/104; Aḥmad, 4/410, no. 19694; Ibn Ḥibbān, 7/191, no. 2834).

And I was on the verge of a similar matter regarding the fast of the middle of Shaʿbān, for I was like the two Shāṭibīs therein. Al-Shāṭibī says: The Salaf made fasting continuous and attached the supererogatory (al-mandūb) to the obligatory (al-wājib). But his followers draw near to God by eating on the day of the middle of Shaʿbān—even though the entire school—Ibn Yūnus, Ibn Abī Zayd, and Ibn ʿArafah in his jurisprudential Dīwān—has explicitly stated the specification of the virtuous days for fasting. He said: And Shaʿbān, especially the middle day thereof; this is his very text. And the Lawgiver has not forbidden fasting on any day of the year except two days specifically: the Day of Sacrifice (al-Naḥr) and the Day of Breaking the Fast (al-Fiṭr). As for the two days following the Day of Sacrifice, our school holds that fasting them is not forbidden (ḥarām), but merely disliked (makrūh). And the fourth day (i.e., the third after the Sacrifice) is fasted by one who has vowed it or one who is in consecutive fasting. The consequence of this is that eating on the middle of Shaʿbān is commendable (mustaḥabb), and its opposite is not disliked; rather, it is merely permissible (mubāḥ). Therefore, one who has vowed it fasts it.

As for the remaining days of the year, the requirement of devotion (taʿabbud) is that one make fasting continuous, as al-Shāṭibī reported from the righteous Salaf.

And it has preceded that the final word with which Ibn Yūnus concluded his jurisprudential Dīwān was: "Taking the little is better than abandoning the whole."

And it has preceded that every believer is desirous of worship, except that heedlessness (al-ghaflah) seduces him and lust (al-shahwah) overcomes him; and by emulation (al-taʾsī) and following (al-iqtidāʾ), his vigor is strengthened.

And it has preceded the transmission of Ibn Bashkuwāl: Whoever is informed of a merit in an act and performs it, God gives him that reward, even if what reached him was not true.

And it has preceded the saying of Muḥibb al-Dīn al-Nawawī: "Act upon it, even if only once."

And it has preceded the saying of ʿIyāḍ: "Everything of devotion that reached me, I performed it, until it reached me about a man that he completed the Qurʾān and then had intercourse with his family, and I followed him in that." But this is not a legal objective (maqṣad sharʿī), nor an intention (niyyah); it is merely a covetous emulation (ghibṭah). And it has preceded the saying of al-Shāṭibī regarding the obligation of the dhikr that al-Kattānī saw in sleep.

So you, O aspirant (murīd), if you cannot make fasting continuous, then specify and fast the days that have particular blessing, such as the six days of Shawwāl. Ibn Rushd said: It is not disliked for anyone to fast them; this is his very text. And he interpreted the wording reported from the Imam (Mālik) in opposition to the Shāṭibīs, who made it a principle and analogized upon it the fasting of the middle of Shaʿbān.

And the expression of Ibn Yūnus in his jurisprudential Dīwān, which is the muṣḥaf of the school, is as follows, verbatim: "Chapter: Fasting the Day of ʿĀshūrāʾ is encouraged." Then he said: "And therein the Kaʿbah is draped every year." And it has been reported that whoever does not intend to fast until morning has the option to fast it or the remainder of it, if he has eaten. And that was related from the Messenger of God ﷺ by more than one of the Salaf.

And Ibn ʿAbbās used to fast two consecutive days (i.e., the 9th and 10th of Muḥarram), fearing that it would escape him; and he would fast it while traveling, and Ibn Shihāb (al-Zuhrī) followed him in that. Then he said: "Chapter: It is reported that the Prophet ﷺ fasted the sacred months, which are Muḥarram, Rajab, Dhū al-Qaʿdah, and Dhū al-Ḥijjah." And he also encouraged fasting the twenty-seventh of Rajab, for therein the Prophet ﷺ was sent; and the twenty-fifth of Dhū al-Qaʿdah, for therein the Kaʿbah was sent down, and with it mercy. And he encouraged fasting Shaʿbān, for the Messenger of God ﷺ used to fast more in it than in any other month.

### | الصفحة 203

ميج فون شق نغ عو للد من ل كن من تس كع أرق يجيد لي مس ارت طاضة___347.

وتنوي في نفسك إن عاقك عائق أن تقضي غير الوتر في وقت آخرء فلك في
هذه أسوة؛ ويكون لك أجر ذلك إن مرضت؛ لقول رسول الله يَق: 'إذا مرض العبد
أو سافر كتب له ما كان يعمل صحيسًا مقيئما”"".

قال في "الإحياء': واختار بعض العلماء أن يكون عدد الرواتب سبع عشرة
ركعة كعد المكتوبة إلا الوتر؛ فالتص قد ورد بأنه لا يقضى؛ وقد تقدم نص النووي
والحاوي أن المؤقثة من النوافل تقضى أبدا. قال السيد الساحلي في بغيته: يلتزم كل
أحد على حسب حاله» بحيث لا يعجز عن القيام في كل الأحوال؛ لأن المطلوب
إثبات أعمال اللزوم كما كان يك إذا عمل عملا أثبته؛ وقد أشار رسول الله يله إلى

نشاطا زاد بحسب نشاطه وحاله؛ قال: ولقد قال والدي: إن عد لزومي من الذكر

وبركة هذا الالتزام أنه إن صده عنه صاد فكأنه فعله للنية الجازمة.

قال الشاطبي في موافقاته: إنما رقع الحرج عن المكلف في ابتداء الأعمال حتى
يدخله حب الخير؛ فحيتدذ يتوخى مطلق الأمر بالعبادة؛ لقوله سبحانه: َبَلق

َيه 4 [الزمسر: 9]» طإوَمَا لفت لانت إلا يبدو (4)2 [الذاريات: 56]. اه
نص "الموافقات”. والعبادة بذل المجهود في مرضاة المعبود؛ وكان فرض الله

# PageV1P204
anchors:
- Root: ن-ف-ق (n-f-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Expenditure, spending upon dependents; from نفق (to spend, to exhaust).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Provisioning for the household as an act of devotional obedience (ṭāʿah), linked to divine bounty.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in financial outlay; metaphorical (majāz) in "expanding" (tawsīʿah) one's means as a sign of gratitude.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ) — "If a servant falls ill or travels, it is written for him..." (idhā marida... kutiba lahu) — the protasis governs the apodosis, indicating the permanence of habitual deeds.
translation:
I say: It is reported in the tradition that on this day deeds are raised [to God]; and there is also encouragement for fasting half of it, and for standing in prayer during that night. This is the end of the text of Ibn Yūnus — and it is upon this that the legal verdict (fatwā) must be based, not upon the saying of one whose statement we have not found in any book: "Fear for the community of Muḥammad what its Prophet did not fear for it."

And from Ibn Yūnus, it is also transmitted concerning expenditure on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, where he said, verbatim: "Encouragement has come regarding spending on one's dependents on that day; and the people of Madīnah would deliberately seek to do so, until it was as if it were a festival day." This is the end of the text of Ibn Yūnus.

And Ibn al-ʿArabī said in his book *al-Masālik*: "Expenditure on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ and the widening of provision is a confirmed practice (makhlūfah) by consensus." Then he recited the verses of Ibn Ḥabīb:

"O soul, may the Merciful not forget ʿĀshūrāʾ — remember it, may you never cease in goodness.
The Messenger, may God's prayers encompass him, said a word — we found upon it the truth and the counsel.
Widen your wealth on ʿĀshūrāʾ, for it has a merit — we found it transmitted in the traditions.
Whoever passes the night of ʿĀshūrāʾ in abundance — shall be joyful in his livelihood throughout the year."

And my shaykh, the master al-Mattūrī, Abū ʿAbd Allāh — may God have mercy on him — would recite to us on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, saying: "The khaṭīb Abū Bakr ibn Juzayy recited to me on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, saying: The khaṭīb Abū ʿAlī al-Farshī recited to me on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, saying: The khaṭīb Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rashīd al-Fahrī recited to me his own composition on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ — and he mentioned to me that he had composed it on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ:

"ʿĀshūrāʾ has come — so fast it, O you who seek the Chosen One's intercession; it is an expiation for the sin of the past year.
And whoever widens [provision] on that day — he shall not cease in his year in a contented life."

And consider, O my brother in God: if you intended in yourself to pray the two units of dawn (Fajr), the two units of forenoon (Ḍuḥā), two units before noon (Ẓuhr), two after it, two before the afternoon (ʿAṣr), two after sunset (Maghrib), two before the night prayer (ʿIshāʾ), and the odd-numbered prayer (Witr) and its pair (Shafʿ) — and you intend in yourself that if an obstacle prevents you, you will make up (qaḍāʾ) all except the Witr at another time — then you have in this a model (uswah); and you shall have the reward of that even if you fall ill, due to the saying of the Messenger of God ﷺ: "When a servant falls ill or travels, there is written for him what he used to do while healthy and resident."

He said in *al-Iḥyāʾ*: "Some scholars chose that the number of the regular supererogatory prayers (rawātib) be seventeen units, equal to the number of the obligatory prayers except the Witr; for the text has come that it is not made up." And the text of al-Nawawī and al-Ḥāwī has already been presented: that the time-bound supererogatory prayers are always made up. Al-Sayyid al-Sāḥilī said in his *Bughyah*: "Each person commits himself according to his own state, such that he is not incapable of standing [in prayer] in all circumstances; for the goal is to establish deeds of constancy (luzūm), just as the Prophet ﷺ, when he did an act, would establish it." And the Messenger of God ﷺ pointed to this in his saying: "The most beloved of deeds to God are the most constant, even if few." So one increases activity according to his activity and state. He said: "And indeed my father said: My constant remembrance (dhikr) reached five hundred times, and I never limited myself to that; indeed I reached thirty thousand. And my constant recitation in prayer was two portions (ḥizb), and I never limited myself to that." Then he mentioned to me the rest of his constant practices. This is the end.

And the blessing of this commitment is that if an obstacle prevents him from it, it is as if he had done it, due to his firm intention (niyyah jāzimah).

And consider: if a man intends a thousand units [of prayer], but does not intend them with absolute firmness so that their making up is not incumbent upon him — there is no doubt that he is not at all like one who does not intend that. And in all this there is wisdom: for al-Shāṭibī said in his *Muwāfaqāt*: "The burden was lifted from the legally responsible person (mukallaf) at the beginning of deeds, so that love of good might enter him; then at that point he pursues the absolute command of worship," due to His saying, Glorified be He: {«وَمَا خَلَقْتُ الْجِنَّ وَالْإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ»} [al-Dhāriyāt: 56]. This is the end of the text of *al-Muwāfaqāt*.

And worship is the expenditure of utmost effort (badhl al-majhūd) in seeking the pleasure of the Worshipped One. And God had made obligatory fifty prayers, then He lightened them for His servant. So whoever intends a hundred units [of prayer] — that is fifty salutations (taslīmah), and that is fifty prayers; and that is the original obligation. And you, O my brother in God, have in this a model; nay, he said:

"If the seeker (sālik) finds in himself [the capacity]..."

# PageV1P205
anchors:
- Root: و-ر-د (w-r-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes arriving at water, a place of watering, or a path leading to it; hence a "litany" (wird) is a fixed portion of recitation or prayer that one "arrives at" regularly.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the spiritual path, wird signifies the appointed devotional portion by which the servant approaches God, mirroring the soul's journey to its source.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: watering-place. Metaphorical: the regular spiritual "station" of worship that the seeker frequents, like camels returning to a well.
- Root: غ-ر-ر (gh-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Deception, delusion, or being heedless; also a white blaze on a horse's forehead (a mark of distinction, but here used for false pretension).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The "deluded" (maghrūrūn) are those who are deceived by worldly appearances or by false claims to spiritual knowledge without true realization.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: to be deceived by a mirage. Metaphorical: the self-deception of those who mistake verbal formulas for genuine gnosis.
- Root: ع-ك-ف (ʿ-k-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cleave to, remain in seclusion, or devote oneself continuously to a place or act of worship.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Iʿtikāf is the ritual seclusion in a mosque for uninterrupted devotion, a Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: to stay in a place. Metaphorical: the soul's persistent clinging to divine service, cutting off worldly distractions.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text uses "if not... then let it be..." (in lam... fa-l-yakun) to express graded obligation, and "even if" (wa-law) for concessive allowance, requiring precise modal rendering.
translation:
I say — may God guide us and you. Know that the ordering of the litanies (awrād) is the path of the wayfarers (al-sālikīn) and the way of the knowers of God (al-ʿārifīn). The author of the Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn (Revival of the Religious Sciences) said: "The least that is transmitted from the litanies of the Companions — may God be pleased with them all — is one hundred rakʿahs in the day and night." And he said in the Iḥyāʾ: "Perseverance upon the litanies is the road to God." And he said in the Book of Delusion (Kitāb al-Ghurūr): "Among the deluded — meaning among the Sufis — is one who claims knowledge of divine gnosis (maʿrifah) yet knows it only through names and words, such that even a farmer abandons his plowing and a weaver abandons his weaving to cling to such a deluded one, catching up those phrases, repeating them as if he spoke from revelation and reported the secret of secrets, claiming for himself that he has attained the Truth — while in the eyes of the masters of hearts he is among the foolish ignoramuses: he never mastered any knowledge, nor refined any character, nor ordered any deed." End quote. Thus he made the ordering of the litanies the methodology of the seekers and the way of the knowers.

And from the Iḥyāʾ also: "The litanies vary according to the varying of times." He made the night litanies five and the day litanies seven. I follow him in this number, and I make the twelve litanies a single wird (litany). If it is not the constant practice of the seeker (murīd) at all times, then let it be at some times — even if only in Ramaḍān and the night of the middle of Shaʿbān. Or let a man be granted success and perform iʿtikāf (spiritual retreat) even for one night and one day. And it is required in iʿtikāf that one make worship continuous for as long as one remains in retreat, so let him observe this ordering that I shall mention.

By this proportion, it would be fitting to begin with the litany of the first part of the night. But I have a purpose in making the litany at the first waking from sleep in the night. So I say:

**The First Litany** — of the twelve litanies — is at the first waking from sleep in the night. In my view, this time is the most deserving of the times for the seeker to observe; for this reason I began with it. For when a man stirs from his sleep, it is as if he is coming from the world of the unseen (ʿālam al-ghayb) to the world of witness (ʿālam al-shahādah), and the soul is inclined toward the demands of the world of witness. So it is fitting that I turn this awakened one away from the world of witness entirely, and direct his face and his aspiration (himmah) to his Lord at the very moment he wakes from his sleep — for this is a foundation for the rest of his day and the observance of his day. For at the very moment God returns to him his spirit — as in the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī: "Whoever wakes in the night..." — the ḥadīth — let him say: "There is no god but God alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise..."

# PageV1P207
anchors:
- Root: ج-ه-د (j-h-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Exertion of effort to the utmost limit; striving against difficulty.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Spiritual striving (jihād al-nafs) in worship; the earnest endeavor to overcome the soul's laziness.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical toil; Metaphorical: the soul's struggle to attain proximity to God.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — The protasis "whoever does not..." governs the apodosis "let him strive," indicating obligation contingent upon circumstance.
translation:
I say — may God grant us and you success in attaining His good pleasure, and may He place us among those who are mindful of His sacred ordinances in every moment:

Know that the one who has not been granted the divine grace (tawfīq) to rise for prayer during these virtuous times must strive earnestly in seizing the excellence of these hours through remembrance (dhikr) and supplication (duʿā'). For the Prophet ﷺ taught us comprehensive words of remembrance for the morning and evening, among which are:

"Praise be to God, and He is over all things Omnipotent: Praise be to God, and Glory be to God, and there is no god but God, and God is Greater, and there is no might nor power except through God. Praise be to God who returned to me my soul and healed my body and permitted me to remember Him. Praise be to God who created sleep and wakefulness. Praise be to God who raised me sound and whole. I bear witness that God revives the dead and He is over all things Omnipotent. There is no god but You, Glory be to You, O God, and by Your praise I seek Your forgiveness for my sin and ask You for Your mercy. My Lord, increase me in knowledge and do not let my heart deviate after You have guided me, and grant me from Yourself mercy; indeed You are the Bestower. O my God, the stars have set, the eyes have slept, the kings have shut their doors, and every lover is alone with his beloved — and here I am, fleeing to You, carrying the heavy burdens of my sins upon my back. I find no intercessor to You better than my knowledge that You are the Greatest of those to whom the distressed flee, the Most Merciful of those upon whom the deluded rely, and the Most Generous of those from whom the destitute and the impoverished seek what is with You."

And you should bring to mind that this time — the latter part of the night — is the very time by which God swore in His Sublime Speech, saying: {«وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا سَجَى»} [Al-Ḍuḥā: 2] ("And by the night when it covers"). And in the authentic ḥadīth, as reported by al-Tirmidhī and Abū Dāwūd, the Messenger of God ﷺ was asked: "Which part of the night is most heard (i.e., when supplication is most answered)?" He replied: "The middle of the night..." — and al-Tirmidhī added: "And after the prescribed prayers."

It is also reported: "Two rakʿahs that a man prays in the depths of the night are better than the world and all that is in it." He ﷺ said: "Were it not that I would burden my community, I would have made them obligatory upon them." Al-Nasā'ī, Abū Dāwūd, and others narrated with a sound chain that ʿĀ'ishah — may God be pleased with her — was asked: "Did the Messenger of God ﷺ pray aloud in the night vigil or quietly?" She said: "Sometimes he would pray aloud, and sometimes quietly."

And in the Ṣaḥīḥ: "Our Lord — Glorified be He — descends when the last third of the night remains." And in Muslim: "When the first third of the night has passed, He says: 'I am the King, I am the King. Who is there to call upon Me that I may answer him? Who is there to ask of Me that I may give him? Who is there to seek My forgiveness that I may forgive him?' — until the dawn breaks." And in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim as well: "Indeed, in the night there is an hour in which no Muslim servant asks God for good of this world or the Hereafter but that He grants it to him — and that is every night."

In sum: remembrance at this time is nothing but the presence of the heart with God. So let a person choose, at this time, that which is most tender to his heart, most gentle to his state, and most fluent upon his tongue. And if prayer is sweet to him, let him stand before his Lord with his intention (qasd) as his goal. Al-Sāhilī said in his *Bughyah*: "Intentions in remembrances are like souls in bodies, and like meanings in words."

Now, if the obstacle (ʿāriḍ) preventing one from prayer is due to his sins, then after completing his prayer he should say: "O my God, the stars have set, the eyes have slept, the kings have shut their doors..." — to the end of the aforementioned supplication. Then he should say: "And You are the One who said in Your firm and noble Book: {«وَمَن يَعْمَلْ سُوءًا أَوْ يَظْلِمْ نَفْسَهُ ثُمَّ يَسْتَغْفِرِ اللَّهَ يَجِدِ اللَّهَ غَفُورًا رَّحِيمًا»} [Al-Nisā': 110] ("And whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks God's forgiveness, will find God Forgiving, Merciful"). O God, O my Master, here I am — I have done evil and wronged myself, and I seek Your forgiveness. So fulfill for me this noble promise in this noble verse, O Most Merciful of the merciful. O God, forgive me. O God, forgive me. O God, forgive me."

And you should select from the formulas of seeking forgiveness (istighfār) that which is most tender to your heart.

But if the obstacle is from creation (i.e., from people or worldly affairs), then your refuge should be the *ḥasbalah* (the phrase "God suffices me"). So say: "O my God, the stars have set... to the end... O God, O Kāf-Hā-Yā-ʿAyn-Ṣād, O Light, O All-Aware, O God, O Most Merciful" — three times, as narrated from ʿAlī — may God be pleased with him. Then say: "O God, forgive me the sins that bring down retribution; forgive me the sins that change blessings; forgive me the sins that increase enemies. O God, forgive me the sins that increase enemies" — and repeat this. Then say: "God suffices me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs" (ḥasbiya Allāhu wa niʿma al-wakīl), and repeat the *ḥasbalah*. For Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq said: "I marvel at the one who fears — how does it escape him to say: 'God suffices me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs'?" For God — Glorified be He — has said: {«حَسْبُنَا اللَّهُ وَنِعْمَ الْوَكِيلُ»} [Āl ʿImrān: 173] ("God suffices us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs") — the verse.

# PageV1P209
anchors:
- Root: ح-س-ب (ḥ-s-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sufficiency, reckoning, and that which suffices one against harm; the root denotes both numerical accounting and the act of one being enough for another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, ḥasbala (saying "Ḥasbī Allāh") signifies the declaration of God's absolute sufficiency (kifāyah) for the servant, entailing trust (tawakkul) and the nullification of all creaturely agency in one's ultimate recourse.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in the sense of "God suffices me"; metaphorical (majāz) when extended to the attributes (al-Ḥalīm, al-Qawī, etc.), where each epithet becomes a distinct locus of divine protection against specific harms.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Consecutive Apposition (al-ʿAṭf al-Bayānī) — The repeated "ḥasbī Allāh" clauses are coordinated by apposition, each carrying its own object of sufficiency (li-dīnī, li-dunyāyā, etc.), requiring the reader to parse each as an independent nominal sentence with an implied predicate of existence.
translation:
I say: Know that the ḥasbala transmitted from Maʿrūf al-Karkhī — may God have mercy on him — is that whoever utters it finds God present with him at its utterance. It is: "God suffices me, and He is the best of trustees; God suffices me for my religion; God suffices me for my worldly affairs; God, the Generous, suffices me for what concerns me; God, the Forbearing, the Strong, suffices me for whoever oppresses me; God, the Severe, suffices me for whoever plots evil against me; God, the Merciful, suffices me at the moment of death; God, the Compassionate, suffices me at the questioning in the grave; God, the Generous, suffices me at the Reckoning; God, the Subtle, suffices me at the Balance; God, the Omnipotent, suffices me at the Bridge (al-Ṣirāṭ); God — there is no god but He — upon Him I rely, and He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne."

And if the affliction be of the calamities of this world, then your refuge is the istirjāʿ (saying "Innā li-Llāhi wa-innā ilayhi rājiʿūn"), for he has said — and you say: "O my God, the stars have set, and the sinners have drawn near; O God, O Kāf-Hā-Yā-ʿAyn-Ṣād, O Light, O Holy, O All-Aware, O God, O Merciful, O Thrice-Beneficent — forgive me the sins that unleash retribution, and forgive me the sins that alter blessings; indeed, to God we belong and to Him we return." And you repeat this as long as your heart remains present; or you recall what is more tender to your heart, for the goal is the gathering of one's resolve and the presence of the heart.

And if the affliction be from bodily illness, then your refuge is the prayer of Ayyūb (Job) — peace be upon him. For Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq has said: "I marvel at one struck by calamity — how does it escape him to say: 'My Lord, indeed harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful'?" And He — exalted is He — has said: {«وَأَيُّوبَ إِذْ نَادَىٰ رَبَّهُ أَنِّي مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ وَأَنتَ أَرْحَمُ الرَّاحِمِينَ»} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 83]. So you say: "O my God, the stars have set, and the sinners have drawn near; O God, O Kāf-Hā-Yā-ʿAyn-Ṣād, O Light, O Holy, O All-Aware, O God, O Merciful, O Thrice-Beneficent — forgive me the sins that unleash retribution, and forgive me the sins that alter blessings, and forgive me the sins that send down calamity; O God, forgive me the sins that send down calamity." And you repeat it; then you say: {«رَبِّ إِنِّي مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ وَأَنتَ أَرْحَمُ الرَّاحِمِينَ»} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 83], repeating it as long as you remain present of mind and collected of heart. Then you say: "O God, hasten my relief and my deliverance; show me the trace of Your mercy; and grant me the coolness of Your pardon and forgiveness, O Most Merciful of the merciful."

And if the affliction be a grief in the heart, then your recourse is the remembrance of Dhū al-Nūn (Jonah) — peace be upon him. Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq said: "I marvel at one overtaken by grief — how does it escape him to say: {«لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا أَنتَ سُبْحَانَكَ إِنِّي كُنتُ مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ»} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 87]." So you proceed as previously mentioned, and you say: "And forgive me the sins that alter blessings; there is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I have been of the wrongdoers."

And if the matter be the seeking of istikhāra (prayer for divine choice), then your recourse is to its established supplication in the authentic ḥadīth. From al-Tirmidhī, who declared it sound: "The nearest that the Lord comes to His servant is in the last part of the night." And it has also preceded from the narration of Muslim: "And when the first third of the night passes" — and the hour of response in the night is hidden; perhaps it is that very hour of yours. So you pray two units: the first with {«قُلْ يَا أَيُّهَا الْكَافِرُونَ»} and the second with {«قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ»}, and you open the known supplication of istikhāra with praise of God and blessing upon the Prophet, and you invoke it seven times, and you close with praise and blessing. Then you await what becomes facilitated for you and what your breast expands toward — for that is the good choice for you.

And consider: if you pray two additional units with the Fātiḥa, and {«وَعِندَهُ مَفَاتِحُ الْغَيْبِ لَا يَعْلَمُهَا إِلَّا هُوَ»} to {«فِي كِتَابٍ مُّبِينٍ»} [al-Anʿām: 59], and in the second unit {«وَرَبُّكَ يَخْلُقُ مَا يَشَاءُ وَيَخْتَارُ»} to {«وَهُوَ اللَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ لَهُ الْحَمْدُ فِي الْأُولَىٰ وَالْآخِرَةِ وَلَهُ الْحُكْمُ وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ»} [al-Qaṣaṣ: 68–70], and you utter the complete blessing upon the Prophet ten times before the supplication and ten times after it — then you act with a balanced inner state, awaiting from God the causes of action and the causes of abstention. This was stipulated by al-Sayyid al-Sāḥilī — may God benefit us with him.

And akin to the istikhāra is the affair of Ibn Ghānim and Ibn Miskīn. ʿIyāḍ mentioned Ibn Ghānim, and noted his religion and virtue, and that our Imām Mālik offered him his daughter in marriage and to reside with him. He had heard from Mālik, and he assumed the judgeship of Ifrīqiya. ʿIyāḍ said: He had a share of night prayer; when he completed it and sat in the final tashahhud, he would present every litigant who sought his judgment before his Lord, saying in his private supplication: "O my Lord, so-and-so has disputed with so-and-so, claiming such-and-such against him, and he has denied the claim —"

# PageV1P210
anchors:
- Root: ق-ض-ي (qaḍā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To settle, adjudicate, decree; the act of finalizing a matter with authority.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine and human judgment; the station of the judge (qāḍī) as one who executes justice in accordance with revealed law.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: passing a legal verdict; metaphorical: the soul's submission to divine decree (qaḍāʾ) in moments of helplessness.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Repeated Protasis (al-sharṭ al-mukarrar) — The phrase "if I am right... if I am wrong" employs parallel conditionals to emphasize the speaker's epistemic humility before God.
translation:
I say — and the text of Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ concludes here.

He was also known as Ibn Miskīn, one of the companions of Saḥnūn and a man of jurisprudence and scrupulous piety (waraʿ). It is narrated that he said: "When Saḥnūn died, I grieved deeply for his death. Then I saw in a dream as though a sword was removed from his neck. So I said: 'By God, I will follow his path and acquire his knowledge.' Then after years, my vision was fulfilled, and I was afflicted with the office of judge (al-qaḍāʾ)." ʿIyāḍ said: "He would stand at night, recounting the cases of the disputants before him one by one, asking God to guide him in them toward what is right."

And among the supplications said at times of distress (al-ghamm): "O Living, O Self-Subsisting, by Your mercy I seek aid." Likewise: "There is no god but God, the Magnificent, the Forbearing; there is no god but God, Lord of the Mighty Throne; there is no god but God, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of the Noble Throne." And he (the Prophet, peace be upon him) said: "O God, I seek Your mercy, so do not entrust me to my soul for the blink of an eye; and set right for me all my affairs — there is no god but You." And he (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever recites the Throne Verse (Āyat al-Kursī) and the closing verses of Sūrat al-Baqarah at the time of calamity, God, Mighty and Majestic, will succor him." And he (peace be upon him) said: "Let one of you seek relief in everything, even in the strap of his sandal." The shisʿ is one of the thongs of the sandal by which its rein is fastened.

And consider also the supplication of relief (duʿāʾ al-faraj): When the caliphate was settled for Abū Jaʿfar (al-Manṣūr), he said to me: "O messenger, go and bring me Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad." So I rose from before him, saying to myself: "What calamity does he intend to do?" And I made him think that I would comply. Then I came to him after an hour, and he said: "Did I not tell you? By God, you will bring him to me, or I will kill him." He said: So I went to him and said: "O Abā ʿAbdillāh, answer the Commander of the Faithful." So he rose with me. When he entered, he greeted, but he (al-Manṣūr) did not return the greeting. He stood and did not sit. Then he raised his head and said: "O Jaʿfar, you are the one who stirred up and magnified." And he said: "My father narrated to me, from his father, from..."

وحدئني أبي عن أبيه عن جده: أن النبي يق قا
من كان أجره على الله؛ فلا يقوم من عباده إلا المتفضلون”7؛ فما زال يقول حتى

له قال: فخرجت فقلت: يا أبا عبد الله تعلم محبتي لك: قال أنت مناء حدثني أبي

# PageV1P211
anchors:
- Root: ح-ر-س (ḥ-r-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To guard, protect, keep watch over something with vigilance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine preservation (ḥifẓ) from spiritual and physical harm; God's eternal watchfulness.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal guarding (ḥaqīqah) vs. metaphorical sheltering under divine care (majāz).
- Root: ك-ن-ف (k-n-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To shelter, encompass, shield from all sides.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): God's encompassing protection (kanaf) that no force can breach.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal wing/side (janāḥ) vs. metaphorical refuge in divine power.
- Root: و-ك-ل (w-k-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To entrust, delegate, rely upon.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Tawakkul — absolute reliance on God, negating self-dependence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal agency vs. theological abandonment to one's own weakness.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Responsive Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — The invocation's clauses follow strict protasis-apodosis patterns, with the optative (duʿā') governed by the subjunctive mood (naṣb) after "as'aluka" (I ask You).
translation:
I say — and success is with God:

Know that the rightly guided (al-muhtadūn) among the early generations (al-salaf) held firm to the prophetic invocations (adʿiyah) in times of distress, and they transmitted them with unbroken chains (asānīd) from their forefathers. Among the accounts that have reached us is what Jaʿfar related — may God be pleased with him — from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A banner will be raised for the treacherous one on the Day of Resurrection, by which he will be recognized." Jaʿfar said: And my father related to me from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever has his reward with God — none among His servants stand forth except the munificent." He continued repeating this until the distress settled within him and softened his state. Then he said to him: "Sit, O Abū ʿAbd Allāh; rise, O Abū ʿAbd Allāh." Then he called for a vessel of fragrant oil (ghāliyah) and anointed him with his own hand, while the oil dripped from between the hands of the Commander of the Faithful. Then he said to him: "Depart, O Abū ʿAbd Allāh, in God's protection." And he said: "O Rabīʿ, follow Abū ʿAbd Allāh with his gift and double it for him."

He said: So I went out and said: "O Abū ʿAbd Allāh, you know my love for you." He replied: "You are a companion." Then he related: My father told me, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The patron (mawlā) of a people is one of them." I said: "O Abū ʿAbd Allāh, you witnessed what we did not witness, and you heard what we did not hear. I entered and saw you moving your lips upon entering his presence." He said: "It was an invocation (duʿā') that I was making." I said: "Is it an invocation you memorized upon entering, or something you transmit from your pure forefathers?"

He said: Rather, my father related to me from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ, whenever a matter grieved him, would make this invocation. And he used to call it the Invocation of Relief (duʿā' al-faraj): "O God, guard me with Your Eye that never sleeps; shelter me with Your Protection that is never assailed; have mercy on me through Your power over me. You are my trust and my hope. How many a blessing have You bestowed upon me, for which my gratitude fell short! And how many a trial have You afflicted me with, for which my patience fell short! O He whose blessing my gratitude failed to match, yet He did not deprive me; O He whose trial my patience failed to endure, yet He did not forsake me; O He who saw me upon sins, yet He did not disgrace me — I ask You to send blessings upon Muḥammad and upon the family of Muḥammad, as You sent blessings upon Abraham and upon the family of Abraham; indeed, You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. O God, aid me in my religion through my worldly life, and in my Hereafter through piety; preserve me in what I am absent from, and do not entrust me to my own self in what I am present for. O He whom sins do not harm and whom forgiveness does not diminish — grant me what does not harm You, and forgive me what does not harm You. My God, I ask You for near relief and beautiful patience. And I ask You for well-being from everything..."

title_en: Section 160 — On Incidental Matters: Supplications and the Night Prayer of Need
arabic_text:
### | الصفحة 211

ميج في شق هن مغ عون للد نكن من تسر كع أرق يجيد لي سركت اطاة 255
ِبليف وأسألك الشكر على العافية: وأسألك الغنى عن الناس ولا حول ولا قوة إلا
بالله”01.

قال الربيع: فكتبته من جعفر؛ فها هو في جيبي: قال ابن سهل: فكتبته من
الربيع؛ فها هو في جييي؛ قال ابن يحبى: فكتبته من ابن سهل؛ فها هو في جربي؛ قال
ابن هارون: فكتبته من ابن يحبى؛ فها هو في جيبي؛ قال المحتسب: فكتبته من ابن
هارون؛ فها هو في جيبي؛ قال ابن القطان: فكتبته من المحتسب؛ فها هو في جيبيء
قال ابن متصور: فكتبته من ابن القطان, فها هو في جيبي: قال أبو عياض: فكتبته من

جيبيء قال العاقولي: فكتبته من اين صخر فها هو في جيبي؛ قال ابن مسرة: فكتبته
من خط طاهرء وكان كتبه من أبي الفتح وأبي الليث؛ ثم قرأته على أبي بحرء وجعله
لنا في جيبه وأراناهء وحدثنا به عن أبي الفتح وأبي الليث: فها هو في جيي؛ قال ابن
عبد الحق: فكتبته من ابن مسرة» فها هو في جبي» قال ابن الطيلسان: فكتبته من ابن
عبد الحق؛ فها هو في جيبي لا يفارقني. وفي حفظي لا أنساء. قال التفزي: فكتبته
من ابن الطيلسان» فها هو في جيبي قال الأستاذ الغافقي: فكتيته من التفزي»
وجعلته في جيبي؛ قال الأستاذ البيري: فكتبته من الأستاذ الغافقي؛ وجعلته في
جيبي؛ قال الأستاذ أبو عبد اله البلدسي: فكتبته من الأستاذ الييري؛ وجعلته في
جيبي؛ قال لي شخي المنتوري: وكتبته من الأستاذ أبي عبد الله البلنسي؛ وجعلته في
وأنا كتبته أيضًا عن شيعخي المنتوري رحمه الله وجعلته في جيبي: وها
هو في حفظي لا أنساه ملتزما ذكره كل ليلة إلا من غفلة.

ومن العوارض أيضًا طلب حاجة؛ وفي صحيح البخاري: "من تعار من اليل
فقال: لا إله إلا اله...”" الذكر المتقدم: ثم قال: اللهم اغفر لي أو دعا استجيب له
فإن هو قام وتوضأ قبلت صلاته؛ فتقصد أيها الأخ في الله بهاتين الركعتين ركعتي

# PageV1P212
anchors:
- Root: ع-ر-ض (ʿ-r-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To appear, occur, or present itself; an incidental or accidental occurrence (ʿāriḍ) as opposed to essential (dhātī).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, that which befalls a person without prior intent — here, the "incidental matters" (ʿawāriḍ) of daily life, including the seeking of a need (ṭalab ḥājah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a side-occurrence; metaphorical: any event that interrupts the normal course of worship, requiring a specific devotional response.
- Root: ت-ع-ر (t-ʿ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To wake from sleep, to stir at night (taʿārra).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The specific act of waking in the night for remembrance — a state of vigilance (yaqaẓah) blessed by prophetic promise.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: to rouse from slumber; metaphorical: spiritual awakening to supplication.
- Root: ح-ف-ظ (ḥ-f-ẓ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To guard, preserve, commit to memory.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The preservation of sacred texts and supplications as an act of religious devotion (ḥifẓ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: keeping something safe; metaphorical: internalizing the transmitted words so they never depart from the heart.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Chain of Transmission (Isnād) — The repeated pattern "قال فلان: فكتبته من فلان" (He said: I wrote it from so-and-so) employs the accusative of specification and sequential conjunction (ʿaṭf) to establish an unbroken oral-written chain, each narrator affirming physical and auditory reception.
translation:
I say — may Allah guide us and you: Know that among the incidental matters (al-ʿawāriḍ) that befall the servant is the seeking of a need from Allah, whether great or small. The rightly guided practice (sunnah) in this is to turn to the Master of Needs with the supplication transmitted from the Chief of the Prophets, upon him be the most excellent of prayers and complete peace.

The chain of transmission for this noble supplication has reached us through a succession of verified narrators, each writing it from his teacher and keeping it in his pocket, as follows:

Al-Rabīʿ said: I wrote it from Jaʿfar; and here it is in my pocket. Ibn Sahl said: I wrote it from al-Rabīʿ; and here it is in my pocket. Ibn Yaḥyā said: I wrote it from Ibn Sahl; and here it is in my pocket. Ibn Hārūn said: I wrote it from Ibn Yaḥyā; and here it is in my pocket. Al-Muḥtasib said: I wrote it from Ibn Hārūn; and here it is in my pocket. Ibn al-Qaṭṭān said: I wrote it from al-Muḥtasib; and here it is in my pocket. Ibn Manṣūr said: I wrote it from Ibn al-Qaṭṭān; and here it is in my pocket. Abū ʿIyāḍ said: I wrote it from Ibn Manṣūr; and here it is in my pocket. Ibn Ṣakhr said: I wrote it from Abū ʿIyāḍ; and here it is in my pocket. Al-ʿĀqūlī said: I wrote it from Ibn Ṣakhr; and here it is in my pocket. Ibn Masarrā said: I wrote it from the handwriting of Ṭāhir, who had written it from Abū al-Fatḥ and Abū al-Layth; then I read it to Abū Baḥr, and he placed it in his pocket and showed it to us, and narrated it to us from Abū al-Fatḥ and Abū al-Layth; and here it is in my pocket. Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq said: I wrote it from Ibn Masarrā; and here it is in my pocket. Ibn al-Ṭaylasān said: I wrote it from Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq; and here it is in my pocket, never leaving me. And in my memory, I do not forget it. Al-Tifāzī said: I wrote it from Ibn al-Ṭaylasān; and here it is in my pocket. The Master al-Ghāfiqī said: I wrote it from al-Tifāzī and placed it in my pocket. The Master al-Bayrī said: I wrote it from the Master al-Ghāfiqī and placed it in my pocket. The Master Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Balansī said: I wrote it from the Master al-Bayrī and placed it in my pocket. My teacher al-Muntūrī said to me: And I wrote it from the Master Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Balansī and placed it in my pocket.

And I also wrote it from my teacher al-Muntūrī — may Allah have mercy on him — and placed it in my pocket. And here it is in my memory; I do not forget it, committing myself to its recitation every night, except when overcome by heedlessness.

And among the incidental matters (al-ʿawāriḍ) is also the seeking of a need. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī: "Whoever wakes in the night and says: 'There is no god but Allah...' [the aforementioned remembrance], then says: 'O Allah, forgive me,' or makes a supplication, it is answered. And if he then rises and performs ablution and prays, his prayer is accepted." So intend, O brother in Allah, by these two units of prayer — the two units [of the night prayer of need] — the fulfillment of your need from the Lord of the Worlds, and ask Him with humility and presence of heart, for He is the Hearer of supplication, the Giver of needs.

# PageV1P213
anchors:
- Root: ح-ا-ج (ḥā-jīm) 
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Need, want, or necessity that impels one toward its fulfillment; a state of lack requiring supply.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological context, the creature's absolute dependence upon the Creator; the supplicant's existential poverty before divine sufficiency.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for material need; metaphorical (majāz) for spiritual yearning — here both converge in the ritual of petition.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Response Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — The protasis "whoever has a need" governs the apodosis of prescribed actions, indicating causal efficacy of the ritual.
translation:
I say — and success is with God: Whoever among the believers is overtaken by a pressing need, let him strive earnestly in the pursuit of the virtuous means (al-asbāb al-fāḍilah). Among these is the prayer of need (ṣalāt al-ḥājah). It is recorded in al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: {«Whoever has a need — whether from God or from any of the children of Adam — let him perform ablution and perfect it; then let him pray two rakʿahs; then let him praise God, Mighty and Majestic, and send blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ; then let him say: There is no god but God, the Forbearing, the Generous; Glory be to God, Lord of the Mighty Throne; Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds; I ask You for the causes of Your mercy and the resolutions of Your forgiveness, and for the gain of every good and safety from every sin; do not leave for us any sin except that You forgive it, nor any distress except that You relieve it, nor any sick person except that You heal him, nor any need in which there is Your pleasure and our welfare except that You fulfill it, O Most Merciful of the merciful.»}

And know that the hour of wakefulness at night — when a person is at ease within himself, having taken his full share of sleep — is a time when he is not distracted by people, for they are asleep. It is likely that this very hour is the hour of response (sāʿat al-ijābah). Al-Ḥilyah states: "A chapter on supplication during all hours of the night, every night, hoping to coincide with the hour of response." In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, he ﷺ said: {«Indeed, in the night there is an hour in which no Muslim man coincides with it, asking God for good of this world or the next, except that He grants it to him — and that is every night.»} There is no act of worship incumbent upon him beyond that; rather, let him seek out what is most tender to his heart. If he wishes to seek forgiveness, the intent that precedes his action has already been mentioned. If he wishes to perform the prayer of guidance (al-istikhārah) or to request a need, the proper conduct for that has already preceded. If he wishes to engage in remembrance (dhikr), then excellent and blessed. And it may be that the one who remembers combines recitation with remembrance — such as making his remembrance the recitation of Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ, finding in its recitation a profound spiritual ecstasy (wajd), whether a thousand times or fewer or more. Al-Dānī has transmitted that he would recite it without the basmalah, and similar is reported by al-Nawawī in his commentary on {«Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High»} [al-Aʿlā 87:1]. I mean: at the beginning of this time — that is, at the onset of the first part of the night.

# PageV1P214
anchors:
- Root: ع-و-ذ (ʿ-w-dh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To seek protection, cling to a refuge; the act of entrusting oneself to a sheltering power.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Qur'anic idiom, istiʿādha denotes the soul's flight from every seductive whisper (waswās) toward the fortress of divine preservation (ʿiṣma).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical sheltering; metaphorical (majāz) — the heart's disengagement from all save Allah, even from one's own self-regard.
- Root: و-س-و-س (w-s-w-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The faint, intermittent sound; the subtle insinuation that creeps into the breast.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The whisper of Satan or the lower self (nafs) that disturbs the certitude of the believer, especially in acts of worship.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Metaphor for the stealthy intrusion of doubt — not a loud call but a barely perceptible murmur.
- Root: ه-ل-ل (h-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To proclaim aloud; the root of tahlīl — the declaration of divine unity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The verbal testimony "lā ilāha illā Allāh" as the seal of sincerity (ikhlāṣ) and the sword against every false object of devotion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the rising of the voice; metaphorical — the elevation of the heart above all multiplicity.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Conditional Inception (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — When the author says "If you pray and turn (fa-idhā ṣallayta wa-tawajjāhta)," the protasis establishes a temporal frame, and the apodosis (fa-l-tastaʿidh) delivers the imperative as a necessary consequence, not a mere option.
translation:
I say — and success is from Allah alone:

Know that when the servant stands in prayer and turns his face toward the Sacred Sanctuary (al-Kaʿba), let him seek refuge and pronounce the Basmala, intending thereby the recitation of the Qur'an. Let him say: "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan; in the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful. Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Self-Sufficient Besought. He begets not, nor was He begotten, and there is none comparable to Him" {«قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ ١ اللَّهُ الصَّمَدُ ٢ لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ ٣ وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌ ٤»} [al-Ikhlāṣ: 1–4]. Then let him say: "Here I am at Your service, my Lord, and at Your pleasure; all good is in Your hands; I am through You and unto You; I declare You free of every partner in truth, and I affirm Your oneness in sincerity." Then, in compliance with Your command, I say: "Allah is the One."

It has already been transmitted from al-Sayyid al-Sāḥilī, on the authority of his father, that the constant recitation of this (sūra) is five hundred times, and it may reach thirty thousand. Ibn al-ʿArabī transmitted in his *Sirāj* that Abū Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) had a thread with one thousand knots, and he would not sleep until he had glorified (Allah) by counting them.

The turning (tawajjuh) may also be performed with the two refuge-sūras (al-Muʿawwidhatān), in the same manner as with Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ. For a person may increase his protection against an envier and a sorcerer. Let him say: "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan; in the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful. Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the Daybreak" {«قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ الْفَلَقِ ١»} [al-Falaq: 1] to its end. Then let him say: "Here I am at Your service; here I stand before You, complying with Your command, and I seek refuge from my envier. So I say as You have commanded me: 'I seek refuge in the Lord of the Daybreak.'"

And if the affliction be from obsessive whisper (waswās), then let him seek refuge with Sūrat al-Nās in this same manner. For only the perfect in faith is tried by waswās — the thief does not break into a ruined house. Therefore, it behooves a man to disregard it. This was stated by Muḥyī al-Dīn.

ʿIzz al-Dīn said: A man may imagine that this waswās originates from his own self, and he wishes to erase it, but that is not within his capacity. This is the meaning of Mālik's statement concerning one who doubts the divorce of his wife — Mālik said: "Say to the wicked one (Satan): 'You have spoken truly.'"

Muḥyī al-Dīn also said: The best means to repel waswās is the tahlīl (declaration of unity). The gateway through which one enters into the remembrance of tahlīl is to seek refuge intending recitation, then let him say: "Know that there is no god but Allah" {«فَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ»} [Muḥammad: 19]. Let him address this discourse to his own soul, then answer it with: "Here I am at Your service, my Lord, and at Your pleasure; here I stand before You, affirming Your oneness by the tahlīl, and I divest myself of all alteration and substitution. So I say: There is no god but Allah." If his heart finds (tranquility) in this, then it may be a healing for his malady.

Al-Sayyid al-Sāḥilī said in his *Bughya*: "The remembrance of presence (dhikr al-ḥuḍūr) is the commitment to known litanies according to specific states, by way of seeking cure from the ailments of the soul and deliverance from the diseases of its attachments." He said: "In their view, when the meaning of the dhikr is prolonged and its words multiply, its meanings branch out over the thought, and thus it does not gather with the remembrance itself."

And the purpose of transcendence (tanzīh) is that you seek refuge intending recitation, pronounce the Basmala, and recite "Glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most High" {«سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى»} [al-Aʿlā: 1], and you address this (verse) to your own self — as I have explained.

# PageV1P215
anchors:
- Root: ص-ل-و (ṣ-l-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes supplication, blessing, and the act of drawing near through devotional address; in its verbal form, it carries the sense of "to pray upon" or "to invoke mercy."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, it signifies divine mercy and the angelic and human act of seeking that mercy for the Prophet ﷺ, as a commanded act of veneration.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in the sense of "turning toward" in prayer; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to the believer's invocation, indicating a spiritual connection rather than physical proximity.
- Root: ت-ب-ع (t-b-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To follow, to pursue, to tread behind another's footsteps.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Quranic context, it denotes obedient adherence to the prophetic example (ittibāʿ), which is the essence of faith.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical following; metaphorical for moral and spiritual emulation.
- Root: و-س-ل (w-s-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A means, a connection, a bond that brings one near to another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The theological term for the Prophet ﷺ as the "means" (wasīlah) to God, a divinely appointed intermediary for guidance and intercession.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for a physical link; metaphorical for the spiritual mediation of the Prophet ﷺ in the seeker's journey.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional and Imperative Sequence (The command to invoke blessings is followed by the seeker's responsive utterance, establishing a grammatical pattern of divine address and human compliance, as in "If you do X, then Y follows.")
translation:
I say — may God guide us and you to the straight path and grant us success in following the noble prophetic way:

Know that when the seeker (al-sālik) completes the recitation of the Qur'anic verses, he should turn his address upon himself and respond to the divine command with the words: "Here I am, my Lord, at Your service, and all good is in Your hands; I am before You, I declare You free of all imperfection, and I affirm Your oneness truly." Then he says, in compliance with Your command: "Glory be to God." And consider also the matter of invoking blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ; for Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Shall I make all my prayer for you?" He replied: "Then your concerns will be fulfilled, and your sin will be forgiven." The Prophet ﷺ also said: "Be steadfast, and you will never fully attain it." This, for the seeker, means that he must remain balanced upon the path of the Sunnah and travel upon the way of the Sacred Law without alteration.

It has been said concerning His words — exalted is He: {«إِنَّ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا رَبُّنَا اللَّهُ ثُمَّ اسْتَقَامُوا»} [Fussilat: 30] — that they did not deviate with the deviance of foxes. And they said: Remembrance (al-dhikr) strengthens the love of following the Beloved. Thus, the mention of the Messenger of God ﷺ is a means to loving him, and loving him is a means to following him; and following him is obligatory. Hence, the command to invoke blessings upon him is emphasized, because it entails love of him, and love of him entails following him. For God — exalted is He — says: {«أَفَأَنتَ تُكْرِهُ النَّاسَ حَتَّىٰ يَكُونُوا مُؤْمِنِينَ»} [Yūnus: 99] — not without messengers; rather, He — glory be to Him — made His Prophet ﷺ a sign pointing us to God, a means (wasīlah) to God, and an intercessor before God. Therefore, we must cling to his stirrup and hold fast to his reins. So invoking blessings upon him is a remembrance of God and a fulfillment of God's command. Thus, when the reciter intends the recitation, he says: {«إِنَّ اللَّهَ وَمَلَائِكَتَهُ يُصَلُّونَ عَلَى النَّبِيِّ ۚ يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا صَلُّوا عَلَيْهِ وَسَلِّمُوا تَسْلِيمًا»} [Al-Aḥzāb: 56]. Then he directs this address upon himself and says: "Here I am, my Lord, at Your service, and all good is in Your hands; here I am before You; I seek intercession through Muhammad, Your Prophet and Your servant, and I invoke blessings upon him in obedience to Your command. O God, bless Muhammad," continuing to the end of your prescribed litany (wird) or to the end of your appointed portion. And you should not depart from your remembrance except for those remembrances that arise from incidental matters — such as when...

title_en: Section 164 — On the Adab of Responding to Natural Phenomena and Fortifying the Heart
arabic_text:
### | الصفحة 215

منهج ني تفن طم على املد ئ لمكن م تمرك لوقت يجيد في تسر الأرات الاضة__ 359
يؤذن المؤذن فتحكيه وتعود لذكرك؛ أو ترى كوكيا ينفض فتقول: ما شاء الله لا
إلا بالهء أو تسمع الرعد فتقول: اللهم لا تقتلنا بغضيك؛ ولا تهلكنا بعذابك؛ وعافنا
قبل ذلك أو تقول ثلانًا: '"سبحان الذي يسبح الرعد بحمده والملانكة من
اعيفته”" أو تسمع نهيق حمار أو نباح كلب فتقول: أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم»
أو تطن أذنك فتقول: اللهم صل على سيدنا محمد ذكر الله بخير من ذكرني؛ أو
اخدرت رجلك فتقول: يا حبيبي يا محمد ييه أو تسمع صراخ ديك فتقول: اللهم
إني أسألك من فضلك؛ وإن هبت ريح فتقول: اللهم إني أسألك خير هذه الريح
وخير ما فيها وخير ما أرسلت به؛ ونعوذ بك من شرها وشر ما فيها وشر ما أرسلت
بهء أو يرعبك شيء فتقول: الله ربي لا أشرك به شيئا اللهم إني أعوذ بك من شرهء
وأدراً بك في نحره؛ اللهم صل على سيدنا محمد وعلى آله وسلم. والحسبلة أيضًا
انعم التحصن مما بخشىء فقد قال معروف في حسيلته المتقدمة: من دعا بها وجد
الله عندهاء ولو لم يكن له ذلك الصدق في ذكره. وكذلك أيضًا ذكروا في
الاسترجاع فالوا: أساس ما يرومه مستنزل اللطف في المصائب الاسترجاع؛ إما
بشرطه من الاخلاص؛ وإما بحاله فقد خصه الله بذلك؛ قالوا: وحال الخاصية لاا
.ينكرء فإذا راعك شيء بل أو انطفاً لك المصباح: فقل: إنا له وإنا إليه راجعون.

# PageV1P216
anchors:
- Root: ذ-ك-ر (dh-k-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Remembrance, invocation, and the act of calling to mind; also used for praise and mention.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the theological sense, dhikr is the heart’s presence with Allah, whether by tongue or inner reflection; it is the counter to heedlessness (ghaflah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for verbal mention; metaphorical (majāz) for the heart’s steadfastness in divine awareness.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Imperative Apodosis (Sharṭ wa-Jawāb) — The protasis (e.g., "if you hear the thunder") is followed by an imperative or supplicatory apodosis, indicating a prescribed response.
translation:
I say — and success is with Allah:

When the mu'adhdhin gives the call to prayer, you should repeat his words and then return to your remembrance (dhikr). Or if you see a star falling, you say: "What Allah wills, there is no power save with Allah." Or if you hear thunder, you say: "O Allah, do not slay us with Your wrath, nor destroy us with Your punishment, but grant us well-being before that." Or you say three times: "Glory be to Him Whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels from His awe." Or if you hear the braying of a donkey or the barking of a dog, you say: "I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan." Or if your ear rings, you say: "O Allah, send blessings upon our master Muhammad — may Allah mention him with goodness as he has mentioned me." Or if your foot goes numb, you say: "O my beloved, O Muhammad." Or if you hear the crowing of a rooster, you say: "O Allah, I ask You of Your bounty." And if a wind blows, you say: "O Allah, I ask You for the good of this wind, and the good of what is in it, and the good of what it has been sent with; and I seek refuge with You from its evil, and the evil of what is in it, and the evil of what it has been sent with." Or if something frightens you, you say: "Allah is my Lord, I associate nothing with Him. O Allah, I seek refuge with You from its evil, and I ward it off by Your might." Then send blessings upon our master Muhammad and upon his family, and grant them peace.

The phrase "Ḥasbunā Allah" (Allah is sufficient for us) is also among the most excellent fortifications against what one fears. For Maʿrūf — may Allah have mercy on him — said in his aforementioned counsel: "Whoever supplicates with it will find Allah at his side," even if he lacks that sincerity in his remembrance. Likewise, they have mentioned concerning the phrase of returning (istirjāʿ): "The foundation of what the seeker of divine gentleness (luṭf) aims for in afflictions is the istirjāʿ — either by its condition of sincerity, or by its state, for Allah has singled it out for that." They said: "The state of the elite (khāṣṣah) is not to be denied." So if something alarms you — or even if your lamp goes out — say: "Surely we belong to Allah, and to Him we return."

And if you find rage within yourself, say: "O Allah, forgive me my sin, and remove the anger from my heart, and grant me refuge from the accursed Satan." And if you find a pain (wajam), place your right hand upon its spot and say: "In the name of Allah, in the name of Allah, in the name of Allah," and then say: "I seek refuge with the might of Allah and His power from the evil of what I find and what I guard against." Repeat this refuge seven times. And if you are struck by an ill omen (taṭayyur) from something, say: "O Allah, none brings good except You, and none removes evil except You, and there is no might and no power save with Allah." Then return to your regular litany (wird) and remembrance.

It behooves this diligent devotee (mujtahid) not to continue [in prayer] until dawn (saḥar). For the Prophet — peace and blessings be upon him — said: "The most excellent prayer is the prayer of Dāwūd: he would sleep half the night, stand [in prayer] for a third of it, and sleep a sixth of it."

title_en: The Second and Third Liturgical Portions (al-Wird al-Thānī wa al-Thālith) — On Night Vigil, Dawn Prayer, and Morning Remembrances

صفرة الوجه والشهرة؛ فمن قام أكثر الليل ونام سحرًا قل نعاسه؛ وفيه استراحة تعين
على الورد الأول من أوراد النهار؛ قال: ونوم هذا الوقت سبب للمكاشفة؛ قال:
.ونعد النوم من جملة الأوراد إذا روعيت آدابه: فعلى هذا أعد هذا النوم بعد تهجد
اورداء وهو:

# PageV1P217
anchors:
- Root: ن-و-م (n-w-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sleep as a natural state of bodily rest; the cessation of sensory activity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Sleep as a metaphor for spiritual heedlessness (ghaflah) when unrestrained, but as a divinely ordained refreshment when disciplined.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical sleep; metaphorical (majāz) for the soul's receptivity to unveiling (mukāshafah) during the pre-dawn hours.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional clause with intent (niyyah) governing reward — the protasis (sharṭ) is the sincere resolve, the apodosis (jawāb) is the recorded divine recompense.
translation:
I say: Abū Ḥāmid [al-Ghazālī] said: "Sleep is the nourishment of the spirit (rūḥ) just as food is the nourishment of the body; and the sleep of Dāwūd (upon him peace) is recommended." He said: "In sum, sleep in the last part of the night is beloved, for it dispels drowsiness in the morning, reduces the pallor of the face and notoriety. So whoever stands [in prayer] most of the night and sleeps at the pre-dawn hour (saḥar), his drowsiness diminishes; and in it there is a rest that aids the first litany (wird) of the day's litanies." He said: "And sleep at this time is a cause for unveiling (mukāshafah)." He said: "And we count sleep among the litanies (awrād) when its etiquettes are observed." Thus, upon this, I count this sleep after the night vigil (tahajjud) as a litany, and it is:

**The Second Litany (al-Wird al-Thānī):** One should intend to rise at the pre-dawn hour (saḥar) before the break of dawn... that he may have in the night two sleeps and two risings, so that this may be part of the strenuous endurance of the night (mukābadat al-layl). He said in the "Iḥyāʾ": "And this is among the most severe and most virtuous of deeds." He said: "And this is the way of Ibn ʿUmar and the resolute ones (ūlū al-ʿazm) among the Companions and the Followers." One should also intend a prayer or a remembrance (dhikr) that he will mention when he rises before dawn, so that the reward is not lost to him if his eye overcomes him. It is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ, according to what Ibn Mājah mentioned, that the Messenger of Allāh ﷺ said: "Whoever intends to rise and pray, and his eyes overcome him until morning, Allāh writes for him what he intended; and his sleep is a charity (ṣadaqah) for him." And [the intent] is the heart's sincerity and its emptiness from distractions — and this is [the essence of] it.

**The Third Litany (al-Wird al-Thālith):** Allāh, Glorified and Exalted, said: {«وَبِالْأَسْحَارِ هُمْ يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ»} [al-Dhāriyāt: 18] — "And in the pre-dawn hours they would seek forgiveness." And it is the time of saḥar. For if Allāh facilitates the return of his spirit to him at the pre-dawn before dawn, that too is a turning (iqbāl) from the unseen world (ʿālam al-ghayb) to the witnessed world (ʿālam al-shahādah). So he should not turn at the first moment except to his Creator, saying: "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" (There is no god but Allāh), as was mentioned at the beginning of the first litany. The Sayyid al-Sāḥilī said in "Bughyat al-Sālik": "And if one's times are filled with his litanies and his constant devotion (hijrah), then there is no doubt that he should employ all that befits all that issues from him or befalls him of movements, and what resembles that of remembrances and supplications." So he says when donning his garment: "Praise be to Allāh who clothed me with what I cover my nakedness with, and beautifies me among people, without any power or strength from me." And may Allāh bless our master Muḥammad and his family. Then when he rises, he says: "O Allāh, grant me vigor in action, and protect me from stumbling and laziness." And may Allāh bless our master Muḥammad and his family. Then when he wipes the sleep from his eyes and beholds the sky, he says: [The supplication continues as recorded by Mālik in al-Muwaṭṭaʾ, 1/131, no. 94].

# PageV1P218
anchors:
- Root: ط-ه-ر (ṭ-h-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Purity, cleanliness — both physical (from filth) and spiritual (from sin)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ritual purity (ṭahārah) as a prerequisite for prayer; inner purification from moral defilement
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal washing of limbs; metaphorical cleansing of the heart from heedlessness
- Root: خ-ب-ث (kh-b-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Malignity, foulness — applied to male and female evil spirits (al-khubth wa al-khabāʾith)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Spiritual impurity seeking refuge from demonic harm
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal filth vs. metaphorical evil whisperings
- Root: ع-و-ذ (ʿ-w-dh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Seeking protection, clinging to a refuge
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine protection (istiʿādhah) as a station of servitude
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sheltering; metaphorical reliance on God alone
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Protasis (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) — "When you enter... say..." (ʿinda + masdar) governing the apodosis of supplication
translation:
I say — and upon entering the privy: "In the name of God; I seek refuge with God from the male and female unclean spirits." This is from al-Nawawī. And when exiting, he says: "Your forgiveness; and praise be to God who has removed from me harm and granted me well-being." And at the siwak: "O God, purify my mouth from sins and idle speech; and may God bless our master Muḥammad and his family." And when standing upright for ablution, ʿIyāḍ transmitted in his *Madārik* that he recites the saying of God the Exalted: {«O you who believe, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces...»} [al-Māʾidah 5:6] — the verse. End quote. Then he says: "Here I am at Your service, my Lord, and at Your pleasure; all good is in Your hands; and I am with You and unto You; here I am, obeying Your command in washing my limbs and wiping them. O God, purify them from burdens and make them forbidden to the Fire. In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate; praise be to God who made water a purifier."

Al-Sabāʾī — one of the saints of God — Ibn Abī Zayd used to say: "Nothing of what we are in except by his blessing." When he wished to perform ablution, he would recite the saying of God the Exalted: {«O you who believe...»} [al-Māʾidah 5:6] — the verse — then say: "Yes, my Lord," repeating this, and wash his limbs under intense fear and yearning. And at the rinsing of the mouth: "O God, purify my mouth from what does not concern me, and employ me in what pleases You from me." And at the snuffing of water into the nose: "O God, do not deprive me of the fragrance of Your bliss." And at washing the face: "O God, whiten my face on the Day when faces are whitened and faces are blackened." And at washing the hands: "O God, give me my book in my right hand, and do not give it to me in my left." And at wiping the head: "O God, shade me under the shade of Your Throne on the Day when there is no shade but Your shade." And at wiping the ears: "O God, make me among those who listen to the word and follow the best of it." And at washing the feet: "O God, make firm my foot upon the Ṣirāṭ on the Day when feet slip." Then you raise your head to the sky and say: "I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, with no partner; and I bear witness that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger. O God, make me among the repentant and make me among the self-purifying."

And if you are in your night with your regular portion (wird), or you occupy it with what draws your heart — then recite the Qurʾān. Muḥibb al-Dīn said: "Reciting the Qurʾān at the end of the night is better than at its beginning." He said: "Likewise, reciting the Qurʾān between the two evening prayers is beloved." And you continue reciting and remembering until the muezzin calls the adhān — then you lend him your ear, imitating him, and you answer the two *ḥayʿalah*s with two *ḥawqalah*s. And when he says: "Prayer is better than sleep," you say: "You have spoken truly and done well." Then you say: "God is greater, God is greater; there is no god but God; Muḥammad is the Messenger of God. I am well-pleased with God as Lord, with Muḥammad as Messenger, and with Islam as religion. O God, Lord of this perfect call..."

62 سيج فزني شق طن مقع عرس ددن سكن من سير كل القت ليجهد في نم لأراك قاضلة
النامة والصلاة القائمة: آت محمدًا الوسيلة والفضيلة؛ وابعثه مقائا محمودًا الذي
وعدته؛ وارزقني العافية في الدنيا والآخرة» وفي الحديث: لما أقام بلال الصلاة وقال:
امت الصلاة: قال النبي ين "أقامها لله وأدامها”"".
اثم تأخ في الورد الرابع: قال السيد الساحلي في قصيدة السلوك:

اوقسم على وقشين وردك يا فنى

ثم قالة

وخذ نصفه بين العشاءين خاليا وخذ نصفه الباقي على أثر الفجر

قال رسول الله يكك: "من كان يؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر فليكرم ضيفه ”7

قال تاج الدين: والنهار ضيف والليل ضيف» قال سعيد بن المسيب: ما من
اليلة تأني إلا نادت: أنا ليلة جديدة؛ لم آ عليكم فط؛ ولا آني عليكم قط بعد.
فاعملوا في خيرا؛ فإنكم مسؤولون عما تعملون في.

وقال المقري ما نصه: رقيغة: كان ابن شاطر يقول: الجديدان حرسان: أحدهما
أبيض؛ والآخر أسود؛ وكلاهما قد أخذ بمجامعدا إلى القيامة؛ ثم يتلو: ون مهنا
ِلَأئهِ) [غافر: 43].

وعن الفضيل: بلغنا أن لله سبحانه وتعالى يقول: "اين آدم؛ اذكرني بعد الصبح
ساعة وبعد العصر ساعة أكفك ما بينهما".

وفي الترمذي وغيره: أن رسول اله يه قال: "من صلى الفجر في جماعة ثم
قعد يذكر الله حتى تطلع الشمس ثم صلى ركعتين كانت له كأجر حجة وعمرة تام
